Highways should be raised for controlled access. One of the Members raised the issue of 
removing the provision for a 2.1 km spur for linking the city of Samastipur with  Package 3 of

rectify all black spots. He raised the issue of stray cattle on NHs an d suggested that Road

The Committee also highlighted the issue of overloaded trucks damaging the city roads which 
are not upto the construction standards of National Highways. The Committee also noted that 
parking of vehicles during night along the National Highways is causing     a lot of accidents 
throughout the country. The Members discussed the problems of the poor quality of 
construction of roads causing rutting a nd collapse of roads soon after they are constructed, 
gaps in construction, the lack of monitoring of roads under construction, stray cattle and 
animals on the highways causing accidents. The Committee enquired about the feasibility of 
the Ministry issuing  guidelines for State Governments to notify some stretch of land parallel 
to the National Highways as area of non -construction, to be acquired at some future point of 
time for construction of service roads. The Committee also discussed about installation o f 
CCTV cameras at every few kilometers in the construction stage itself for monitoring the 
progress of construction on site and desired to know whether such plans can be included at 
DPR stage itself. A Member also enquired about utilisation of CRIF Fund in  the country and 
the criteria for selection of CRIF works and sought clarifications on some of the provisions 
under it. He pointed out the large number of litigations pending in courts involving 
contractors engaged   in road construction and   desired to kno w about the process of 
appointment of arbitrators. The Committee also sought more information and a presentation

such ducts.

REPORT 
 Tourism is generally regarded as a recent phenomenon but even in ancient times, people 
travelled not only for trade, business and religious purposes, but also to explore new unfamiliar 
places and cultures. Since ancient times, India has enjoyed a thriving trade and bilateral cultural 
relations with other countries via foreign travelers and  voyagers who visited India over the 
centuries in  search of knowledge and wisdom  and Indian traders who served as cultural 
ambassadors abroad and brought home ide as, impressions and customs of the distant lands. The 
Greek historian and diplomat Megasthenes travelled to Pataliputra in 302 BC during the reign of 
Chandragupta Maurya and introduced the world to the richness of Indian culture and customs 
through his boo k Indica, followed by the accounts and observations of other distinguished 
travelers like Fa -Hien, Ibn Battuta, Al -Biruni, Marco Polo and many others. The ancient Indian 
Universities like Nalanda and Vikramashila were the most important centers of cultural  interaction 
attracting large number of students and scholars from all over the world. Education, religion, trade 
and commerce were the dominant factors in tourism growth as they served to highlight India as a 
dream destination for traders and scholars, mystics and pilgrims alike in the ancient world.  
 
2. After independence in 1947,  a large number of Embassies and Missions were set up to 
play a pivotal role in political and economic cooperation, cultural promotion and interaction, trade 
and investment pro motion, press and media liaison, and scientific cooperation in bilateral and 
multilateral contexts and consular services. Overseas Tourism Offices were also set up by the 
Ministry of Tourism as early as in 1950 -60s and their restructuring was also done in 2018-19, 
under which 14 offices were co nsolidated into 8 t o coordinate with the Indian Miss ions and 
Embassies to carry out promotional activities showcasing India as an all year round  Tourist 
Destination. Despite the endeavours to synergize the efforts of the Ministries of External Affairs 
and Tourism, India is yet to realize its full potential as a tourist destination. India stands at 2 3rd 
rank in terms of international  tourist arrivals and 12th in terms of foreign exchange earnings from 
tourism for the year 2019; its percentage share in International Tourist Arrivals is a lowly 1.2 4. A 
country which boasts of one of the seven wonders of the world, 40 UNESCO World Heritage 
Sites, a seemingly inexhaustible number of forts, palaces, historical monuments, c aves and 
sculptures, geographically diverse and blessed with natural beauty and biodiversity, reported less 
International Tourist Arrivals in 2019 as compared to its geographically smaller Asian neighbour, 
Thailand. To realize the immense potential of the Indian tourism industry in building India a five 
trillion dollar economy as envisioned by the government, a “3T” (Trade, Technology and Tourism) 

2 
 
strategy has been implemented for the Indian Missions wherein their functioning would be judged 
by their abilit y to boost trade, tourist inflows and facilitating technology transfer to Indian 
companies. 
 
3. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and 
Culture, in this backdrop, decided to take up the subject „Role of Indian Miss ions Globally for the 
growth of Tourism in India‟ for examination and report thereon. As a sequel to examination of the 
subject, the Committee called for Background Notes and Replies to Questionnaires formulated to 
obtain exhaustive information on the stra tegies employed by the Ministries of Tourism and 
External Affairs for promotion of Indian Tourism in foreign markets . The Committee heard the 
views of the Secretary, Ministry of Tourism and Senior Officers of Ministries of Tourism and 
External Affairs, on the subject, in its meeting held on 31st May, 2022. 
  
4. The representatives of the Ministries of Tourism and External Affairs , through their oral 
and written submissions, highlighted the importance of Tourism as an engine for economic growth 
given its pot ential as a vehicle for job creation, economic growth and development. Globally, 
strong economic growth has generated millions of new travellers looking for exceptional travel 
experiences, be it business or leisure, domestic, regional or international, and  this trend is expected 
to continue with sustained momentum. Before the Covid pandemic, International Tourist Arrivals 
(ITA) in India had been consistently growing since 2003; however, India ranks 2 3rd position in 
Inbound Tourism and 12th rank in terms of Foreign Exchange earnings from tourism in 2019 and is 
yet to realize its full potential for Inbound Tourism. Inbound Tourism  covers all international 
tourist traffic entering a country and is also known as “export tourism” because although touris ts 
enjoy their travel experience within the destination country, they are paying for it using foreign 
currency.

7. The Committee observes that in concordance with UNWTO, International Tourist 
Arrivals (ITA) include both Foreign Tourist Arrivals (FTA) and NRIs and from 2014 
onwards the Ministry of Tourism has started to compile the arrivals of NRIs on annual basis.  
Proper segregation of data regarding number of NRIs visiting India to meet their families 
and the actual number of foreign tourists coming for tourism purposes needs to be separately 
maintained as this data will help in the  formation of tourism policies. Since NRIs constitute a 
significant share of IT As, there has been a rise in ITAs since 2014, perhaps contributing to 
the rise of India to the 2 3rd rank in ITAs though still below even small countries like 

4 
 
Thailand, Austria and Poland The growth of FTAs however has been much slower taking a 
decade to double from 5.78 million in 2010  to 10.93 millions in 2019.   Other developing 
nations like Thailand r eported high er international tourism receipts. The Committee 
recommends that the promotional tactics of Thailand to utilize diplomacy and tourism 
promotion to attract foreign tourists despite their small population and geographical area as 
compared to Indi a may be assessed, and may be applied  in the Indian tourism sector, if 
found beneficial for the growth of Inbound Tourism in India. 
 
8. The Committee notes that there is no dearth of scenic places in India which are at par 
or even better than international locales but the latter  draw more international f ootfalls.  
Kashmir for example has similar weather and terrain as Switzerland but the l atter is more 
famous and draws more international tourists.  Similarly, Goa, Kochi, Kumarakom have 
beautiful beaches at par with international beaches.  The Committee is of the opinion that 
the Ministry should adopt a proactive policy to promote internationally such tourist places in 
India at par with those abroad.    
 
ROLE OF MINISTRY OF TOURISM 
9. The Secretary, Ministry of Tourism,  briefed the Committee that the Government launched 
„Incredible India‟ campaign to tap into the vast tourism potential of the country in an organized 
manner. The campaign highlighted various facets of Indian culture and history such as yoga, 
spirituality, festivals and monuments. The Incredible India campaign is one of the most successful 
campaigns that placed India on the world tourism map. Now the Ministry of Tourism has launched 
Incredible India Reconnect 2022  Campaign to position India as a preferred to urism destination in 
tourism generating markets.  However, Inbound Tourism  strategy should not be confined to  
campaigns and therefore Government of India has adopted a holistic appro ach to promote Inbound 
Tourism. Indian Missions and India Overseas Offices will execute a strategized, targeted approach 
tailored to each host country to promote Inbound Tourism to India. In order to forge partnership 
with Indian Missions for Inbound Tourism  and ensure effective implementation, the MoT in 
consultation with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), 
Ministry of Civil Aviation (Ministry of Civil Aviation) and Ministry of Commerce (MoC) has 
formulated a detailed stra tegy document covering the vision and objectives, key strategic areas, 
key operational areas and governance of the institutional arrangement  for promoting Inbound 
Tourism to India. The key objectives of the Strategy are:  

5 
 
(i) Position India as the most favoured tourist destination  
(ii) Create right perception about India as a tourism destination  
(iii) Promote India as a 365 days destination  
(iv) Promote specific themes, destinations and products of Indian Tourism  
(v) Strengthen India‟s role in various multilateral and bilateral forums on Tourism 
 
10. A Programme Implementation Committee under the Chairmanship of the Additional 
Secretary (Tourism) was set up to take forward the project. Two meetings have taken place so far. 
Steering Committee under the Chairmanship of Secretary, Tourism will look after overall direction 
and guidance for the program. 
 
11. KEY FEATURES OF TOURISM STRATEGY  
 
a) COUNTRY- SPECIFIC STRATEGIC PLANS  
 The Ministry of Tourism in consultation with Ministry of External Affairs and other 
relevant Ministries and Industry Stakeholders will identify the top source markets including 
established as well as emerging markets. In addition, focus areas such as Buddh ist Markets will be 
identified.  The Ministry of Tourism will accordingly prepare country specific multi -year strategic 
plans for marketing in these Key Markets on the basis of the needs, requirements and preferences 
of travelers.  Apart from generic measu res applicable to all the markets, the plans may also have 
targets for specific markets.  
 
b)  MEGA FAMILIARIZATION TOURS 
 Mega familiarization tours for specific countries covering specific tourism offerings such 
as Culture and Heritage, Yoga and Wellness, Medical Value travel, Adventure Tourism. 
 
c)  INTERNATIONAL ROADSHOWS  
 Plans for International roadshows in consultation with Indian Missions and Industry 
Stakeholders for various markets, which will showcase the relevant Indian Tourism products and 
offerings.  
  
(d) CONNECT WITH INDIAN DIASPORA  
 Missions will leverage their connect with Indian Diaspora to motivate them to travel to 

6 
 
various Indian Destinations. The Mission will also strategize how the diaspora can be leveraged to 
promote Indian tourism in their host countries.  
 
 (e)  ANNUAL EVENTS TO BE HOSTED BY INDIA  
 Plans for important events for promotion of Inbound Tourism  shall be prepared in 
consultation with Indian Missions and Industry Stakeholders. Some of the key events are 
International Buddhist Conclave, India Tourism Mart, Yoga Day etc.  
 
(f) ANNUAL INTERNATIONAL EVENTS WHERE INDIA PARTICIPATES  
 Plans for important international tra vel marts such as WTM, ITB etc which help in 
promoting Inbound Tourism shall be prepared in consultation with Indian Missions and Industry 
Stakeholders.  
 
(g) SPECIFIC STRATEGY FOR MEDICAL AND WELLNESS TOURISM 
 Medical tourism, especially wellness tourism and AYUSH may be promoted to position 
India as a health and wellness destination.   
 
(h) SPECIFIC STRATEGY FOR MICE TOURISM 
 MICE Tourism (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, Exhibitions) constitute an important 
element of tourism and has a multiplier effect on the economy. A specific strategy to promote 
India‟s MICE offerings and winning bids for international events need to be planned.  Support 
from the Indian Missions will be crucial for winning the bids for hosting the events in India.  
 
11.1 The Committee appreciates that the tourism strategy has country specific strategic 
plans and targets specific markets . Different countri es have different social, economic and 
political situations and   country specific strategic plans would help to appeal to the general 
consciousness and expectations of the people of different countries. The Committee notes that 
the general assessment of the earlier tourism promotional campaigns of India  was that  
though impressive, they lacked focus on products and themes and failed to convey a clear cut 
message about India and that not much publicity w as given to the new and urban India, its  
new deve lopments and luxury properties. The Committee is pleased to note that the new 
strategic approach addresses these shortcomings and is tailored to suit specific markets.  
 

7 
 
11.2 The Committee notes that various tourism circuits such as „Buddhist Circuit,‟ 
„Ramayana Circuit‟ can provide tourists with enriching religious experiences. The 
Committee also observes that in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic, the importance of 
shorter distances in travel has become more pronounced and regional tourism is likely to 
grow. India should therefore leverage its cultural similarities such as the Buddha‟s trail with 
its neighbhours. The Committee recommends t hat necessary steps be taken to revive circuit 
tourism by organizing FAM trips and Buddhist Circuit Family Tours and Conferences with 
the help of Indian Overseas Tourism Offices and Missions to boost tourism in country.   
 
11.3 The Committee appreciates that strategic promotion of MICE tourism has been given 
importance. The Committee notes that there is a surge in business travel to India and 
promotion of MICE tourism would capitalize on the blossoming image of India as a n 
important MICE destination. India already has many cities which have good infrastructure 
for hosting conferences or are in the process of developing the same.  What is required is the 
connectivity between the cities to enable the growth of MICE tourism in India.  
 
11.4 India is a hub of holistic streams of medicine such as Ayurveda, Homeopathy, 
Naturopathy and the birthplace of Yoga.  Yoga has caught the world‟s imagination with 21 
June being declared as Yoga Day. Yoga and wellness retreats are now in great demand in the 
aftermath of the pandemic.  India has huge wellness tourism potential and the Committee 
appreciates its inclusion in the tourism strategy. India receives most of its medical tourists 
from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Oman, Bangladesh, Maldives, Nigeria, Kenya and Iraq. There is 
a huge potential for India to realize and aggressively advance towards attracting medical 
tourists from other parts of the world, including Europe and America. 
 
(i) FACILITATING VISA 
 Ministry of Home Affairs is developing e -VISA mobile application, which can be 
expedited.  
(j)  FACILITATING DIRECT CONNECTIVITY 
 South East Asia, Eastern Europe and South America have huge potential for increasing 
foreign tourist arrivals to India.  Therefore, it is important to introduce direct flight connectivity 
from these markets which have the potential to contribu te to tourist  traffic to India.  MoCA may 
look into initiating direct flights between India and countries that are witnessing a rise in the 

8 
 
number of outbound international tourists. 
 
11.5 The Committee observes that South Asia is home to many tourism based economies 
such as Nepal, Maldives, Bhutan and tourists also use India as transit to other places in the 
South Asian region and South Asian nations are often markete d as a part of a package tour 
and therefore connectivity between India and its South Asian neighbours i s of utmost 
importance for Indian tourism sector.

1) Creating database for the respective country of travel agencies, tour operators, independent travel 
planners, MICE agencies, travel &  consumer Media and other relevant stakeholders in the travel 
industry.   
2) Monitor relevant tourism trends and opportunities and prepare quarterly market reports that 
can be shared with Ministry of Tourism and the private sector stakeholders  
 
 (l) PUBLIC RELATIONS AND COMMUNICATIONS 
 The Missions and India Tourism Overseas Offices need to undertake the following 
public relations and communication activities relevant to tourism promotion:-  
(i) To track and report articles related to India in the local media 
(ii) To ensure placement of positive news stories in trade and consumer media 
(iii) To ensure placement of official press releases from MoT 
(iv) Image building and to counteract negativity publicity as and when required 
(v) Active presence on Social Media 
 
(m) RELATIONSHIPS AND OUTREACH  
The Missions and India Tourism Overseas Offices  may build relationships with various 
stakeholders to create awareness about India tourism products, engage with museums, universities, 
trade organizations, local clubs, bring annu al conferences of travel and hospitality associations in 
the identified markets to India , identify eminent opinion makers, celebrities, TV teams, tour

advise in the selection of travel shows for participation.

(n) INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION AND ENGAGEMENT WITH 
 MULTILATERAL/BILATERAL FORUMS 
 Active engagement in multilateral forums like UNWTO, G -20, ASEAN, BRICS, IBSA, 
SAARC need to be pursued. Partnerships may be explored with SAARC and ASEAN countries to 
develop and promote common packages on themes that link the countries such as the Buddhist 
circuit, Ramayana circuit, Himalayan circuit, Heritage circuit that would yield excellent dividends 
to all participating nations.  
 
11.6 Apart from geographical proximity, the historical and cultural linkages between India 
and its South Asian neighbours offer great potential for d evelopment of regional tourism.  
The Committee is of the opinion that c ooperation with other South Asian countries on joint 
tourism and advertising campaigns and steps to facilitate seamless travel of tourists between 
India and its neighbourhood would promote Inbound Tourism in India 
 
(o) FACILITATE FDI INTO TOURISM SECTOR  
Government of India has allowed 100% FDI in hospitality sector. India is developing various 
destinations and actively promoting investment from Private sector includi ng Public Private 
Partnerships. The Missions can engage with the trade/ industry to promote  and encourage 
investment in tourism and hospitality sector in India.  
 
(p) GOVERNANCE AND MONITORING 
The Ministry of Tourism will set up a digital platform to bring visibility to all the stakeholders 
about the activities to promote Inbound Tourism . It will have a dashboard on trends and track 
performance of Inbound Tourism  from various countries .  The Ministry will organize quarterly 
meetings with relevant Ministries, participating States and Industry Stakeholders to review the 
progress on various initiatives and activities.   
Ministry of Tourism will designate a nodal agency for implementation of the program. There will 
be a Steering Committee and program implementation committee for overall direction, guidance,

11.9 The Committee notes that the Incredible India Campaign was the first campaign to 
promote India uniformly as a destination offering a wide range of experiences and was 
hugely successful but marketing Campaigns are only part of the challenge.  Tourism requires 
easy visa clearances, hotels, flight, train and road connectivity and above all the promise of a 
safe, secure and convenient travel. In order to build a successful brand, all aspects of tourism 
infrastructure and services and supply -demand gaps must be given utmost importance and 
this can be achieved only by coordinated efforts of all the stakeholders. The Committee 
appreciates the holistic and targeted approach of the Government for promotion of Inbound 
Tourism and recommends that systematic monitoring of the coordinated efforts of all the 
stakeholders may be done by the Programme Implementation Committee

FILM TOURISM   
14. Upon query by the Committee, the Secretary informed that the Ministry of Tourism has 
issued guidelines dated 25.07.2012 for extending financial support to State Governments/ Union 
Territory Administrations, for promotion of „Film Tourism‟.   Financial assistance is provided up 
to Rs.2.00 Lakh per film for compone nts such as Space Hiring/Filming charges, Facilitation Fee 
etc.  
 
15. Government of India (Ministry of Information and Broadcasting), has launched scheme 
relating to incentives to foreign film producers for shooting in Indian locales . Under the scheme, 
international film production companies can claim a reimbursement of up to 30% on Qualifying 
Expenditure in India subject to a maximum of INR 2 crore. Foreign films shooting in India can 
claim an additional 5% bonus up to a maximum of INR 50 lakhs (USD 65,000 ) as additional 
reimbursement would be granted for employing 15% or more manpower in India.  
 
16. The Committee notes that countries offer various types of incentives to encourage film 
producers to use beau tiful locations to shoot films.  Most countries offer tax sops in the form 
of VAT refunds ranging from 10 -20% depending on the location and the budget of the film.  

12 
 
Sometimes the governments even bear some cost of the production as films act  as 
advertisements for the country and huge ben efits are accrued. The Spain Tourism Board 
partnered with the Bollywood film “Zindagi Na Mile gi Dobara” for promotions and got a 
huge influx of tourists that year.  The incentives offered by the Indian government appear to 
be meager compared to the interna tional norm s and the considerable payoffs. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism may review the incentives provided to 
foreign film producers as per internationally competitive rates.  
 
OVERSEAS INDIA TOURISM OFFICES UNDER MINISTRY OF TOURISM  
17. The Ministry of Tourism (MoT) has restructured its overseas offices by consolidating 14 
offices into 8 offices, currently located in Beijing, Dubai, Frankfurt, London, New York, 
Singapore, Tokyo, and Moscow (currently in the process of identifying a location for 
establishment). The overseas offices help the Ministry to connect with foreign operators, provide 
human interface and ensure that the Incredible India brand penetrates deep in the source markets.  
The purpose behind consolidating the 14 overseas India To urism Offices into 8 offices is carrying 
out effective/focused promotional activities and to reduce the financial implication in handling 
these overseas offices. The eight Overseas Tourist offices also look after count ries other than the 
one they are stationed in.

fairs/exhibitions, organizing „Incredible  India‟ Road shows and „Know India Seminars,‟ Joint 
Promotion & Joint Advertising, etc.  
 Enhancing visibility: Undertaking advertising campaigns in the Print, TV, Radio, 
Online/digital including social media and outdoor media. 
 Facilitation: Extending brochure support to foreign tour operators, promotional events with 
Indian Missions, production and distribution of publicity material in local languages.

32. The MEA acts as an effective coordinating point for smooth implementation of visa related 
policies between the MHA and Missions/Posts abroad while Missions/Posts abroad act as 
implementing agencies.  
33. Indian visas are primarily issued under (i) Regu lar/Paper Visa Scheme by Indian 
Missions/Posts abroad; (ii) e -Visa Scheme by Bureau of Immigration and (iii) Visa -on-Arrival 
Scheme by Bureau of Immigration. Under Regular Visa Scheme  Visa Sticker of appropriate 
category and duration is pasted on the passport of an applicant.  The Indian Missions/Posts process 
visa application, as per the MHA‟s guidelines, for 19 categories of visas. The e -Visa scheme has 
been expanded from e -Tourist visas to include new categories viz  e-Business visa, e -Medical 
visa, e-Conference and e -Medical Attendant. Nationals of 171 countries were eligible to avail e -
Visa scheme prior to its suspension in March 2020 (due to onset of Covid-19 pandemic).  
 
34. However, post Covid -19 pandemic e -Visa Scheme has been fully restored, in graded 
manner, for nationals of 156 countries. The Visa-on-Arrival scheme is available to select eligible 
nationals of three countries (i.e. Japan, RoK and UAE) visiting for the purp ose of business, 
tourism, conference and medical.   The process involved filling up of an application form which is 
required to be submitted at the Visa -on-Arrival desk on arrival along with Disembarkation Card.  
After due verifications and payment of applicable fee, the passport of these nationals are stamped 
with Visa-on-Arrival stamp with 60 days/double entry facility by the immigration officer.

abroad or to the Outsourcing Age ncy (where Visa services are outsourced).    The applicant is also

a Pilot project w.e.f. 26 January, 2022 for 24 Missions/Posts abroad facilitating applicants  to

ETA (Electronic Travel Authorisation) through registered email to facilitate their travel  into India.

scheme to nationals of eligible countries. The e -visa service, including e -Tourist Visa, under the 
scheme is being rendered in time -bound manner and decision is communicated to applicant via e -
mail within 72 hours of making online application. Initially the scheme was open for e -Tourist

extending the facilities t o nationals of other countries.  Now, 28 Indian airports an d 5 Indian Ports

avail e-Visa scheme prior to its suspension in March 2020 (due to onset of Covid -19 pandemic). 
However, in the post Covid -19 pandemic e -Visa S cheme has been fully restored, in graded 
manner, for nationals 156 countries only.  e-Visas issued under e -Visa scheme are of Single, 
Double, Triple and Multiple entry/entries facilities.

68. The Committee observes that many of the tourist spots and places of religious 
importance are located near the National Highways yet the state of the last mile connectivity 
from the National Highways to the tourist spot leaves much to be desired. The Committee 
feels that good quality last mile connectivity is important to ensure a positive experience for 
tourists visiting a tourist destination in the country, which in turn, helps attract more tourists 
through word-of-mouth publicity.  The Committee therefore recommends that Ministry ma y 
examine the state/quality of last mile connectivity roads at all such tourist spots near the 
National Highways at the earliest and ensure their construction and maintenance with the 
concerned Ministries/agencies to make the tourist places more accessible  to tourists, both 
domestic and international, which will invariably increase the number of tourists visiting 
such places.

policymaking, high percentage of women are employed in the global tourism industry as 
compared to other sectors, i.e. women make up over 54% of the labour force in the tourism

industry. Women have mo re opportunities for advancement and assuming roles once 
dominated by men such as tour guides. However, Indian tourism industry still lags behind 
with only 12.1 percent share of female employment. The Committee desires to be apprised of 
the coordinating mechanisms formulated by the MoT to generate employment opportunities 
for women in Indian tourism industry.

RECOMMENDATIONS/ OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
 
 The Committee observes that in concordance with UNWTO, International Tourist 
Arrivals (ITA) include both Foreign Tourist Arrivals (FTA) and NRIs and from 2014 
onwards the Ministry of Tourism has started to compile the arrivals of NRIs on annual basis.  
Proper segregation of data regarding number of NRIs visiting India to meet their families 
and the actual number of foreign tourists coming for tourism purposes needs to be separately 
maintained as this data will help in the formation of tourism policies. Since NRIs constitute a 
significant share of ITAs, there has been a rise in ITAs since 2014, perhaps contributing to 
the rise of India to the 23 rd rank in ITAs though still below even small countries like 
Thailand, Austria and Poland The growth o f FTAs however has been much slower taking a 
decade to double from 5.78 million in 2010 to 10.93 millions in 2019.  Other developing 
nations like Thailand reported higher international tourism receipts. The Committee 
recommends that the promotional tactics  of Thailand to utilize diplomacy and tourism 
promotion to attract foreign tourists despite their small population and geographical area as 
compared to India may be assessed, and may be applied  in the Indian tourism sector, if 
found beneficial for the growth of Inbound Tourism in India. 
(Para 7) 
*India Tourism Statistics 2019: 
The Committee notes that there is no dearth of scenic places in India which are at 
par or even better than international locales but the latter draw more international footfalls.  
Kashmir for example has similar weather and terrain as Switzerland but the l atter is more 
famous and draws more international tourists.  Similarly, Goa, Kochi, Kumarakom have 
beautiful beaches at par with international beaches.  The Committee is of the opinion that 
the Ministry should adopt a proactive policy to promote internationally such tourist places in 
India at par with those abroad.    
(Para 8) 
ROLE OF MINISTRY OF TOURISM  
The Committee appreciates that the tourism strategy has country specific strategic 
plans and targets specific markets. Different countries have different social, economic and 
political situations and   country specific strategic plans would help to appeal to the general 
consciousness and expectations of the people of different countries. The Committee notes that 
the general assessment of the earlier tourism  promotional campaigns of India was that 

33 
 
though impressive, they lacked focus on products and themes and failed to convey a clear cut 
message about India and that not much publicity was given to the new and urban India, its 
new developments and luxury prop erties. The Committee is pleased to note that the new 
strategic approach addresses these shortcomings and is tailored to suit specific markets.  
(Para 11.1) 
The Committee notes that various tourism circuits such as „Buddhist Circuit,‟ 
„Ramayana Circuit‟ ca n provide tourists with enriching religious experiences. The 
Committee also observes that in the aftermath of the COVID pandemic, the importance of 
shorter distances in travel has become more pronounced and regional tourism is likely to 
grow. India should therefore leverage its cultural similarities such as the Buddha‟s trail with 
its neighbhours. The Committee recommends that necessary steps be taken to revive circuit 
tourism by organizing FAM trips and Buddhist Circuit Family Tours and Conferences with 
the help of Indian Overseas Tourism Offices and Missions to boost tourism in country.   
(Para 11.2) 
The Committee appreciates that strategic promotion of MICE tourism has been given 
importance. The Committee notes that there is a surge in business travel to India and 
promotion of MICE tourism would capitalize on the blossoming image of India as an 
important MICE destination. India already has many cities which have good infrastructure 
for hosting conferences or are in the process of developing the same.  What  is required is the 
connectivity between the cities to enable the growth of MICE tourism in India.  
(Para 11.2) 
India is a hub of holistic streams of medicine such as Ayurveda, Homeopathy, 
Naturopathy and the birthplace of Yoga. Yoga has caught the world‟s  imagination with 21 
June being declared as Yoga Day. Yoga and wellness retreats are now in great demand in the 
aftermath of the pandemic.  India has huge wellness tourism potential and the Committee 
appreciates its inclusion in the tourism strategy. India  receives most of its medical tourists 
from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Oman, Bangladesh, Maldives, Nigeria, Kenya and Iraq. There is 
a huge potential for India to realize and aggressively advance towards attracting medical 
tourists from other parts of the world, including Europe and America. 
(Para 11.4) 
The Committee observes that South Asia is home to many tourism based economies 
such as Nepal, Maldives, Bhutan and tourists also use India as transit to other places in the 
South Asian region and South Asian nat ions are often marketed as a part of a package tour 

34 
 
and therefore connectivity between India and its South Asian neighbours is of utmost 
importance for Indian tourism sector. 
(Para 11.5) 
Apart from geographical proximity, the historical and cultural linkag es between 
India and its South Asian neighbours offer great potential for development of regional 
tourism. The Committee is of the opinion that cooperation with other South Asian countries 
on joint tourism and advertising campaigns and steps to facilitate seamless travel of tourists 
between India and its neighbourhood would promote Inbound Tourism in India. 
(Para 11.6) 
The Committee notes that the Incredible India Campaign was the first campaign to 
promote India uniformly as a destination offering a wide range of experiences and was 
hugely successful but marketing Campaigns are only part of the challenge.  Tourism requires 
easy visa clearances, hotels, flight, train and road connectivity and above all the promise of a 
safe, secure and convenient travel. In order to build a successful brand, all aspects of tourism 
infrastructure and services and supply -demand gaps must be given utmost importance and 
this can be achieved only by coordinated efforts of all the stakeholders. The Committee 
appreciates the holistic and targeted approach of the Government for promotion of Inbound 
Tourism and recommends that systematic monitoring of the coordinated efforts of all the 
stakeholders may be done by the Programme Implementation Committee 
(Para 11.9) 
FILM TOURISM 
The Comm ittee notes that countries offer various types of incentives to encourage film 
producers to use beautiful locations to shoot films. Most countries offer tax sops in the form 
of VAT refunds ranging from 10 -20% depending on the location and the budget of the  film.  
Sometimes the governments even bear some cost of the production as films act as 
advertisements for the country and huge benefits are accrued. The Spain Tourism Board 
partnered with the Bollywood film “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara” for promotions and go t a 
huge influx of tourists that year.  The incentives offered by the Indian government appear to 
be meager compared to the international norms and the considerable payoffs. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Tourism may review the incentives pr ovided to 
foreign film producers as per internationally competitive rates. 
(Para 16)

OVERSEAS INDIA TOURISM OFFICES UNDER MINISTRY OF TOURISM  
The Committee notes that out of the 31 posts in the Overseas Tourism Offices, only 7 
have been filled while 24 l ie vacant. More than 12 vacancies have been vacant for more than 
5 years. There are 6 vacancies in the local staff strength of 19 also. The Committee is 
dismayed to note that three fourths of the posts in the Overseas Tourism Offices are vacant, 
many of th em for years altogether despite the fact that these offices were established 
specifically for the purpose of promotion of tourism and incur huge expenditure. The 
Committee notes that most Offices are manned by a single person and fails to see how the 
Overseas Tourism Offices could have functioned effectively with a bare minimum staff in 
position. The Committee desires to be apprised of the reason for such delay in filling these 
vacancies and bottlenecks faced in this regard and recommends that necessary steps be taken 
to fill the positions lying vacant for more than 5 years. 
(Para 22) 
The Committee also observes that as per relevant surveys, not many travellers to 
India were aware of the existence of an India Tourism Office in their country and even less 
felt that the information and guidance provided by the Office was adequate.  The Committee 
has been informed that the Indian employees appointed to the Overseas India Tourism 
offices were not required to be proficient in the local language which the Committee  feels is 
an oversight.  The first point of contact for a potential tourist is often the Overseas India 
Tourism office and it is essential that the employees of the Tourism office should be able to 
give their guidance in the local language.  The brochures and website of India tourism should 
also be available in the local language. The Ministry has informed that the Incredible India 
website is presently available in 8 different foreign languages apart from English and Hindi 
and after revamp it would be avail able in 20 + vernacular and foreign languages.  The 
Committee urges that the brochures and website may be made available in as many 
languages as possible as language plays a crucial role in global industries like tourism. It is 
essential that potential tou rists are given clear information in the language that they are 
familiar with to give them the confidence to visit countries where they may encounter 
language barriers.   
 (Para 23)

in terms of tourism promotion and can provide professional and impartial service at all times

is equally important.  The Committee observes that the Overseas Tourist Offices do not seem 
to have a Visa help desk for information and guidance of both tourists and agents.  Visa rules 
change from time to time and it is essent ial that the agents and tourists are kept updated of 
the same. In many countries, the visa issuance has been outsourced and tourists have to be 
informed clearly about any extra handling charges apart from the normal visa fees.  The

the responsibility of tourism promotions have now been consolidated to only 8 offices, the 
mandate of promotion of Indian tourism abroad is now effectively with the Indian Missions. 
The Committee has been informed that Tourism O fficers, who are either IFS/MEA 
personnel have been designated in 20 Missions who will be responsible for the holistic 
promotion of India as a tourist destination, creating country specific strategies among others.

1  
REPORT 
 
 
India has a significant maritime sector with 12 Major and over 200 Non -Major Ports 
situated along its 7500 km long coastline and a vast network of navigable waterways. Maritime 
Trade which is an important component of the maritime sector, influences the pace, structure and 
pattern of development of the country. Ports play a critical role in development of the maritime 
sector of the nation  and the region as well as a huge volume of cargo containing industrial, 
domestic commodities is traded between India and foreign countries through ports. By linking 
maritime trade with inland transportation such as rail -road-air effectively, ports serve as a main 
mode in supply chain transportati on, connectivity of national and international traffic and 
economic growth of the nation. The country ’s maritime sector plays a crucial role in its overall 
trade and growth, with 95% of the country ’s trade volume and 65% of the trade value being 
undertaken through maritime transport. 
 
2. Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPS&W) has been entrusted with the 
responsibility to formulate policies and programmes on aforesaid subjects and their 
implementation. The Ministry looks after shipping and waterways  sectors which include Major 
Ports, National Waterways, Inland Water Transport, Shipbuilding and Ship -repair etc. As ports 
play a vital role in the EXIM trade of the country, the focus of the government continues to be on 
the capacity augmentation of the p orts, so that they are able to meet ever increasing trade 
requirements of the country. The total installed capacity of the Major and Non -Major ports 
during 2020-21 was 2554.61 MTPA (1560.61 MTPA Major Ports & 994.00 MTPA non -Major 
Ports). This has been possible on account of various infrastructure projects undertaken at various 
ports for construction of new berths and terminals, mechanization of existing berths and 
terminals, capital dredging for deepening of drafts for attracting large vessels in port chan nels 
etc. 
 
3. The Ministry also informed the Committee that to be globally competitive, the Indian 
Ports have made progress in mechanization and adoption of technology to improve productivity 
and establish ancillary services within port premises to improve ca rgo evacuation time. With an 
aim to achieve approximately 5% share in world exports, India ’s exports need to grow 
aggressively in next 5 to 10 years. It is also imperative for Indian Ports to strengthen maritime 
capabilities in view of the increase in port  connectivity to handle heavier cargo volumes and 
bigger size of container vessels, in near future. Besides maritime trade, another aspect which has 
enormous potential to develop and is closely  related to port development and connectivity, is 


2  
cruise touris m, which can increase the number of tourists, both in international and domestic 
circuits. Cruise shipping can benefit the economy of the country  and can also generate 
employment. For cruise shipping to develop, tourist terminal facilities and connectivity of ports 
to the places of tourist interest is crucial. To give focus on cruise tourism, a Task Force has been 
constituted in the year 2015 with the coordinated efforts of Ministry of Ports, Shipping & 
Waterways (MoPS&W) and Tourism. 
 
4. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and  
Culture, in this backdrop, decided to take up the subject “ Connectivity and Tourist Terminal 
Facilities at Ports” for examination and report thereon. The Committee heard the views of the 
Senior Officers of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways, Chairmen of various Ports and 
Chairman, Railway Board, in its meeting held on 18 th May, 2022 as well as in visits undertaken 
by the Committee. The Committee also heard the views of the Senior Officers  of Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping & Waterways and the Ministry of Tourism, in its meeting held on the 1 st June, 
2022. 
 
5. The Committee is aware that ports have been centers of commerce for centuries 
and they remain crucial to the economy even today. Every year, hundreds of billions of 
rupees worth of products move through ports. Ports generate substantial business activity 
through their operations. The Committee notes that n ation’s major ports are an important 
part of our  national economy and transportation system. Over 95% of India’s trading by 
volume and 65% by value is done through maritime transport. In addition to their impact 
on the national economy, ports also have an impact on local and regional economies of the 
states on which the ports are situated. The Committee is also of the opinion that a 
substantial portion of business activity in a variety of industries is driven by international 
trade, and the value of foreign  trade has risen substantially over the years. Although trade 
volumes are affected by global economic conditions and have decreased slightly over the 
past few years due to COVID pandemic, trade volumes are expected to rise in the future, 
increasing the imp ortance of ports and waterways in terms of export and import. The 
Committee recommends that at this crucial juncture of expected increase in global 
maritime trade, appropriate policy measures may be taken to increase maritime trade 
through port connectivity to boost the economy of the country. 
 
6. The Committee observes that with the increase in port capacity to handle heavier 
cargo volumes and bigger size of container vessels in near future, there will be a need for 
development of modern terminal development,  which will also challenge the ability of 


3  
terminals to handle increasing cargo volumes. The Committee recommends that 
appropriate guidelines and coordination mechanisms may be formulated to facilitate the 
development of modern terminals to handle increased  cargo volumes and bigger container 
vessels in near future which will decrease the challenges of terminal operators as well. 
 
SAGARMALA PROGRAMME 
 
7. Sagarmala is a National Programme aimed at accelerating economic development in the 
country by harnessing the potential of India ’s 7,500 km long coastline and 14,500 km of 
potentially navigable waterways. Sag armala was announced by the Hon’ ble Prime Minister in 
2014. The concept of Sagarmala was ap proved by the Union Cabinet on 25th March 2015. The 
vision of Sagarmala is to reduce logistics cost for both domestic and EXIM cargo with minimal 
infrastructure investment. Studies under Sagarmala have identified opportunities for reducing 
overall logistics costs, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the economy and increasing 
competitiveness of exports. 
 
8. Currently, there are 802 projects worth investment of ₹ 5.48 lakh crore s for 
implementation under the “Sagarmala Programme”  by 2035. Out of which, 201 projects worth ₹ 
99,281 crores have been completed and 216 projects worth ₹ 2.12 lakh crores are under 
implementation. Further, 384 projects worth ₹ 2.3 Lakh crore are under various stages of 
development. In addition to this, 73 5 projects with estimated investment of ₹ 1 lakh crore have 
been identified for carrying out holistic development of coastal districts. The Table below 
provides a breakup of the projects on the basis of their present status:

(HPRCL), ₹ 10 crore for developing  and operating Chabahar Port in Iran after taking over 
from India Ports Global Limited (IPGL) in 2018-19, ₹ 50 crore in SPV formed with NHAI for

10. The Committee notes that SDCL was incorporated on 31st August, 2016 for 
implementation of Sagarmala and currently out of 802 projects, 202 projects have been 
completed, 216 projects are under implementation, while 384 are under various stages of 
development. Hence, only about 25% of the total projects under Sagarmala are complete as 
on date. The Committee expresses serious concern at the slow progress of work and 
recommends that Sagarmala, being a crucial step in the progress of India’s shipping sector, 
which seeks to bring about port connectivity needs to be expedited. The Committee also 
desires to know whether there has been cost escalation and time overrun as compared to 
original cost and timeline of the projects. The Committee while underlining  the speedy 
implementation of the Sagarmala projects, also desires to know the precise reasons for 
delays, port-wise and concrete steps taken to address the delays. 
 
 
MARITIME STATES DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE (MSDC) 
 
11. Maritime States Development Committee (MSDC) is an apex advisory body for the 
development of the maritime sector and aims to ensure integrated development of Major and 
non-Major Ports. The MSDC was constituted in May, 1997 to assess in consultation with State 
Governments, the future developmen t of existing and new Minor Ports by the respective 
Maritime States either directly or through captive users and private participation. Further, MSDC 
also monitors the development of minor ports, captive ports and private ports in the Maritime 
States with a view to ensure their integrated development with Major Ports and to assess the 
requirements of other infrastructure requirements like roads/rail/IWT and make suitable 
recommendations to the concerned Ministers.

PORT CONNECTIVITY AND INFRASTRUCTURE 
 
13. Connectivity is one of the critical enablers for ports as it is the end -to-end effectiveness 
of the logistics  system that drives competitiveness for industry. Port connectivity challenges 
exist in India and even new ports that have world class equipment can see their turnaround times 
hamstrung because of poor connectivity. 
 
14. The Committee was also informed that this poor conne ctivity constrains India’s trade 
competitiveness and increases industrial production costs. India's hinterland connectivity is 
mainly based on road and rail networks. Railways are the mainstay for carrying long lead 
distance and bulk cargo. But the expansi on of rail network has not been able to keep up with the 
growing demand. Hence, the implementation of road and rail connectivity projects attains 
importance for enhancing the country's overall freight efficiency. 
 
15. The “Sagarmala Programme,”  which is the ke y initiative by MoPS&W has identified 
connectivity between ports and domestic production and consumption centers, through rail, road, 
pipeline, MMLP under the pillar of port connectivity.

19. The Committee notes that the Government has taken up large number of projects 
to remove the bottlenecks in road and rail connectivity to ports. The Committee has no 
doubt that once the  projects are implemented, the connectivit y problems may be resolved 
to a great extent. However, despite  the enormous importance of the  connectivity of ports, 
the Committee feels that the pace of work under the Port, Rail and Road connectivity 


7  
Projects have been slow. The Committee is of the opini on that more coordinated efforts are 
required to complete the connectivity projects by involving Railway Authorities/NHAI etc., 
addressing all technical aspects. The Committee emphasizes that interconnectivity of roads, 
ports, airports, railways, waterways  etc. should be part of the infrastructure planning 
process, right from inception stage. The Committee is also of opinion that approach to a 
port from  hinterland can be critical enough to make  or mar  a Terminal, because  it 
determines the  turn round time an d evacuation time -vital to  the functioning of the port. 
Evacuation is a vital component of any port project as the capacity and efficiency of the 
port vitally depend on the rate at which the cargo can be evacuated from  the terminal. The 
efficiency, viability and business depend on how well connected the port is.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the plans for the connectivity of a port to the roads 
and railway networks, to airports, to service roads connecting nearby towns and villages 
should be an essential component of the project from the its formulation stage itself and 
should be a part of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) so that the integrated infrastructure 
can be developed with proper connectivity and interlinking.

direction and such parks, if planned at strategic locations in the country would bring down 
logistics costs and boost the national economy. The parks will enable the shift from a point-
to-point to a hub –and-spoke model in logistics sector, eventually helping to bring down 
logistics costs and enabling more efficient movement through new -generation vehicles. The 
importance of a modern and effic ient logistics network cannot be overemphasized. Poor 
connectivity across various logistics modes not only increases the wear and tear of 
transport means and damages to goods, but also leads to uncertainty in supply chains 
leading to further decrease in th e route utilization by trade and thus, increasing 
transportation costs for the remaining users. Sagarmala aims at construction of wider 
roads for connectivity of Ports to another point. However, unfortunately, the Committee 
noticed that in some cases the S agarmala Projects are undertaken only up to major cross 
roads on the route and thereafter no effort is made to construct road up to point envisaged 
in the Sagarmala Project. The Committee is constrained to note that in such a situation the 
wider roads/conn ectivity between the Port and the point envisaged in the Sagarmala 
Project beyond the point of cross roads will remain unfulfilled. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the point –to–point Sagarmala connectivity envisaged may be 
implemented irrespective of the fact that there exists major cross roads in between. The 
Committee stresses that road connectivity under Sagarmala should not be only point to 
point but encompass the entire peripheral network of roadways interlinking nearby towns, 
villages, servi ce roads, important tourist places, national monuments etc. for the overall 
development of the areas. The Committee emphasizes that  service roads should be 
included in the DPR itself, and given as much importance.

24. The Committee was also informed by the MoPSW of the following specific issues 
regarding connectivity to ports:- 
 
Improvement of Rail Share at Paradip Port 
I - Infrastructure Improvement: 
(i) Direct Rail Connectivity to Mines: The nearest railway sidings to various Iron Ore mines 
like Nuagaon, Gandhamardan and Gonua are situated in the vicinity of 20 -30 km. Iron Ore 
is transported by road to the railway sidings in the first mile connectivity, which leads to 
higher cost and environmental hazards. Steps may be taken to develop railway sidings close 
to the mine -heads by  obtaining necessary statutory clearances, to maximize  the rail 
movement of Iron Ore. 
(ii) Nayagarh – Koira – Barbil Railway Line: Feasibility of laying a new railway line from 
Nayagarh to Barbil via Ko ira may be examined. The above line will reduce the distance 
from mines of Sundargarh District, Odisha to Paradip Port and increase the rail share. 
(iii) Doubling of Sukinda – Jaroli Section: Original TDC of ongoing Sukinda – Jaroli doubling 
project is June 2022 , which is likely to get delayed for want of MoEF clearance and land 
acquisition. The above pro ject may be expedited for early completion to increase Ore rake 
movement. 
(iv) Improvement of Road Connectivity: Gandhamardan Iron Ore mines are  situated in 
Keonjhar District of Odisha. The nearest railway siding is at Naranpur (NANR) which is 
about 20km away from the mines. Condition of the existing road leading to the railway 
siding from the mines is not good, which needs to be developed to facilitate faster 
movement of Iron Ore to siding for further despatch by rail. 
 
II -Policy Issues: 
(i) Iron Ore Pellet and Export traffic of Iron Ore has been categorized under priority “D” as per 


11  
the “Iron-ore Policy 2021,” which is affecting rake allotment. Hence the Users like  
Triveni/BRPL are converging the Iron Ore Pell et by road (around 250 trucks/ day). 
Necessary changes in categorization may  be made to bring Iron Ore Pellet and Export Iron 
Ore under higher priority. 
 
III- Rake Availability: 
(i) JSW has developed  a 10 MMTPA capacity Iron Ore Terminal inside Paradip Port on PPP 
basis for loading of Iron Ore/ Pellet. They have more than 100 indents pending with SE 
Railway for supply of rakes for movement of their cargo from mines to Paradip Port for 
further despatch especially to their Steel Pla nt at Dolvi, Maharashtra through coastal 
shipping. Since supply of rakes is not adequate, they are despatching some Iron Ore by 
road to Port (500 trucks/ day). Hence, more BOXN rakes may be supplied by SE Railway, 
as per the demand, for movement of Iron Ore from Mines to Paradip Port. 
(ii) The Port is having a stock of more than 3 MMT of import cargo waiting for evacuation. 
More than 250 indents for rakes are pending with Railways. At least 22 rakes on daily basis 
may be supplied to the Port for loading of the import cargo.

Rail Connectivity Issues pertaining to Visakhapatnam Port Authority 
(i) Visakhapatnam Port Authority (VPA) is one of the largest Major Ports in the country and 
handles ~ 75 Million Tonnes per annum. The rail co -efficient of VPT is ~ 60% and is 
largely dependent on the Indian Railways for transportation of its EXIM cargo. The current 
cargo handling capacity of VPA is 127 Million Tonnes and will further increase in the next 
few years. VPA is largely dependent on Indian Railways for transporting its EXIM cargo 
and 80% of this Rail bound cargo is transported via the Raipur-Vizianagaram route (RV). 
(ii) Due to delay in completion of Electrification and Doubling works of the Titlagarh - Raipur 
and Titlagarh - Sambalpur sections on the RV line, during periods of peak demand, VPA as 
well as the Indian Railways experience severe congestion which causes heavy detention to 
rolling stock. 
(iii) As per the latest information ascertained from the Zonal Railways, it is understood that the 
TDC for electrification and doubling in the Titlagarh -Raipur and Titlagarh - Sambalpur 
sections are during 2022 -23. It is also to mention that as per the past experience that TDC 
has been regularly shifted to later dates due to certain project related constraints in the 
sections. 
(iv) In this regard, the Railway Board may be suitably addressed to strictly adhere to the TDC 
in the above two sections for facilitating quick transportation of EXIM cargo from / to 
VPA and thus enabling “Win-Win” situation for both the Indian Railways and VPA.

developed are equipped with state -of-the-art facilities and amenities including 
comfortable passenger lounge, immigration counters, sign boards in various relevant 
languages, clean washroom facilities etc. for  the tourists, to offer them a comfortable 
experience. The development of terminals may be planned with a long-term analysis 
of the estimated capacity requirements so as to be able to efficiently handle a large 
number of tourists in the upcoming years. 
 
40. The Committee further notes that  the tourist  terminal/ cruise  facilities being 
developed at present are for the Government controlled port terminals only. The 
Committee recommends  that the Ministry may devise ways to promote the 
development of cruise tourist terminals at privately managed ports as well, as there are 
many existing and upcoming private ports, which have the potential to attract tourists 
due to their opportune location. 
 
41. From the data furnished by MoPS&W with regard to pre-Covid and post-Covid 
scenario of cruise s hips/passengers handled by Indian Ports, the Committee notes that 
while there was a discernible pattern of growth in terms of cruise ships/passengers 
handled by Indian Ports from FY 2016 -17 to FY 2019 -20, the onset of the Coronavirus 
pandemic has had a sub stantial deterrent effect on the number of vessels/passengers 
handled. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & 
Waterways and Ministry of Tourism may undertake  necessary remedial measures to 
boost the revival of the cruise tourism se ctor over and above the pre -Covid levels, at 
the earliest. 
 
 
MARITIME INDIA VISION (MIV) 2030 
 
42. The Committee was apprised regarding the following prioritized 
Initiatives/Actionable Points under MIV 2030:- 
A) Ocean Crushing: 14 actionable points are identified under this category 
B) Inland and Lighthouse: 2 Actionable Points are identified under this category 


21  
C) Inland/ River Crushing: 3 Actionable Points are identified under this category. 
 
 
43. The Committee notes that the ports and port–terminals, situated near industries 
and tourist sites/monuments, will play a vital role in shaping key theme of Maritime 
India Vision, 2030 through their capabilities to handle bulk cargo and heavy tourist 
traffic simultaneously. The Committee recommends that terminals be develope d under 
the MIV 2030 through linkages with modern transport system, globalized supply 
chains, tourist places and coastal communities and also by taking the views of 
stakeholders for improvement of terminal designs. 
 
Transshipment Hubs 
 
44. The Ministry informed the Committee that as per the new policy of the Government 
many transshipment hubs are being created in the  country to increase the  share of India in 
the transshipment of goods worldwide. In this direction Andaman and Nicobar Islands is 
being developed as a major transshipment hub, for which DPR has already been awarded. In-
principle Government approval for development of a major port at Vadhavan in Maharashtra 
has also been awarded. This port intends to develop the port infrastructure  and also establish 
connectivity to hinterland through the PPP model. With the development of Vadhavan port, 
India will break into the league of countries with top 10 container ports in the world. 
 
45. The Committee appreciates the new policy of the Government  to create 
transshipment hubs across the country, which will create connectivity to the areas near 
the coastal regions and also bring about growth in economy and generate employment. 
The Committee welcomes the development of Andaman & Nicobar Islands as 
transshipment hub and the development of Vadhavan  Port. The Committee also notes 
that Lakshadweep Islands is  strategically placed near the busiest worldwide 
commercial shipping routes. The Committee therefore desires that the Ministry may 
explore the possibility of setting up a transshipment hub at Lakshadweep Islands. This 
will also give a boost to the tourism, besides creating job opportunities for the youth.

22  
RECOMMENDATIONS/ OBSERVATIONS AT A GLANCE 
 
 
The Committee is aware that ports have been centers of commerce for centuries and  
they remain crucial to the economy even today. Every year, hundreds of billions of 
rupees worth of products move through ports. Ports generate substantial business 
activity through their operations. The Committee notes that nation’s major ports are an 
important part of our  national economy and transportation system. Over 95% of 
India’s trading by volume and 65% by value is done through maritime transport. In 
addition to their impact on the national economy, ports also have an impact on local and 
regional economies of the states on which the ports are situated. The Committee is also 
of the opinion that a substantial portion of business activity in a variety of industries is 
driven by international trade, and the value of foreign trade has risen substantially over 
the years. Although trade volumes are affected by global economic conditions and have 
decreased slightly over the past few years due to COVID pandemic, trade volumes are 
expected to rise in the future, increasing the importance of ports and waterways in terms 
of export and import. The Committee recommends that at this crucial juncture of 
expected increase in global maritime trade, appropriate policy measures may be taken to 
increase maritime trade through port connectivity to boost the economy of the country. 
(Para 5)  
 
The Committee observes  that with the increase in port capacity to handle heavier 
cargo volumes and bigger size of container vessels in near future, there will be a need for 
development of modern terminal development, which will also challenge the ability of 
terminals to handle increasing  cargo volumes. The Committee recommends that 
appropriate guidelines and coordination mechanisms may be formulated to facilitate 
the development of modern terminals to  handle increased cargo volumes and bigger 
container vessels in near future which will decrease the  challenges of terminal 
operators as well. 
(Para 6) 
 
SAGARMALA PROGRAMME 
The Committee notes that SDCL was incorporated on 31st August, 2016 for 
implementation of Sagarmala and currently out of 802 projects, 202 projects have been 
completed, 216 projects are under implementation, while 384 are under various stages of 


23  
development. Hence, only about 25% of the total projects under Sagarmala are complete 
as on date. The Committee expresses serious concern at the slow progress of work and 
recommends that Sagarmala, being a crucial step in the progress of India’s shipping 
sector, whi ch seeks to bring about port connectivity needs to be expedited. The 
Committee also desires to know whether  there has been cost escalation and time 
overrun as compared to original cost and timeline of the projects. The Committee 
while underlining the speedy implementation of the Sagarmala projects, also desires to 
know the precise reasons for delays, port -wise and concrete steps taken to address the 
delays. 
(Para 10) 
 
RAIL CONNECTIVITY 
The Committee notes that the Government has taken up large number of projects to 
remove the bottlenecks in road and rail connectivity to ports. The Committee has no 
doubt that once the  projects are implemented, the connectivity problems may be 
resolved to a great extent. However, despite the enormous importance of the connectivity 
of ports, the Committee  feels that the pace of work under the Port, Rail and Road 
connectivity Projects have been slow. The Committee is of the opinion that more 
coordinated efforts a re required to complete the connectivity projects by involving 
Railway Authorities/NHAI etc., addressing all technical aspects. The Committee 
emphasizes that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways, waterways etc. 
should be part of the infras tructure planning process, right from inception stage. The 
Committee is also of opinion that approach to a port from  hinterland can be critical 
enough to make  or mar  a Terminal, because  it determines the  turn round time and 
evacuation time-vital to the functioning of the port. Evacuation is a vital component of 
any port project as the capacity and efficiency of the port vitally depend on the rate at 
which the cargo can be evacuated from  the terminal. The efficiency, viability and 
business depend on how well  connected the port is.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the plans for the connectivity of a port to the roads and railway 
networks, to airports, to service roads connecting nearby towns and villages should be 
an essential component of the project  from the its formulation stage itself and should be 
a part of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) so that  the integrated infrastructure can be  
developed with proper connectivity and interlinking. 
(Para 19)  


24  
 
INITIATIVES UNDERTAKEN BY MOPS&W TO EXPEDITE IMPL EMENTATION 
OF PORT CONNECTIVITY PROJECTS 
The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the various Ministries to expedite the 
implementation of the Port Connectivity Projects. It also notes that the Ministry of Road 
Transport & Highways and NHAI has also ca rried out a detailed prioritization exercise 
and had shortlisted  38 road connectivity projects which are at DPR stage and likely to 
be awarded by the 
F.Y. 2022. The Committee is of the opinion that such a capital intensive infrastructure 
project which seeks to improve port, rail and road connectivity involving various 
ministries, State Governments can be successful, only if all the concerned agencies give 
utmost attention to the time -bound completion of the portion of work allocated to 
each one and maintain close coordination and cooperation amongst themselves. The 
Committee hopes that all out efforts would be made by all the stakeholders to complete 
the work allocated within the time schedule. The Committee also desires to know the 
status of the award of work rel ating to the 38 road connectivity projects and the 
percentage of work completed. 
(Para 21)  
 
The Committee further notes that a SPV under NHAI viz. National Highways Logistics 
Management Ltd. (NHLML) has been incorporated in 2020 to develop Multimodal 
Logistic Parks (MMLPs) and works related to National Highways connectivity to ports. 
The Committee is of the firm opinion that the MMLPs is a step in the right direction 
and such parks, if planned at  strategic locations in the country would bring down 
logistics costs and boost the national economy. The parks will enable the shift from 
a point-to-point to a hub–and-spoke model in logistics sector, eventually helping to 
bring down logistics costs and enabling more efficient movement through new -
generation vehicles. The importance of a modern and efficient logistics network  cannot 
be overemphasized. Poor connectivity across various logistics modes not only 
increases the wear and tear of transport means and damages to goods, but also 
leads to uncertainty  in supply chains leading to further decrease in the route 
utilization by trade and thus, increasing transportation costs for the remaining users. 
Sagarmala aims at construction of wider roads for connectivity of Ports to another 
point. However, unfortunately, the Committee noticed that in some cases the Sagarmala 


25  
Projects are underta ken only up to major cross roads on  the route and thereafter no 
effort is made to construct road up to point envisaged in the Sagarmala Project. The 
Committee is constrained to note that in such a situation the wider 
roads/connectivity between the Port and  the point envisaged in the Sagarmala  Project 
beyond the point of cross roads will remain unfulfilled. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the point –to–point Sagarmala  connectivity envisaged  may be 
implemented irrespective of  the fact that there exis ts major cross roads in between. 
The Committee  stresses that  road connectivity under Sagarmala should not be only 
point to point but encompass the entire peripheral network of roadways interlinking 
nearby towns, villages, service roads, important tourist places, national monuments etc. 
for the overall development of the areas. The Committee emphasizes that service 
roads should be included in the DPR itself, and given as much importance. 
(Para 22) 
 
The Committee appreciates the initiative of the MoPS&W under the PM’s “Gati Shakti” 
Programme, to carry out an intensive exercise to find connectivity gaps and that 52 
last mile road connectivity projects have been identified in consultation with Major 
Ports and State Maritime  Boards. The requirement of these projects has been 
conveyed to MoRTH for assessment and development on 1st April, 2022. The 
Committee may be furnished the information regarding the on -ground 
implementation of these road connectivity projects. Similarly, the Committee desires to 
know the status of sanction surveys to be conducted by Ministry of Railways (MoR) to 
determine the feasibility of rail connectivity  to ports which have sizeable freight traffic 
but are still not connected by rail. 
(Para 23) 
 
ISSUES WITH CONNECTIVITY TO PORT 
The Committee notes the specific instances of connectivity issues. It notes with concern 
the lack of road connectivity from railway sidings at Paradip Port to iron -ore mines at 
places like Nuagaon, Gandhamardan and Gonua, which leads to higher road 
transportation cost. It also notes the lack of railway line to reduce mine -port distance at 
Nayagarh. While at places like Sukinda - Jaroli, iron-ore rake movement is decreased 
due to delay in environmental clearance for  doubling projects. The Committee is of the 
opinion that since railways is the fastest transport mode and can transport huge quantity 


26  
of ore at one go and also causes less environmental pollution as compared to road 
transport, all out efforts should be made to hasten the Mine -to-port road projects in the 
said projects. Environmental Clearances should also be fast tracked to expeditiously 
complete the projects. The Commi ttee also recommends that necessary steps may be 
taken to develop railway sidings near mines and for obtaining necessary statutory 
clearances to maximize the rail movement of Iron Ore. The Committee notes that some 
of the Rail and Road projects connecting the Paradip Port are pending for years due to 
various reasons. The Committee recommends that the Ministries of Railways; Ports, 
Shipping & Waterways; and State Governments should make concerted efforts to 
complete the projects at the earliest. Secretary, M inistry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways may take the initiative to complete the projects without delay. 
(Para 25)  
 
The Committee notes  that Vishakhapatnam Port is  one of  the largest  Major Ports in 
the country handling 75 MTPA with a 60% rail co -efficient, and is largely dependent on 
the Indian Railways for transportation of its EXIM cargo. The delay in electrification 
and doubling work  on this rail route is causing severe congestion at Port and also on 
railway lines. The Committee recommends that necessary steps should be taken to 
rectify the problem. 
(Para 26)  
 
The Committee is aware that Odisha is the largest iron ore producing Indian 
State playing a crucial role in the development of iron and steel industries across the 
nation as well as development of transportation system, aircraft industry, automobile 
industry, real estate and building industry etc. The Committee recommends that all out 
efforts should be made to ensure quick  movement of iron ore from Paradip Port and 
connecting roads should be repaired in a time bound manner and policies should be 
framed in this regard, to ensure growth of aforesaid industries, which will result in 
economic growth of the country. 
(Para 27)

Shipping & Waterways in coordination with the Ministry of Tourism to develop the 


27  
required infrastructure and facilities for cruise tourism and for promotion of the same

India and requires well thought out, concerted efforts of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping

meetings regularly and if required, the Task Force may seek consultations fro m

plan for the development of cruise tourism in the country.

The Committee notes from the projections regarding the potential for cruise shipping in

Tourism and Culture deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Culture on the

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
NATIONAL LIBRARY, KOLKATA 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee fails to comprehend how the National Library could be expected to 
function to its maximum potential when the top -level post of Director-General of the Library 
has been lying vacant for several years on the run. The Committee recommends that the post 
of the Director -General in the National Library should not be kept vacant for such a lon g 
time and steps be taken to fill it up immediately. The Committee strongly recommends that 
urgent action needs to be taken for filling up the human resource requirements of the 
National Library. 
(Para 13)  
 Reply of Ministry  
1.1 The vacancy has been advertised in Employment News for the week 29 th January - 4th 
February, 2022 for filling up the post of DG, NL. All the necessary actions are being initiated 
in this regard. 
 
CENTRAL SECRETARIAT LIBRARY, DELHI 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes that Central Secretariat Library, a premier library  
situated in the heart of the capital, is a big attraction for politicians, bureaucrats and  
scholars. In view of its locational advantage, the Committee is of the view that CSL  
should undertake the r ole of advising decision makers on matters of library information 
services. The Committee also desires that CSL should play a lead role to coordinate with 
national and international agencies, associations, Non -Governmental 
Organizations (NGOs), publishers and other stakeholders for the development of  
library services in the country and for deriving benefit from huge collections of  
Government reports and gazettes. 
(Para 17)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
2.1 This Ministry vide Letter dated 06.04.2022 has directed CSL to take necessary action 
as recommended by PSC.  
 
 

3 
 
CHALLENGES 
 Legislation 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the Ministry should bring  
pressure on state governments to enact library legislation in the states where it has not been 
enacted covering all aspects like structure of buildings, staff requirement,  
preservation of valuable manuscripts etc. for their proper growth. Libraries in  
Southern States may be emulated in this regard. 
(Para 37)  
Reply of Ministry  
3.1 This Ministry vide D.O Letter dated 13.04.2022 and subsequent reminders dated 
04.07.2022 &  31.08.2022 requested all States/UTs Authorities to take necessary steps for 
implementation of the recommendations of the Committee. Response received in this regard 
from 05 States namely Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tripura, Sikkim and Chandigarh may be seen 
at Annexure- C. 
 Financial Resources 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the State Governments may be  
guided to frame rules/amendments in the Act in a manner that money collected for the 
purpose is utilized properly and spent only for the libraries. It should not go to other  
State accounts and be used for other purposes. 
(Para 42)  
Reply of Ministry 
4.1 Information on the money collected and expenditure incurred is being obtained from 
State/ UT Authorities. An interim reply with the data received from 9 States has already 
been provided to the DRPSC (Annexure-A). Other States are also being pursued constantly.
