1 
 
REPORT 
The Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Culture on the 
recommendations/observations as contained in its Three Hundred and Eleventh Report on 
‘Creation of Regulatory Framework for Protection of Historical Sites and Monuments ’ which 
was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 3rd February, 2022. 
2. The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 29th July, 13th October 
and 25 th October, 2022 in respect of all the recommendations/observations contained in the 
311th Report. The replies have been categorized as follows:— 
Chapter-I: 
Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the Ministry:  
Paragraph Nos.:  35A, 39, 41, 52 
Total:   4 
Chapter-II: 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the replies of the Ministry: 
Paragraph Nos.:  14, 15, 16, 18, 33, 35 
Total:   6 
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have 
not been accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.:  23, 34, 43, 47, 48, 48A, 50  
Total:   7 
Chapter-IV: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final replies of the 
Ministry are still awaited: 
Paragraph Nos.:   Nil  
Total:   Nil 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Efficacy of the existing Regulatory Framework to deal with the specific issue of 
encroachment of the Historical Sites and Monuments  
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee recommends that wherever possible, the Ministry/ASI should develop 
the area in the vicinity of the ancient monuments as green space with amenities for tourists 
since doing so will not only curb encroachment of that area but also bolster touri sm in the 
region.  
(Para 35A)  
Reply of Ministry  
1.1 The suggestion is noted for action, wherever possible.  
 
Review of existing provisions for grant of permission required for construction or 
repairs within the prohibited/ regulated areas of Centrally protected monuments  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee fails to see why a person living in the Regulated Area of a CPM 
should be required to seek permission from the Competent Authority under the AMASR Rules 
for carrying out innocuous maintenance activities such as filling of cracks, whitewashing , 
replacement of windows etc. The Committee feels that such uncalled -for interference makes 
lives harder for people living nearby the monuments and could slowly cause feelings of 
anguish towards the monument itself. Given the large number of monuments acro ss the 
country and the limited budgetary resources available with the Government, it is pertinent 
that people residing near the monuments are encouraged to look after the monuments and 
protect them. Besides, placing such unnecessary curbs and implementing them is a wastage 
of limited Government resources and turns the focus away from where it should be - actually 
protecting and preserving the monument itself. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry may undertake a thorough review of the AMASR  Act and Rules and omit any 
provisions that provide for seeking permissions for minor works where the same is not 
actually needed and streamline the process for applying for permission in case where the 
same is actually needed. Steps may urgently be taken to make it possible for the entire 
process for seeking permission for construction activities in prohibited and regulated areas, 
to be completed online so as to not cause any hassle to bona fide residents living near the 
monuments.  

3 
 
(Para 39)  
Reply of Ministry  
2.1 Recommendation is noted for action as appropriate. 
 
Evolving ways for participation of municipalities and village panchayats in the process 
of protection of regional Historical Sites and Monuments 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. Given the large number of historical monuments and sites located across the country, 
many of which are not under any sort of protection from the Central/State Governments, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation made in para 5.7.23 of its 294 th Report on the 
subject ‘Development and Conservation of Museums and Archaeological sites - Challenges 
and Opportunities ’ and recommends that the Ministry should find ways to institutionally 
integrate municipalities and village panchayats in the process of protection of historical  
monuments and sites across the country and if needed, create a dedicated body to implement 
the regulatory framework for the same.  
(Para 41)  
Reply of Ministry  
3.1 Noted for action as appropriate. 
 
Miscellaneous  
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee recommends that ASI may frame Disaster Management Plan for the 
monuments at the earliest since disasters can cause irreversible damage to our invaluable 
historical monuments and sites and sincere efforts have to be made to have plans in place  to 
minimize the damage caused due to such adversities.  
(Para 52)  
Reply of Ministry  
4.1 Noted for compliance.  
  

4 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. In light of the observations made by various experts on the subject and the lack of any 
specific reasoning behind the limit of 100 metres and 300 metres around the CPMs as 
prohibited and regulated areas, the Committee is of the strong view that the Ministry must 
undertake a holistic, in -depth review of the restrictions imposed by the AMASR Act on 
construction activities near the CPMs since it does not seem logica l to have restrictions on a 
uniform amount of area across the highly diverse types of monuments under the protection of 
the Central Government. The Committee takes serious notice of the observation made by one 
of the experts that the 2010 amendment was bro ught about without any inputs from the ASI 
and recommends that the review of the existing legislation should be carried out in 
consultation with existing and former senior officials of ASI, and other subject experts. The 
Committee recommends that the area to be deemed as prohibited and regulated area should 
not be set in stone for all the monuments and should instead be decided on a case -to-case 
basis, with due consideration to the individual requirements of the monument/site. There is 
no denying the fact t hat there needs to be a mechanism for keeping a check on the 
construction activities in the vicinity of a historical monument but utmost care must be taken 
to ensure that doing so causes least possible disruption in the lives of people who have had 
been li ving in harmony with the monuments since decades, duly factoring in the specific 
requirements for such checks given the unique nature of the individual historical monuments. 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should urgently work towards creating a  
regulatory framework that has provisions for the least possible restrictions on construction 
activities in a manner suitable to the specific requirements for individual monuments while 
ensuring that no structural or visual damage is caused to the monument  by any construction 
activities and does not unnecessarily impinge on the rights of people living nearby the 
monuments. 
(Para 14)  
 Reply of Ministry  
1.1 The issue has been taken into consideration under proposed amendment in 
consultation with other experts also. 
 
 
 

5 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee agrees with the concerns raised by one of the experts regarding the 
prohibitions imposed by the AMASR (Amendment) Act, 2010 on appointment of any person 
who has held any post with the ASI or the Ministry of Culture, as the Chairman or member of 
the NMA. The Committee feels that having the services of personnel who have had actual 
field experience working for the preservation and protection of the historical monuments and 
sites, could help NMA fulf ill its mandate in a more effective manner but many people with 
such experience would be those who have had worked with the ASI or Ministry of Culture 
and thus would be deemed ineligible to be appointed as the Chairman or member of the NMA 
as per the exist ing provisions of the AMASR Act. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry may revisit the rationale behind the restrictions imposed by Section 20F(3) of the 
AMASR (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2010 and consider the pros and cons behind 
imposing such a restriction on the appointment of Chairman and members of the NMA. 
Further, the Committee notes that the NMA has also been given the responsibility of 
classification and gradation of monuments in consultation with ASI. The Committee 
recommends that NMA may complete the classification and gradation exercise at the earliest. 
The Committee feels that doing so, alongwith preparation of heritage byelaws for all CPMs, 
would permit the Ministry to come up with provisions for restrictions best suited for each 
monument instead of blanket bans that fail to serve the intended purpose. 
(Para 15)  
Reply of Ministry  
2.1 The issue has been taken into consideration under proposed amendment. Actions are 
also initiated for enabling the work of preparation of Heritage Bye-laws at faster rate.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may introduce the concept of 
Transferable Development Rights to enable people having properties in the vicinity of the 
monuments to monetize their properties. The Committee feels that this would act as a 
deterrent to encroachment of monuments, especially in case the monument is located in a 
congested urban area.  
(Para 16) 
Reply of Ministry  
3.1 Transfer of Development rights is not within the jurisdiction of MoC. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee takes note of the extensive list of suggestions made by the expert 
regarding the new Rules/ Regulations/ Policies/ Legislation/ Amendments that can be 

6 
 
introduced in order to ensure better protection of the Historical Sites and Monuments. The 
Committee reiterates its recommendation made in Para 14 of this Report and recommends 
that the Ministry may thoroughly examine the above -mentioned suggestions made by the 
expert while undertaking the review of the AMASR Act. The Ministry must ensure that t he 
review of the existing legislation may factor in feedback from experts in the field of 
conservation, preservation, archaeology, law as well as all the stakeholders who are 
impacted by the AMASR Act.  
(Para 18)  
Reply of Ministry  
4.1 Stakeholder consultations w ere done while working on AMASR Amendment and  
their views have been suitably taken into consideration.  
 
Efficacy of the existing Regulatory Framework to deal with the specific issue of 
encroachment of the Historical Sites and Monuments  
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee notes the existing provisions in place in order to deal with the issue of 
encroachment of Centrally Protected Monuments and the loopholes/ gaps/ glitches pointed 
out by various experts. The Committee agrees with the suggestion made by one of the experts 
that amendments are required in order to ensure that encroachment of monuments are 
removed as quick as possible in fast track courts. The Committee feels that doing so can 
permit the encroachment to be removed befo re any permanent structure is constructed in the 
vicinity of the monument, thus preventing any sort of possible damages to the monument.  
(Para 33)  
Reply of Ministry  
5.1 The issue of removal of encroachments is suitably being addressed in the proposed 
amendment.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may undertake a thorough review of the 
AMASR Act as well as the AMASR Rules in terms of the powers available with ASI to tackle 
the issue of encroachment of monuments, keeping in view the various loopholes and gap s 
pointed out by legal experts. The Committee feels that the Ministry should incorporate 
provisions similar to those relating to encroachment in the Indian Forest Act, 1927, in the 
AMASR Act in order to empower ASI to effectively deal with the issue of enc roachment of 
monuments. The Committee further recommends that the AMASR Act should grant power to 
ASI to seal the site of illegal construction till the time the demolition can be done, so that any 
delay in the same does not cause any further damage to the monument and there is no 

7 
 
incentive for encroachers to undertake any illegal construction near the monument. The 
Ministry should request the Ministry of Finance to provide it with separate budget to carry 
out the demolition of unauthorized constructions tha t have taken place in the vicinity of 
Centrally Protected Monuments.  
(Para 35)  
Reply of Ministry  
6.1 The issue of removal of encroachments is suitably being addressed in the proposed 
amendment. As per the AMASR Rules, 1959 the demolition of unauthorised constructions is 
to be carried out at the cost of defaulter. 
 
 
 
  

8 
 
CHAPTER-III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Suggestions for creation of Regulatory Framework for protection of Historical 
Monuments presently not under the protection of both Central and State Governments 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry may consider coming up 
with a legislation to amend the Constitution adding ―ancient and historical monuments 
other than those declared to be of national importance to the Concurrent List, in order to 
permit the Central Government to enforce at least some set of provisions for the basic 
protection and conservation of archaeological monuments and sites which are presently not 
under any sort of protection by Central and State Governments. A separate Herita ge 
Commission may thereafter be established to look after such monuments. Since a 
Constitutional amendment is a time -taking process, the Committee recommends that in the 
meanwhile, the Ministry may come up with policy guidelines which can be adopted by the  
State Governments across the country for looking after neglected archaeological sites and 
monuments. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry may request for certain 
budgetary allocation to allow ASI to carry out urgent conservation measures at such 
miscellaneous monuments, possibly in coordination with concerned State Archaeology 
Departments.  
(Para 23)  
Reply of Ministry  
1.1 ASI has provisions to undertake conservation measures at ancient monuments which 
are not of national importance. Certain budgetary allocation is also made for this purpose.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
1.2 The reply furnished by the Ministry does not  state whether it has taken any 
action to frame policy guidelines which can be adopted by the State Governments across 
the country for looking after neglected archaeological sites and monuments . The 
Committee desires to be informed whether the Ministry has taken any action in this 
regard. Further, the Committee may be apprised regarding the budgetary allocation 
made and u tilized by ASI for monuments which are not of national importance and 
what are the guidelines/ rules in place for taking up such conservation works. 
 
 

9 
 
Efficacy of the existing Regulatory Framework to deal with the specific issue of 
encroachment of the Historical Sites and Monuments  
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee is concerned to note that the final notification of declaration of an 
ancient/historical monument/site/remains as of national importance, is not published by ASI 
in most cases. The Committee recommends that a time-bound limit may be prescribed for ASI 
to publish the final notification, alongwith the site map, for monuments under its protection 
since the purpose of the same is to verify the physical structure and to determine the 
portion/part/extent of the monument that is required to be within the protected limits.  
(Para 34)  
Reply of Ministry  
2.1 Declaring any monument as of national importance and publication final notification 
therefor involve consultation with State Government,  Stakeholder, Management Committee 
or sometimes land owners. Such formalities may consume much time -case to case basis and 
are beyond the jurisdiction of ASI/MoC Sometimes, legal issue may crop up. As such it 
appears not feasible to specify a fix time limit to publish final notification. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
2.2 The Committee notes that the declaration of any monument to be of national 
importance and publication of final notification therefor is a time -consuming process 
since it involves consultation with State Government, Stakeholder, Management 
Committee or sometimes land owners.  However, the more extensive the tasks, the 
greater is the need for setting time limits.  The Committee feels that having a clear time -
limit for publication of the final notification is required to mitigate the present situation 
wherein the final notification of declaration of an  ancient/historical 
monument/site/remains as of national importance, is not published  at all  by ASI in 
many cases, even after passage of very long time  since publication of preliminary 
notification. The Committee  strongly recommends that t he Ministry may prescribe  a 
well-defined time-bound limit for ASI to publish the final notification  of declaration of 
an ancient/historical monuments/site/remains as of national importance , along with the 
site map, for monuments under its protection.  While deciding upon the time -limit to be 
fixed for this purpose, the Ministry may duly factor in the time-consuming nature of the 
process for publication of final notification. 
 
Preparation of monument -specific conservation plan and bye -laws for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments across the country 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee opines that the Ministry/ASI/NMA should carry out an exercise to 
prepare monument -specific conservation plans and heritage bye -laws for all Centrally 

10 
 
Protected Monuments across the country, since there cannot be a uniform plan for all the 
monuments and the unique conservation requirements of each monument can only be 
reflected through dedicated conservation plan for each monument. Such an exercise would  
undoubtedly require sufficient manpower and resources. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should ensure that swift action is taken to ensure that ASI is adequately staffed at all 
times and staffing requirements should be anticipated well in advanc e since recruitment of 
quality personnel is often a time-taking exercise. The Committee further recommends that the 
Ministry should formulate the budgetary requirements for creation of dedicated conservation 
plans for all CPMs and request the Ministry of F inance to grant the same as a special one -
time grant.  
(Para 43)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
3.1 For the conservation of monuments an annual conservation programme is prepared by 
the Circles concerned as per the requirement and priority of the monuments/ sites. B ased on 
the approved annual conservation programme, conservation works are carried out. In  
addition, Site Management Plans (SMPs) for select WH monuments have also been prepared 
by ASI. 
3.2 Promotions held in ASI during 2021 and 2022 (till date) are attac hed at Annexure-I. 
Further, plan for filling up vacant posts and promotion for upcomi ng years are also given at 
Annexure-II. 
3.3 Annual budget for the conservation of monuments is provided by the Ministry of 
Culture to the Archaeological Survey of India. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.4 The Committee observes that the annual conservation programme prepared by 
the Circles concerned is as per the requirement and priority of the monuments/ sites. 
The Committee, however, feels that the requirements and priority of conservation work 
at the monuments/ sites cannot be effectively gauged unless monument -specific 
conservation plans are prepared for all monuments in the respective circles  and 
therefore, recommends that provisions may be introduced to prepare m onument-
specific conservation plans so as to ensure suitable state of conservation for all Centrally 
Protected Monuments. 
 
3.5 The Committee notes the details furnished by the Ministry regarding the status 
of direct recruitment to the various posts in ASI and is concerned to note  that more  
than 2,000 vacancies exist at various posts in ASI at present. In this regard, the 
Committee may be apprised whether ASI factors in the time taken by the recruiting 
agencies to complete the recruitment process, while repo rting its vacancies to such 
agencies. Given the evident scarcity of manpower available with ASI in view of the large 
number of Centrally Protected Monuments across the country, anticipating the delays 
in the process of recruitment while reporting vacancies / upcoming vacancies, is of 

11 
 
crucial importance. Effective steps, therefore, must be taken in this regard to ensure 
that ASI is adequately staffed at all times  and recruitment process is put in motion well 
in advance for the same,  so as to ensure sufficient  protection and preservation of our 
tangible cultural heritage. 
 
Security policy for all Centrally Protected Monuments 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may carry out an exercise to figure out 
the requirements for security infrastructure as well as for posting security personnel at each 
monument. The data thus obtained may be used to frame a comprehensive security  policy for 
all the Centrally Protected Monuments so as to ensure a satisfactory level of protection of 
CPMs across the country. The Committee acknowledges the budgetary constraints faced by 
the Ministry and recommends that the Ministry may request the Min istry of Finance to 
provide sufficient budget to allow it to post security personnel at all CPMs across the 
country. Outsourcing should be done to appoint staff for security of the monuments and 
guides should be trained and they should also be made respons ible for taking care of the 
property.  
(Para 47) 
Reply of Ministry  
4.1 Noted for action as appropriate. Action has to be taken up by the Ministry of Culture.  
 
4.2 Guides- Guide matter is handled by the Ministry of Tourism ( MoT). Therefore, MoT 
may take suitable action.   
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.3 The Committee desires to be apprised whether the Ministry of Culture has taken 
any action to seek sufficient budget from the Ministry of Finance to allow it to post 
security personnel  at all Centrally Protected Monuments across the country  and 
whether any action has been taken on the issue of training of guides by the Ministry of 
Tourism. Further, t he Committee is of the view that given the extensive knowledge  
possessed by ASI regarding Centrally Protected Monuments across the country, having 
a suitable mechanism for coordination between ASI and Ministry of Tourism will help 
improve the training standards of Tourist Guides working at such sites.  Sensitization 
programmes for guides may also be carried out in coordination with the Ministry of 
Tourism to encourage them to look after the Centrally Protected Monuments while 
guiding the tourists. 
 
 

12 
 
Improving the mechanism for coordination between ASI and State Government 
Departments  
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may issue guidelines to the State 
Government Departments concerned to approach the ASI in cases where the State protected 
Monuments require the technical expertise available with ASI for better protection and 
preservation of State -protected monuments. The Committee further recommends that the 
regional offices of ASI should proactively review the status of protection and preservation of 
State-protected monuments and in case gross neglec t in the same is observed, the matter 
should be taken up with the State Government Department concerned. The Committee feels 
that a mechanism should be put in place to enable periodic exchange of information about 
the developmental/ conservation/ protection measures taken by ASI and State Departments.  
(Para 48)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
5.1 The point is noted for compliance. However,  wherever necessary, ASI provides 
technical expertise and guidance to the State Governments for undertaking conservation of 
State-protected and unprotected monuments.  In addition, if requested by the State 
Governments, ASI also takes up conservation of State Protected / Unprotected monuments.  
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
5.2 The Committee desires to be apprised of the procedure under which ASI 
provides technical expertise and guidance to the State Governments and the details of 
such instances in the last 3 years.  
 
Miscellaneous  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee recommends that the Ministry/ASI, in coordination with the State 
Government Archaeology/Culture Department concerned, should take up the restoration of 
historical/ religious sites having heritage value and architectural and cultural significa nce 
such as temples which are more than 100 years old and which have been converted into 
mixed-use buildings such as residential property or government building, to their original 
shape. A time -bound implementation programme should be made for the same and  
accountability of officials working on these projects should be fixed so that the restoration 
works are completed on time and in a satisfactory manner. The Ministry may approach the 
Ministry of Finance to allocate separate budget for this purpose. The Com mittee further 
recommends that it should be mandated that the management bodies for religious sites shall 
get periodically audited regarding the state of conservation, safety and security of the 
monuments and the amount of funds/donations received and spen t, so as to ensure that such 

13 
 
funds are not diverted for unrelated purposes.  
(Para 48A)  
Reply of Ministry  
 
6.1 ASI provides technical  expertise and guidance to the State Governments to take up 
the restoration of historical/ religious sites having heritage value and architectural and 
cultural significance. 
 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
6.2 The Committee reiterates its recommendation made under  ‘Further 
Recommendation/Observation’ at para 5.2 of Chapter III of this Report. 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry is working on a much -needed 
amendment of the AMASR Act,  1958. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may 
incorporate the recommendations made by the Committee in this Report and factors in 
feedback from experts and stakeholders in the amendment of the AMASR Act.  
(Para 50) 
Reply of Ministry  
 
7.1 The final Draft Cabinet Note and Bill has been prepared after considering comments 
received from various State Governments, consultation with heritage experts and inter 
ministerial consultation. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
7.2 The Committee notes that the reply furnished by the Ministry does not make any 
mention of the recommendations made by the Committee in its 311 th Report having 
been incorporated in the final Draft Cabinet Note and Bill . The Committee desires to be 
apprised in this regard.

REPORT 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation on the recommendations/observations as contained in its T hree Hundred Fourteenth 
Report on Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Ministry of Civil Aviation which was presented 
to both the Houses of Parliament on 14th March, 2022.  
 
2.  The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 3rd June, 2022  and 13 th 
July, 2022 in respect of all the observations/ recommendations contained in the Report. The 
replies have been categorized as follows:-

Total: 10

of the replies of the Ministry:

91, 97, 104, 110 & 112 
Total: 24 
 
Chapter-III: 
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not been 
accepted by the Committee: 
Paragraph Nos.:  13, 23, 48, 51, 55, 62, 76, 94, 99 & 105 
Total: 10 
 
Chapter-IV:  
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final replies of the Ministry are 
still awaited:

Total: Nil 
 
 
 
 
 
 

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
 
Assessment of Demands for Grants (2022-23) of the Ministry 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that while the projected  demand of the Ministry for 2022 -23 was 
Rs. 11,183.10 crores, an allocation of Rs. 10,667.00 [Rs. 10,590.54 (Revenue) + Rs. 76.46 
(Capital)] crores has been made, which indicates a shortfall of Rs. 516.10 crores. It also noted 
that shortfall is mainly on a ccount of decreased allocations for AIAHL and RCS, while budget 
for projects and programmes have been adjusted as per priority of execution. The Committee is 
of the opinion that the decreased allocation for AIAHL is justified, in view of the fact that the 
process of disinvestment of Air India is almost complete, however, not agreeing to the 
projections for the RCS by a staggering amount of Rs. 101.28 crores is cause of concern. The 
Committee feels that the RCS Scheme, which has given a big boost to affordab le connectivity, 
should have been encouraged by the Government, through sufficient budgetary support. A 
curtailment of funds at this stage may hamper the smooth development of this important scheme. 
The Committee is aware that the Civil Aviation sector is reeling under stress and different 
players have also suffered massive losses due to COVID -19 pandemic and need a helping hand 
from the Government at this critical juncture, yet the Ministry has not been allocated the desired 
projected amount for B.E. 2022 -23. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry‟s 
request for additional funds for all schemes/ heads, including RCS scheme at the R.E. 2022 -23 
stage may be favourably considered by the Ministry of Finance. 
(Para 8) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The observations of the Committee have been noted. Regarding the budgetary provision 
under RCS Scheme, it is submitted that the budget allocation under the scheme  at BE 2022 -23 
has been made considering the status of the progress of the projects  covered under R CS. The 
status of the UDAN airport  is reviewed from time to time and if required, the Ministry will take 
up the matter with MoF for enhanced budget at RE stage in FY 2022-23. 
 

3 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee also notes the decrease in allocation for B.E. 2022 -23 (Revenue) as 
compared to projected amount for 2022 -23 for DGCA by Rs. 37.08 crores, BCAS by Rs. 22.62 
crores and National Aviation University by Rs. 8.60 crores. There has also been a decrease in 
B.E. 2022-23 (Capital) for BCAS by Rs. 13.31 crores and AAIB by Rs. 3.40 crore, where less 
than one-fourth of the projected amount of Rs. 4.40 crores has been allocated. The Committee 
expresses serious concern at the decrease in funds for the agencies looking after the security and 
safety in Civil Aviation sector such as DGCA; BCAS; and AAIB, despite the increased security 
concerns in the sector and recommends that Ministry should be given additional funds at R.E. 
2022-23 stage. 
(Para 9) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The recommendations of th e Committee for allocation of additional funds  for DGCA, 
BCAS and National Av iation University have been noted and depending upon request received 
from these organizations, the matter will be taken up with Ministry of Finance at RE 2022 -23 
stage. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes that over the last five years, the percentage of allocated budget at 
R.E. stage, on projected demand has varied from 56.36%, 59.19% and 34.78%. While in 2020 -
21, it was substantially raised to 84% of the projected demand. In 2021 -22, the Ministry was 
allocated Rs. 72,652 crores, which was more than the projected demand of Rs. 67,844.62 crores 
and the higher allocation was on ac count of “Disinvestment of Air India Limited‟. For this year 
also, 86.80% of the total allocation of Rs. 10,667.00 crores was for AIAHL (SPV), leaving only a 
meager portion of 13.2% amounting to Rs. 1407.09 crores for allocation to the rest of the heads. 
The Committee is of the opinion that such a low allocation over the years will seriously affect the 
growth of the Civil Aviation sector, which is already suffering from a downturn caused by 
COVID-19 pandemic. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the issue of low allocation 
may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance at R.E. stage and need for higher allocations may 
be stressed upon. 
(Para 12) 

4 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The observation of the Committee regarding low allocation over the years has been noted 
and depending upon request received from different organizations of the Ministry, the matter will 
be taken up with the Ministry of Finance at R.E. 2022-23 stage for higher allocations. 
 
Greenfield Project, Brownfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee noted that in the next two to three years, there would be a proposal for six 
to seven new Greenfield airports. From the recent experiences, it has been noticed that the 
Greenfield airports which were developed during the last decade have saturated on their existing 
capacities and need further expan sion and augmentation of facilities, however, lack of land 
availability is limiting the scope of expansion of Greenfield airports. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that every Greenfield airport must be planned in such a way that it should meet the 
requirements of at least next 40 years. Necessary land for the airport may be acquired based on 
the futuristic planning; construction; and development can be undertaken in the future 
depending on the requirements. 
(Para 24) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 Noted. The Master Plans are developed for Airports considering the future forecast. 
However, the development plans are prepared for undertaking the construction in phases. Due to 
the dynamic nature of development, the Master Plans are reviewed regularly based on the revised 
growth forecast. Based on the futuristic traffic projections adequate facilities are  created and 
planned at the airports, such that it would be able to meet all the future traffic demand. 
 
Defence Brownfield Projects 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. In addition to the aforesaid land transfer issues between MoD and AAI, another issue 
relates to the restrictions imposed by the MoD and creation of “no fly zones” over defence 
airfields for over flying by civilian aircrafts. The Committee understands that though restrictions 
are justifiable for civilian aircrafts over flying high security defence airports, yet it feels that the 
problems faced by the civilian aircrafts must be kept in mind. The civilian aircrafts in such cases 

5 
 
have to traverse a longer route to avoid “no fly zones” which results in longer duration of flights 
and higher fuel consumption and leads to higher passenger fares. The Committee is of the 
opinion that wherever possible, the MoD should allow domestic airlines to fly over defence 
airfields in consultation with the Ministry. Hence, the Ministry should take up this issue 
expeditiously with the MoD. 
(Para 28) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Ministry of Civil Aviation in coordination with Ministry of Defence has undertaken the 
issues of FUA (Flexible Use of Airspace) under which the upper airspace of Restricted Airspace 
Volume, at and above 33,000 feet in the Northern Sector and above 25,000 feet in the Southern 
Sector, have been converted as Temporary Reserved Airspace (TRA). 119 Conditional Routes  
(CDRs) have been promulgated so far. Moreover, 24 danger areas have been de -notified in 
coordination with Army.  
 
Airports Authority of India 
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee is also of the view that security and safety measures, presently available 
at the airports are generally not upto standards, due to which there are frequent security lapses. 
The ILS systems are also lacking at airports, which makes night landing and landing during 
rainy seasons risky. The Committee, therefore, recommend s that at all under construction 
airports, security and safety equipment of world -class level should invariably be installed. The 
latest ILS systems and night landing facilities should also be incorporated at the planning stage 
of airports, so that the flights can operate smoothly even in bad weather conditions, reducing the 
need for diversion of flights. The Committee is also of the view that planning for airport 
construction should be futuristic, so that there is no need for expansion and alterations for 
installation of ILS or security/ safety apparatus, at a later stage, which inconveniences the 
passengers and also disturbs the flight operations at airports. 
(Para 39) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The suggestions of the Committee have been noted and the sugge stions/ observations of 
the Committee will be adhered to, while developing airports in future. 

6 
 
Installation of HEPA Filters at Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that HEPA filters are not effective against 
COVID-19 virus and that it is also not technically feasible to install such systems at airports. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that as per ISHARE guidelines, UVGI systems and 
MERV-13 filters may be installed at all the airports in the country, espec ially the ones where 
there is international arrivals from countries where COVID -19 cases are still prevalent. The 
Committee desires to know the airport-wise status of installation of UVGI systems and MERV-13 
filters across the country and the action plan o f the Ministry to combat future waves of COVID -
19. 
(Para 74) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Action for installation of UVGI system and MERV -13 filters in the existing AHUs 
depending upon feasibility at AAI Airports has already been initiated in accordance with the 
guidelines issued by ISHARE on "Operating of Air conditioning and ventilation system to 
control spread of Corona Virus Disease (COVID - 19) in Residence, Workspaces and Healthcare 
Facilities". 
  
7.2 At 30 AAI airports, UVGI system has been installed, wh ile 2 AAI airports have been 
installed with MERV -13 filters. Action is being taken to install UVGI and MERV -I3 filters at 
balance airport depending upon the feasibility.  At 28 airports, installation of UVGI system and 
MERV-13 filters is not feasible due absence of centralized air-conditioning system. 
  
7.3 The airport wise details are attached Annexure - A. Status report of UVGI and MERV 13 
filters at Airport operated by State Government and PPP partners is attached under Annexure – 
A1. 
 
Connectivity of Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
8. Considering the importance of the issue, the Committee had earlier taken up the issue in 
its 297th Report on the subject „Functioning of Airports Authority of India‟. The Ministry in its 

7 
 
action taken notes on the aforesaid Report informed that the project of National Master Plan 
incorporating the Airports, Roadways, Railways, Shipping, Gas pipe lines, Power (existing and 
proposed) all have been combined to create a National Master Plan, which will be inaugurated 
by Hon‟ble Prime Minister. Additionally, letters have been sent by Chairperson, AAI to Chief 
Secretaries of various State Governments to align and relate the City Master Plans also with the 
Airport Master Plans. 
(Para 98) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Noted. 
 
Leveraging Tourism through Airports 
Recommendation/Observation 
9. The Committee feels that airports act as a first gate of entry for both the domestic and 
international tourists visiting a particular city with iconic destinations. Hence, the visuals at the 
airports leave a lasting impact on the mind of a tourist and also create interest in them to 
explore the places of tourist interest. In view of this, the Committee feels that leveraging tourist 
places through airports assumes significance. The Committee, t herefore, recommends that 
besides offering tourist destinations suggested by Ministry of Tourism for RCS -UDAN bidding 
for promoting tourism, MoCA should also design airports to portray the local art and culture of 
the city at the airports through statues, murals, paintings and sculpture displays. The Committee 
recommends that promotional signages for promoting tourism can be explored through 
commercial concessionaires. The AAI can explore the possibility of completely removing rentals 
for Government agencie s instead of charging 50% concession on rental for promoting tourism. 
At the Jaipur airport, the Ministry may impress upon the PPP partner for synchronising the 
Master Plan of the airport, portraying the local theme, art and culture. The Ministry can also 
explore the possibility of engaging marketing personnel at airports to provide professional 
assistance and guidance, especially to the international tourists, which will help in promotion of 
tourism in the country. 
(Para 115) 
 
 

8 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
9.1 The suggestions of the Committee regarding promotion of tourism and portraying of local 
art and culture of the city at the airports through statues, murals, paintings and sculpture displays 
have been noted.  
 
9.2 With regard to synchronizing the Master Plan of Jaipur Airport, portraying the local 
theme, art & culture, it is to inform that the Concessionaire i.e. Jaipur International Airport 
Limited vide their email dated 15.12.2021 have informed that the Master Planning of Jaipur 
Airport for the future development has been considered to have sense of place with local theme. 
 
Evacuation of Stranded Indians in Ukraine 
Recommendation/Observation 
10. The Committee notes that the Government has embarked upon a massive operation 
namely, „Operation Ganga‟, to evacuate stranded Indian nationals, especially, students, from the 
war torn region of Ukraine. Some private airlines and Indian Air Force are engaged in this 
effort, through special flights. The Committee understands that the Government of India is also 
exploring options for evacuating the stranded nationals through corridor/ cross border roads to 
neighbouring countries and thereafter bringing them back to the country by air. The Committee 
applauds this well-coordinated humanitarian efforts of the Ministries of Civil Aviation; Defence; 
and External Affairs and recommends that airlift and all the other possible means of evacuation 
efforts should continue till all the stranded Indian nationals in Ukraine are evacuated safely. 
Presumably, the Ministry would also bear the requisite cost of transport, if required and make 
arrangements for their transport to their native places. 
(Para 116) 
Reply of the Ministry 
10.1 The Ministry of Civil Aviation notes with gratitude the words of encouragement from  the 
Committee. Around 22,500 Indian nationals returned from Ukraine to India from 1 February – 
11 March, 2022. 90 evacuation flights were operated under Operation Ganga, including 14 
Indian Air Force flights. The air fare for all the flights operated under Operation Gang a has been 
borne by the Government of India. 
  

9 
 
CHAPTER-II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Budget Allocation for Combined Headquarter Building 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that a Combined Headquarters (HQ) building has been planned for 
DGCA, BCAS, AAIB & AERA and allocation has been made under the B.E. (2022 -23) Capital 
Section and all the four aforesaid organizations will be contributing for the expendit ure of the 
said building. The Committee appreciates the fact that all the four organizations viz., DGCA, 
BCAS, AAIB and AERA, which are dealing with the security and safety in Civil Aviation Sector 
are being housed in the same building which will ensure be tter coordination among them and 
will ensure best results in the civil aviation security. The Committee, however, notes that no 
capital allocation has been made for B.E. (2022 -23), though Rs. 20.00 crores has been given as 
„Grants-in-Aid‟ to AERA in B. E. 2022-23 (Revenue) head. The Committee desires to know the 
reasons for no allocation at AERA under Capital Head and how the Ministry proposes to ensure 
contribution on the part of AERA for timely completion of its HQ building. The Committee also 
desires to know whether there are any expected cost and time overruns for construction of HQ 
building. The Committee recommends that the HQ building may be built within a fixed timeline 
so as to avoid cost escalation at a later stage. The Committee may be provided wi th a brief Note 
on the proposed Combined Headquarters. 
(Para 16) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Regarding allocation of budget under Capital Section for AERA, it is clarified that AERA 
being an autonomous body, the entire expenditure for its maintenance, Salary  and Capital 
creation is provided through Grants -in-aid from the budget of MoCA. The budgetary allocation 
of Rs 20.00 crore for the FY 2022-23, as Grants-in-aid, is inclusive of Rs 8.00 crore as GIA – for 
Creation of Capital Assets and this amount of alloc ation will be utilised by AERA for payment 
of its share of cost of construction of combined office complex. 
 
 

10 
 
1.2 It may be stated that a Civil Aviation Office Complex at Safdarjung Airport has been 
approved by the competent authority at a cost of Rs. 303. 80 crore. It will accommodate the 
offices of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation/(DGCA), Bureau of Civil Aviation 
Security/(BCAS), Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau/(AAIB) and Airports Economic 
Regulatory Authority/(AERA). Presently, these offic es are scattered in different places in 
Delhi.  The present office premises of these organizations are not able to accommodate all 
the personnel at one place.  
 
1.3 The execution of the project has been entrusted to Airport Authority of India/(AAI), a 
statutory organiz ation under this Ministry. An Mo U has been signed on 24th November 2016 
among AAI, DGCA, BCAS, AAIB and AERA.  As on 31.05.2022, 82% of the construction has 
been completed. AAI has informed that the probable date of completion of the project is  
31.12.2022.

Greenfield Project, Brownfield Project and Defence Brownfield Project 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The committee feels that the Ministry is off mark as regards the understanding on 
creation of white paper for policy makers, as to how and why Green Field Projects are the future 
of the nation. The Ministry has had a long experience of developing airports which were owned 
by the State Governments or by Airport Authority of India. While a long time vision is always 
envisaged for an Airport project to grow for next few decades, however the Committee feels that 
the Brown Field Projects are important to enhance  the footprint of aviation network in the 
country but given an option of redoing an existing airport to that of a Green Field project, there 
should be a clear and ambitious policy of the Government to identify locations for furtherance of 
New Airports. Ind ia being a country with large population, the comparison of number of 

11 
 
aircrafts per person in India is far less than those of United States of America and China which 
have a comparable population figure and geographical area. 
(Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Greenfield airport is conventionally referred as an aviation facility being developed on 
empty land or previously undeveloped land and an airport whose commissioning, planning & 
construction process is carried out from the scratch / grass root level. 
 
2.2 Advantages of Greenfield Airports are:  
 Sites can be planned as per the governing guidelines for intended critical aircraft. Land is 
available & is comparatively cheaper than land at Brownfield airports. 
 Land for future expansion of Airport can be earmarked at initial stage & kept as reserved 
for future growth. 
  
2.3 However, to enhance the footprint of aviation network in the country, 
upgradation/modernization of existing brownfield Airports is also being done. In this regard, 
Private Airport Concessionaires and   AAI has embarked upon a CAPEX plan of more than Rs. 
90,000 crore during year 2019 -2024 for development/ upgradation/ modernization of various 
airports in the country to meet the requirement of Air traffic which includes New Greenfield 
airports, expansion/ modification of existing terminal, new terminals, expansion/ strengthening 
of existing runways, aprons, ANS works like control tower, technical block etc. Such works 
leads to more Aircraft Parking Bays, Better runway efficiency and safety, i ncrease operational 
efficiency, capacity of terminal building which will further facilitate seamless movement of 
Aircraft and enhance the passengers' experience. 
 
2.4 Government of India (GoI) has formulated a Greenfield Airports (GFA) Policy, 2008 
which provides guidelines, procedure and conditions for establishment of new Greenfield 
Airports in the country. As per the Policy, an airport developer or the respective Sta te 
Government willing to establish an airport is required to send a proposal to the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation (MoCA) in the prescribed format available at www.civilaviation.gov.in. There is a 2 -
stage process for approval of the proposal i.e., 'Site Cleara nce' followed by 'In -Principle' 

12 
 
approval.  In accordance with this policy, MoCA receives proposals from the State Governments 
or Airport Developers from time to time for establishment of airports. After due examination, the 
approval for development of a ne w Greenfield Airport is granted. The responsibility for project 
implementation such as land acquisition, project funding, obtaining other mandatory clearances, 
etc. lies with the concerned airport developer or the State Government, as the case may be. 
Under the GFA Policy, GoI has accorded 'In -Principle' approval for development of 21 
Greenfield airports, out of which 08 airports have been operationalized. 
 
2.5 Ministry of Civil Aviation launched Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) - UDAN 
(UdeDeshkaAamNagrik) to stimulate regional air connectivity and making air travel affordable 
to the masses. The primary objective of RCS is to facilitate / stimulate regional air connectivity 
by connecting unserved/underserved airports/heliports/water aerodromes. UDAN is a m arket 
driven scheme. Interested airlines based on their assessment of demand on particular routes 
submit their proposals at the time of bidding under UDAN. An airport which is included in the 
awarded routes of UDAN and requires upgradation / development fo r commencement of RCS 
operations, is developed under "Revival/upgradation of unserved and underserved 
airports/heliports/water aerodromes" Scheme. The Government of India has approved a budget 
of Rs. 4500 crore for revival of existing unserved / underserve d airports / airstrips of the State 
Governments, Airports Authority of India, Public Sector Undertakings and Civil Enclaves. 
 
Recommendation/Observation

Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes with serious concern that out of the total MRO services turnover of 
Rs. 15,353 crores, the annual turnover of the Indian MRO industry is just Rs. 2,300 cro res, 
which is just 15% of India‟s civil MRO expense. The balance 85% MRO services amounting to a 
colossal amount of Rs. 13,053 crores are availed from MROs b ased abroad in Singapore, 
Malaysia, Middle East, EU and USA etc. The massive amount of the MRO services availed from 
abroad can be gauged from the fact that the amount is more than the total B.E. allocation of Rs. 
10,667 crores for 2022 -23. The Committee l aments the huge outgo of avoidable foreign 
exchange. It is of the opinion that Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) organizations play 
a major role in the economy of airline operations. Since, 85% of these activities are carried out 
abroad, there is a strong case to bring these MROs to India as the MRO expenditure is expected 
to grow further with the growth in civil aviation sector. The issues which come within the ambit 
of foreign suppliers can also be addressed by giving them incentives to operate in th is country. 
India with its large technical manpower base can easily provide the manpower for MRO 
services. The reasons for carrying out MRO services abroad, include tax anomaly with global 
MROs in terms of GST/ levies/ surcharges etc.; high airport charges  for land rentals, airport 
royalty, lack of availability of hangar space etc. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should take up the aforesaid issues with the Ministry of Finance and other concerned agencies 
and try to address the issues at the earliest. The issues which are within the ambit of the Ministry 
itself viz. airport charges, hangar space etc. should be expeditiously resolved by the Ministry and 
AAI. 

17 
 
(Para 34) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 Keeping in view India‟s growing aviation market, technology and skill base, Government 
announced new MRO Guidelines on 1st September, 2021 with a view to create a congenial 
atmosphere in the country for the development of MRO industry for aircraft/ helicopter/ drones 
and their engines and other parts. The salient features of the guidelines are as follows: 
a. Concession fee, in any manifestation including royalty, shall not be leviable on new/ 
renewal of existing contracts. 
b. Selection of agency and procedures for allotment of land/ space under rationalized land/ 
space rental for new MRO contracts and renewal of existing MRO contracts, shall be 
through e-tender by AAI. 
c. The renewal of the existing land leases/ space license of MRO service providers/ 
Aircraft Maintenance Organizations (AMOs) shall be on the basis of bidding wherein 
Right of First Refusal (RoFR) shall be given to the existing lessee/ licensee to match the 
first rank bid in terms of the selection criteria provided its bid is within 15% of the most 
competitive bid received. 
d. The quoted/ accepted lease fee shall be escalated @15% after every 3rd year. 
e. The maximum period of contract, new or renewal, for allotment of land/ space shall be 
30 years from the date of handing over of site.  
 
7.2 The new guidelines would encourage the MRO organizations and OEMs to setup 
workshops in India and create a conducive environment towards making India global hub of 
MRO.

at 5 Airports viz. Bhopal, Chandigarh,  Chennai, Begumpet (Hyderabad) and  Juhu Airports.

i. GST on MRO has been reduced from 18% to 5% with full input tax credit from 1 
April, 2020 so as to promote Indan MRO industry and ease cash flow issues for the 
MRO and aviation industry. 
ii. Transactions sub-contracted by foreign OEMs/ MROs to domestic MRO are treated 
as "exports" with zero-rated GST w.e.f. 1 April, 2020.

Rationalisation of Air Fares and Cancellation Charges in Domestic Sectors 
Recommendation/Observation 
20. As regards pricing of the tickets, the Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that at 
present, air fare is neither regulated nor fixed by the Government and airlines are free to fix the 
reasonable tariff under the provision of Sub -rule (1) of Rule 1 35, Aircraft Rules, 1937 having 
regard to all relevant factors including the cost of operation, characteristics of service, 
reasonable profit and the generally prevailing tariff. Also, as regards the concern of the 
Committee regarding extra fare for seat s election, the Ministry has stated that travel by air is a 
contractual matter between airline and passenger, which is commercial in nature. The 
Committee is of the opinion that for Civil Aviation sector to grow in an open market, it is 
justifiable that the private airline operators should be given a free hand to fix the air fares as 
they are governed by competition. However, the Committee would like to draw the attention of 
the Ministry to the provision of the  Aircraft Rules, 1937, which  specifically mention s that the 
fares should be reasonable and should maintain reasonable profit. In the above context, the 
Committee feels that the reply of the Ministry stating that air travel is purely a contractual 
matter between the airline and the passenger, is not at al l justified. The Committee is of the 

36 
 
opinion that a balance also must be maintained between the commercial interests of the airlines 
and the interest of the passengers. The Committee feels that the passengers should not be fleeced 
in the garb of commercial ization and therefore recommends that the Ministry should maintain a 
close watch on the fare pricing by the airlines to ensure that it is not exorbitant. It also 
recommends that at least for the same sector, route and duration of flight, in all the private  
airlines, the Ministry should issue guidelines so as to ensure similar or least variation in fares 
among all airlines. The Committee is also of the opinion that fixing of different fares for 
selection of seats in the same flight is arbitrary and unjustifi able. Hence, Committee on the 
principle of equity feels that all the seats in a same flight should have same fare. The Committee 
also recommends that the Ministry should strictly enforce the DGCA Charter and ensure that 
under no circumstances, the airlines  levies cancellation charges more than the basic fare plus 
fuel surcharge. The Committee may be informed about the mechanism adopted by the Ministry to 
ensure that the Aircraft Rules, 1937 and DGCA Charter is being followed in letter and spirit by 
all private airlines. 
(Para 91) 
Reply of the Ministry 
20.1 Under the provisions of Sub Rule(1) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937, every air 
transport undertaking engaged in scheduled air services require to establish tariff having regard 
to all relevant fact ors, including cost of operation, characteristics of services, reasonable profit 
and the generally prevailing tariff. Airlines are free to charge reasonable air fares as per their 
operation viability subject to compliance of above said provision. The airli nes remain compliant 
to the Sub Rule (2) of Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 1937 as long as fare charged by them is in 
line with fare displayed on their website. 
 
20.2 Further, fare capping was also put in place by the Government during the COVID -19 
pandemic as a special measure in order to safeguard the passengers' interest. The lower as well as 
upper air fares (excluding User Development Fee (UDF), Passenger Service Fee (PSF) and GST) 
were fixed sector -wise on the basis of duration of flight time. The far e capping is currently 
applicable on rolling basis for a 15 days' cycle. 
 

37 
 
20.3 With a view to maintain transparency, Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) 
started monitoring of airfares on certain routes selected on random basis to ensure that the 
airlines do not charge airfares outside the range declared by them.

Requirement of Air Traffic Controllers (ATCOs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes with serious concern that there is a huge backlog of 708 vacancies

with DPE only recently. The Committee is of the opinion that the demand for ATCOs will rise 
exponentially with the growth of the aviation sector in the country and feels that the Ministry 
should have anticipated the requirement of more number of ATCOs well in advance and inducted 
ATCOs continuously over the years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that proc edural 
issues regarding manpower requirements of ATCOs should be addressed immediately to ensure 
operationalization of new airports that are being constructed in near future do not suffer due to 
lack of ATCOs.

Flying Training Organisations (FTOs) 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee notes that there would be a growing requirement of around 1000 pilots 
every year in the near future. The Committee also notes that a liberalized FTO policy has also 
been brought out, wherein new and attractive incentives have been given to pr ivate entities who 
want to start an FTO. The Committee supports the new initiatives of the Ministry as it is of the 
opinion that with the expected growth of the Civil Aviation Sector in the country, there would be 
increased demand for trained pilots. The M inistry should therefore gear up for the requirement 
of FTOs and set up FTOs in a time bound manner. The Committee also notes that the Ministry 
has taken up the issue of reduction of GST on AvGas and funding support to FTOs as a priority 
sector, with the M inistry of Finance and it has also taken up relevant issues with State 
Governments and Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. The Committee recommends that the 
issues may be forcefully taken up with the concerned stakeholders and the Committee may also 
be apprised of the progress in this regard. The Committee also recommends that keeping in view 
of the Atmanirbhar Bharat, sufficient Flight Training Organisations (FTOs) may be established 
in various parts of the country to ensure that our boys and girls are not going to foreign 
countries to get pilot training.  
(Para 55) 
5.1 Reply of the Ministry 
i) There are currently 35 DGCA -approved Flying Training Organisations (FTO) in the 
country.  IGRUA at Amethi (UP) is under the administrative control of the Central 
Government. Eight FTOs are under State Governments and 26 are owned by the private 
sector. Indian FTOs had 229 aircraft for flying training as on 30 Nov 2021.  
ii) The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) follows a five -phase certification 
process for setting up a FTO to check all the laid down rules and regulations. The 
Directorate of Flying T raining (DFT) at DGCA conducts scheduled annual inspections 
and unscheduled spot checks at FTOs.  
iii) India had 28 FTOs as on 31 st March 2016.  The number of FTOs was above 40 in 2015, 
but was reduced drastically after a comprehensive review of all FTOs by DGCA in 2015 
and subsequent closure of FTOs that did not meet the specified requirements.  

47 
 
iv) From 28 FTOs in March 2016, the number of FTOs is likely to increase to 43 by 
December 2022 and to 58 by December 2023, that is, an over 100% increase in a matter 
of two years.  
v) Airports Authority of India (AAI), on 25 September 2020, approved a liberalised Flying 
Training Organisations (FTO) policy wherein the concept of airport royalty (revenue 
share payment by FTOs to AAI) was abolished and land rental charges were 
significantly rationalised.   
vi) Under the old policy, around 13% royalty was charged on FTO revenue and land rentals 
were linked to local land rates.  These contributed to the financial distress, closure of 
training operations and long-drawn legal disputes between the FTOs and AAI.   
vii) Due to the investor-friendly liberalised FTO policy, AAI received bids for all nine FTO 
slots in March 2021 despite the airline sector going through a serious financial crisis due 
to Covid.   
viii) AAI issued award letters on 31 May 2021  and 29 October 2021 for nine FTOs to be 
established at five airports at Belagavi (Karnataka), Jalgaon (Maharashtra), Kalaburagi 
(Karnataka), Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) and Lilabari (Assam). Soft launch of two 
FTOs at Kalaburagi was done on 15 August 2021 and at Lilabari on 12 April 2022.  
ix) In the second round of FTO creation, tender process is in progress for establishing 15 
FTOs at 10 Airports viz Cooch Behar, Tezu, Jharsuguda, Deoghar, Meerut, Kishangarh, 
Hubli, Kadapa, Bhavnagar and Salem Airports. 
x) DGCA has introduced new Online On Demand Examination (OLODE) for the AME 
and flight crew (FC) candidates with effect from November 2021. These license 
examinations provide an opportunity to the candidates to choose date and time to appear 
in the examination as per his/her choice on the available slots of the examinations. 
xi) DGCA has modified its regulations to empower Flying Instructors with the right to 
authorise flight operations at FTOs. This will help increase the flying hours and aircraft 
utilisation at each FTO and lead to faster completion of the CPL requirements. 
xii) Currently there is no shortage of pilots in the country. However, there is a shortage of 
commanders on certain types of aircraft and the same is being managed by utilizing 
foreign pilots by issuing Foreign Aircrew Temporary Authorization (FATA). Currently, 
there are 87 FATA holders in India.  

48 
 
xiii) Currently, there are around 9,000 pilots employed with various airline operators in 
India. Given the fleet projections, it is felt that India may require aroun d 1000 pilots per 
annum over the next five years.

xviii) The number of CPL holders produced by Indian FTOs in 2021 is 504, an all-time high.  
xix) The good performance by Indian FTOs in 2021 is despite severe disruptions due to the 
Covid second wave, Cyclone Yaas, Cyclone Tauktae, early onset of monsoons and a 
rising cost of imported aviation fuel. 
xx) Typically, around 40% of Indian CPL holders do their flying training at a foreign FTO.  
Based on stakeholder feedback, the cost of doing flying training abroad is around Rs. 
1.2-1.5 crore per cadet.  This works out to a direct loss of foreign exchange to t he tune 
of Rs. 500 crore annually.  The multiplier effect in terms of loss of revenue and jobs on 
account of this exodus is far higher and needs to be reversed, under the Atmanirbhar 
Bharat Abhiyan.  

49 
 
xxi) Cost of AvGas used by FTOs is a challenge. AvGas is not manufactured in India and 
hence we are completely dependent on imports. The IGST levied on import of AvGas is 
18%, additionally 18% GST is levied on the sale of AvGas.  The landed price for FTOs 
works out to Rs. 184.5 per litre as on March 9, 2022.  
xxii) Cost of AvGas is at a 98% premium to the cost price of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), 
which is being sold to airlines at Rs. 94 per liter at Delhi, as on March 3, 2022. It may 
be noted that, to begin with, the cost of ATF in India itself is one of the highest in t he 
world. 
xxiii) In value terms, the IGST earned by the Government from AvGas imports is a mere Rs. 
3-5 crore per annum.  The tax levied on AvGas is ultimately recovered from a small 
base of flying schools. These flying schools have no option but to  charge the students. It 
increases the cost of training for students. In order to make cost of training affordable to 
children from all the sections of our society and not just the affluent, it is important to 
reduce IGST/GST on import and sale of AvGas to „Zero‟ or a bare minimum level. 
xxiv) Ministry of Civil Aviation has requested Ministry of Finance to consider requesting the 
GST Council to reduce the IGST and GST levied on import of AvGas from 18% to zero 
or one percent; This, along with various measures being undertaken by the Ministry of 
Civil Aviation will go a long way in making our FTOs stronger and India a global 
training hub by 2030. 
xxv) Under Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan, Indian Oil is planning to produce AvGas at Koyali 
Refinery located in Vadodara (Gujarat).  The first  batch of AvGas is expected to be 
dispatched in June 2022, subject to quality certification by competent authorities.

51 
 
Facility of Aerobridges 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that despite charging passengers, 
PBB or aerobridge facilities are not being used by private airlines to reduce operational cost. 
Due to this, passengers, especially the aged ones have to bear the brunt and have to climb the 
stairs of the parking stand to board an aircraft. The Committee deplores this apathetic and 
unreasonable attitude of the private airlines and strongly recommends that its circular on the 
aforesaid subject may be strictly enforced. The Committee also recomme nds that regular 
surprise checks should also be carried out by the Ministry to ensure compliance of the circular 
and in case there is a default, the concerned private airlines should be penalized. 
(Para 76) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 DGCA has discussed the matter with airport &airline operators. The airlines have 
informed that the usage of Bridge Mount Equipment (such as Aerobridges) at  airports are 
attributed to commercial issues i.e. at times it adds to financial burden and increases turn -around 
time of the aircrafts and hence is not commercially viable to use such facilities at airports. Since 
this is a  commercial issue between an airport & an airline and it does not affect the safety of 
operations, DGCA/Ministry cannot issue directions for mandatory usage  of Bridge Mount 
Equipment (PCA/FEGP) at airports. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
7.2 The Committee notes that the DGCA/Ministry cannot issue directions to airport or 
airlines for mandatory usage of aerobridges at airports which causes major issues to 
passengers, especially the aged ones.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
the Ministry may at least issue necessary instructions to all the airports/ airlines to provide 
assistance to aged/differently abled passengers to board an aircraft  with the usage of 
passenger boarding ramps, wheelchairs and hydraulic lifts.        
 
Seaplane Policy 
Recommendation/Observation 

52 
 
8. The Committee expresses serious concern that the seaplane policy is still not in place and 
is still being finalized in consultation with stakeholders. The Committee also laments the fact that 
the first seaplane that was operationalized, was stopped due to technical reasons. It expresses 
concern at the lack of seriousness of the Ministry, as regards Seaplane policy. The Com mittee 
has repeatedly pointed out the need for Seaplane policy in view of the fact that our country is 
endowed with rivers and lakes. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a feasibility study 
may be conducted in the North -Eastern Region for operation o f Seaplanes in the big lakes and 
rivers of the North -Eastern Region. The Committee also stresses on the expeditious finalization 
of Seaplane policy. It also recommends that proper planning should be done before start of the 
operations, so that the operations are not halted. 
(Para 94) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 India has about 400 airstrips lying unused and about 7500 km long coastline. As such, 
there is vast potential to operationalise these airstrips and coastline with small aeroplanes, 
helicopters and seaplanes to provide last mile air connectivity to the common people living in far 
flung and remote areas of the country. 
 
8.2 Accordingly, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) after extensive consultations with 
States/ UTs, Airlines and other key stakeholders of  the Industry has proposed to promote small 
aircraft operations including seaplanes and helicopters with more focus to the small aircraft 
operations for last mile connectivity and introduce a sub-scheme under UDAN. 
 
8.3 Small Aircraft Scheme (SAS) includin g the operation of seaplane has been issued by the 
Honourable Minister of Civil Aviation launched on 26.03.2022 at WINGS Hyderabad.  As per 
the provisions for Seaplanes in SAS, proposals are being invited from airlines under the special 
round of bidding UDA N 4.2 for cancelled routes of previous rounds and the Sea Plane routes 
proposed by Sagarmala. Start date of submission of the bid is 28.04.2022. 
 
Further Recommendation/ Observation 
8.4 The Committee notes that Small Aircraft Scheme (SAS) which includes the 
operation of Seaplane was launched on 26.03.2022 , however a Seaplane Policy has yet not 

53 
 
been finalized by the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendation 
that a S eaplane Policy may be formulated expeditiously in consultation with various 
stakeholders, which will provide last mile air connectivity to the common people living in 
far flung and remote areas of the country. The Committee also desires to know the status of 
the bidding process for the seaplane routes proposed by Sagarmala.

The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Por ts, 
Shipping & Waterways on the recommendations/observations as contained in its Three 
Hundred and Sixteenth Report on „Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of the Ministry of Ports, 
Shipping & Waterways ‟ which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 14th 
March, 2022. 
 
2. The Action Taken Replies were received from the Ministry on 20th June, 202 2 in 
respect of all the recommendations/observations contained in the Report. The replies ha ve 
been categorized as follows:-

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes a significant gap in the overall budgetary allocation of the 
Ministry in the Financial Year ( F.Y.) 2022 -23 as compared to its projected requirements. 
Against the proposed demand for Rs. 2542.43 Crores in B.E. 2022 -23, only Rs. 1709.50 
Crores have been allocated, registering a shortfall of Rs. 832.93 Crores i.e. 32.76% of the 
overall budgetary requirement of the Ministry for the F.Y. 22-23, and is certain to have an 
adverse bearing on the implementation of various port projects of the Ministry. The 
Committee observes that under several crucial heads such as Sagarmala Development 
Company, Indian Maritime University, Kolkata Port Trust, Inland Water Transport etc., 
significantly lesser allocation/no allocation has been made against the projected demand of 
the Ministry. The Committee desires to be apprised of the different schemes/projects under its 
ambit which will be adversely affected because of the shortfall in B.E. 2022-23 along with the 
course of action planned by the Ministry to deal with this shortfall. The Committee observes 
that the growth of In dia‟s maritime sector is of paramount importance and needs to be 
accelerated to strengthen our position of eminence in the global maritime sector. Since the 
Ministry has to play a vital role in shaping India‟s maritime prowess into an engine of 
economic development, availability of adequate financial resources is a prerequisite towards 
propelling India to the forefront of the global maritime sector. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should ensure a good pace of utilization of allocated funds in 
initial quarters of F.Y. 2022-23, deploy their resources in a more efficient way and request 
the Ministry of Finance to enhance budgetary allocation at the R.E. 2022-23 stage so that the 
various programmes and projects that the Ministry has planned for F.Y. 22-23 can stay on 
course. 
(Para 6) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1. Under Sagarmala Scheme funds have been allocated for development of projects
