2 
 
 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
II) ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. From a perusal of Table No. 2, the Committee is constrained to note that there is a 
substantial underutilization of the budgeted funds during the FY 2021 -22. Against the RE 2021 -
22 allocation of Rs. 969.80 crore, only 47.70% amounting to Rs. 462.55 crore could be spent till 
the 31st January, 2022. It means that the remaining expenditure would have to be squeezed in 
the last two months of FY 2021 -22. Since as per norms stipulated by the Ministry of Finance, 
there is a ceiling o f 25% on expenditure in the last quarter, occurrence of huge savings is a 
certainty. It may be pertinent to mention here that a zero based budgeting exercise which 
requires that budget request be evaluated thoroughly, starting from zero base, is in practic e and 
the financial outlays are earmarked based on factors like past trend of expenditure, stages of 
formulation/implementation of various projects, the pre -projects approvals etc. Therefore, 
savings of Rs. 1056.97 crore vis -à-vis the BE 2021 -22 allocation  not only betrays fiscal 
indiscipline by way of underutilization of the earmarked funds which will have an adverse 
bearing on infrastructure development oriented activities of the Ministry, but is also indicative of 
shortcomings in budgetary planning and m onitoring of the budgeted funds. The Committee 
observes that a resource constrained country like India cannot afford to keep a vast chunk of its 
resources locked up and surrendered towards the end of the financial year. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends  that realistic projection of fund requirements should be given utmost 
priority at the highest level of the Ministry so that the Budget Estimates are formulated with 
application of proper financial yardsticks and large variations between the Budget Estimat es, 
Revised Estimates and Actual Expenditure needs to be avoided. The Ministry must also pay 
attention to streamlining its monitoring mechanism and ensure optimal and more efficient 
deployment and utilization of its financial resources for smooth execution  of its programmes 
within the approved cost and designated timeline. 
(Para 20) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The observations/recommendations of the Hon‟ble Committee have been taken note of.  
It is submitted that during the financial year 2021 -2022, against the RE allocation of Rs. 969.80 
crores, the Ministry could incur expenditure to the tune of Rs. 803.90 crores, which comes to 

3 
 
 
82.89%. There are a several reasons which led to less expenditure by the Ministry during the first 
two quarters of the financial ye ar. The pandemic situation was still prevailing in the country and 
the implementation of various Schemes of the Ministry was severely affected.  Further, the 
Swadesh Darshan Scheme was under review by the Government and no new projects we re 
sanctioned during the year. The Global Media Publicity was not carried out due to the pandemic 
situation and ban on operation of international commercial flights resulting in  lack of 
international tourism. 
1.2 Major two schemes of the Ministry of Tourism viz. Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD are 
being implemented by the State/UT Governments and further release of the fund depends based 
on timely utilisation of fund earlier provided.  
1.3 Pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee, suitable instructions were g iven to 
the Program Divisions of the Ministry to apply due diligence while projecting budgetary 
requirements. The Ministry is closely monitoring the expenditure status periodically at the 
highest level. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee also takes a serious note of keeping the unspent provision of Rs. 1056.97 
crore till the close of financial year 2021 -22 despite reduction in the budgetary outlay at the RE 
2021-22 stage, in disregard of the provisions of General Financial Rules requiring the unsp ent 
provisions in a grant to be surrendered to the Ministry of Finance as soon as these are foreseen, 
without waiting for the last day of the financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry should exercise greater fiscal prudence, an d ensure that unspent budgetary 
provisions are surrendered timely in future. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The observations/recommendations of the Committee are noted for compliance in future.  
It is, however, submitted that the allocations under RE and BE were decided by the Ministry of 
Finance at the RE Meeting held in October, 2021 and the Ministry of Financ e is aware of the 
additional resources available by way of cut imposed on the BE allocation of the Ministry. After 
communication of the RE/BE ceiling, and before communication of the Technical Surrender, the 
Ministry is required thoroughly review the alloc ation to be made to each Scheme/components of 
a Scheme and Non -Scheme activities keeping in view the reduced allocation. It is humbly 
submitted that the Ministry of Tourism has 20 Domestic and 7 Overseas Offices under it besides 
the Ministry. It operates s everal Schemes and there a number of components under different 
Schemes.  Also the non-Scheme segment has a number of activities spread over the Ministry, all 
India Tourism Offices and Overseas Offices. The technical surrender of funds would have to be 

4 
 
 
done Scheme -wise/Head-wise and before intimating the surrender, the actual requirement of 
funds, based on the RE allocation, under different Heads of Account - both Scheme and Non -
Scheme is required to be assessed based of inputs from all the concerned agenci es. Once the 
funds are surrendered to the Ministry of Finance, Head -wise, no further adjustment would be 
possible. Accordingly, intimation of the Technical surrender of funds took some time. However, 
as per the recommendation of the Committee, the Ministry  would certainly make all efforts to 
intimate the technical surrender at the earliest. 
 
 
III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee observes that despite the fact that India offers a diverse portfolio for 
travel and touris m, the share of India's International Tourist Arrivals (ITAs) in the ITAs of the 
world was merely 1.57 per cent in 2020. There is increased competition among various countries 
to attract foreign visitors. There is, therefore, an imperative need for India t o prepare suitable 
market strategy to attract foreign visitors. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Ministry in collaboration with a professional body should carry out market research of foreign 
tourist source markets to identify the expectations , requirements, psychographics, demographics 
and many other aspects of a foreign tourist willing to travel to India, thereby enabling to create 
a strategic plan to revive inbound tourism. The research should be conducted with an objective 
to provide an aut hentic feedback, roadmap and recommendations to the Ministry of Tourism 
with respect to inbound tourism in India and provide a blueprint on the various policy objectives 
and infrastructure development needed to strengthen inbound tourism in the country. 
(Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted. 
 
 
 
 
 

5 
 
 
V. INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF TOURIST CIRCUITS AROUND SPECIFIC  
THEMES (SWADESH DARSHAN) 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee recommends that the various circuits under the Swadesh Darshan 
Scheme should be developed using the Hub and Spoke Model which can draw tourists from the 
popular religious destinations towards other unexplored destinations that are positioned near 
the major destinations. 
(Para 80) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The suggestion of the Committee is noted. 
4.2 The Ministry of Tourism has now revamped its Swadesh Darshan Scheme in the form of 
Swadesh Darshan 2.0. As per the guidelines, the vision of the Swadesh Darshan 2.0. is to 
develop sustainable and responsible tourism desti nations in the country  and with the mission to 
create a robust framework for integrated development of tourism destinations in partnership with 
the States/UTs and local governments for promoting sustainable and responsible tourism in the 
country. 
4.3 As per the guidelines for  SD 2.0, the States will prepare a S tate Perspective Plan 
analysing tourism potential of various destinations based on the following: 
(i) Major tourism attractions, offerings and themes; 
(ii) Connectivity by Air, Rail and Road including local travel; 
(iii) Connectivity to any tourist circuit; 
(iv) Current tourism eco system at the destination; 
(v) Future tourism potential at the destination; and 
(vi) State support for the destination 
 
4.4 The Ministry will select 2 -3 destinations of the State for development based on the State 
Perspective Plan and availability of funds. 
 
 
VIII. CRUISE TOURISM 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee observes that despite being endowed with 7500 km coastline and a vast 
network of lakes and rivers, and a steady increase in the number of ships and cruise passengers 

6 
 
 
calling on Indian ports over the past few years, cruise tourism in India is still at a nascent stage. 
Though various initiatives have been taken by the Ministries of Tourism and Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways to develop India as destination as well as source market for cruise tourism and 
increase the number of cruise shipping calls  and passenger arrivals, India's enormous cruise 
potential still remains untapped. While appreciating the initiatives taken by the Ministries of 
Tourism and Posts, Shipping and Waterways to develop India as an attractive cruise tourism 
destination, the Committee recommends that the following measures may also be taken: 
(i) Training institutions for various services in cruise tourism be developed. 
(ii) The taxation structure in this segment may be revamped to bring down cost for passengers, 
making cruise shipping aff ordable for middle class population that constitute the major 
portion of Indian demographics. This will go a long way in boosting participation of the 
middle class in this segment of tourism. 
(iii) Synergy between the various stakeholders of this industry like c ruise companies; tour 
operators, and immigration and customs departments may be utilised to optimise the gains 
for all. 
(iv) An effective promotional campaign be developed to put Indian Cruise industry on the 
Global map. 
(Para 98) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 Recommendations of the Committee are noted. 
 
IX. DOMESTIC PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY (DPPH) SCHEMEINCLUDING  
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee observes that in most countries with a large population, domestic tourism 
is the foundation of a vibrant tourism industry. India also has a strong domestic tourism base 
which is evident from the fact that Domestic tourism visits were 2321.98 million during 2019. 
However, owing to the prolonged COVID -19 pandemic, the erstwhile booming tourism and 
hospitality sector has taken a severe beating due to which the number of domestic tourists 
slumped to 610.22 million during 2020 registering a negative growth of 73.3%. The trajectory of 
international tourism remains uncertain because new COVID -19 variants are emerging in some 
parts of the world due to which new restrictions are being introduced. With the rapid pace of the 
nation-wide COVID vaccination, the revival of the Indian economy has gained momentum and 
Indian tourist destinations have ri sen to prominence as a result of strong pent -up demand and 

7 
 
 
the relaxation of domestic restrictions. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the publicity 
campaigns of the Ministry should be focused on following safety protocols and helping restore 
confidence among tourists and promoting domestic tourism. 
(Para 106) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 It is submitted that the Ministry of Tourism  through in its social media handles, 
undertook campaigns focusing on following in safety protocols and promoting India as a safe 
destination for tourists to visit and highlighting the latest Covid-19 protocols for travelling to and 
within India. The social media handles are also being used to bring forward and highlight many 
lesser known destinations all over the country so that domestic tourists can have many more 
options. 
6.2 Further, the recommendations of the Committee have also been noted for compliance. 
  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee observes that high net worth Indian nationals opt for foreign tourism 
instead of domestic tourism. One of the reasons behind this is the exhaustion of the timeworn 
tourist destinations and absence of new avenues. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
unexplored and unexploited tourist destinations should be identified, developed and marketed to 
revive the curiosity of high -end domestic tourists and the publicity campaign should aim at 
persuading high end domestic tourists to substitute domestic tourism for foreign tourism. 
(Para 108) 
Reply of the Ministry 
7.1 The suggestion of the Committee is noted. 
7.2 Domestic tourism holds substantial promise for the growth of  tourism in the country, 
which can significantly contribute to the Indian economy. The Government has launched 
“Dekho Apna Desh”, a major campaign for promoting domestic tourism.  The Ministry of 
Tourism has now revamped its Swadesh Darshan scheme in the fo rm of Swadesh Darshan 2.0 . 
As per the guidelines, the vision of the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 is to  develop sustainable and 
responsible tourism destinations in the country. The Scheme will focus on developing Tier -II 
and Tier-III destinations to create more opportunities for domestic travellers. 
 
X HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
7. The Committee notes that tourism is a labour -intensive industry and a multi -sector 

8 
 
 
activity characterized by multiple services provided by a range of suppliers and,  therefore, this 
sector has huge potential for generation of jobs and absorption of a substantially higher 
workforce. The Committee notes from the Market Pulse data supplied by the Ministry , that the 
hospitality and allied sectors face huge deficit in trai ned manpower. As against annual 
requirement of 902890 for 2022, the total supply including attrition is only 84128 and the 
demand-supply gap is to the extent of 818762. Tourism sector is likely to witness a boom post 
pandemic because there is lot of pent-up demand for travel. This boom may bring an exponential 
demand for the workforce at managerial, supervisor and skilled levels in hospitality and tourism 
sector. This leads the Committee to the irresistible conclusion that the existing institutional 
capacities would be unable to fulfill the estimated additional requirement of manpower in the 
hospitality 80 and allied sectors. The Committee is of the view that since training is a key 
intervention and issues of human resource development and capacity building are extremely 
important, the r ealization of the country's huge, barely tapped tourism potential cannot be 
realized without addressing the challenges of capacity constraints. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry should adopt a proactive interventionist approach to give  a major 
boost to the various initiatives relating to human resource development for the hospitality and 
tourism sector through convergence with the private sector. 
(Para 120) 
Reply of the Ministry 
8.1 Noted for compliance. 
8.2 Ministry of Tourism is imple menting Scheme for Capacity Building for Service Provider 
under which various private institutions have been involved to conduct various capacity-building 
programs. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

9 
 
 
 
CHAPTER-II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
II) ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2022-23 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that although there has been marginal increase in the budgetary 
outlay for the Ministry from Rs. 2026.77 crore for FY 2021-22 to Rs. 2400.00 crore for FY 2022-
23, it is still lesser than the BE 2020 -21 allocation of Rs. 2499.83 crore. Though the BE 2022-23 
allocation is 18 -41% higher than the BE 2021 -22 outlay, there is a substantial shortfall of Rs. 
537.92 crore vis-à-vis the projected demand of Rs. 2937.92 crore by the Ministry for FY 2022 -23 
and that too at a time when this sector is reeling under losses in the wake of COVID -19 
pandemic. The Committee notes that this budgetary outlay for 2022 -23 has been reduced to Rs 
416 crore as compared to the BE 2021 -22 of Rs. 668.72 crore under the head - Promotion and 
Publicity. The Committee find s this reduction alarming because the tourism and hospitality 
sector has been hit the hardest by COVID-19 pandemic and with massive job and revenue losses,

Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 The Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance has examined the matter. The 
comments are submitted as under:   
2.2 Export of Services is defined at section 2(6) of the IGST Act, 2017 as " the supply of any 
service when the supplier of service is located in India; the recipient of service is located outside 
India; the place of supply of service is outside India; the payment for such se rvice has been 
received by supplier of service in convertible foreign exchange...... and the supplier of service 
and the recipient of service are not merely establishments of a distinct person....".  Thus, there 
are few conditions for service to qualify as export. In the issue under consideration, place of 
supply of tour operator service is the place where the service is performed. The place of supply 
of hotel accommodation service is the location of the premise. Accordingly, such services do not 
qualify as export as place of supply is not outside India. 
2.3 Tour operator services supplied to a foreign touri st are also not zero rated as “ zero rated 
supply” means any of the following supplies of goods o r services or both, namely: -(a) export of 
goods or services or both; or (b) supply of goods or services or both to a special Economic Zone 
developer or a special Economic Zone developer or a special Economic Zone unit"  (Section 16 
of IGST Act, 2017 refers). 
2.4 Only supply of goods manufactured in India to certain specific recipients are classified 
as deemed exports under section 147 of the CGST Act , 2017 . “Deemed exports ” means such 
supplies of goods as may be notified under Section 147. ( Section 2(39) of the CGST Act, 2017 
refers). 
2.5 The GST Council in its 47 th meeting held on 28 th and 29th June, 2022 has recommended 
relief to the tour operators by recommending the foreign component of a tour provided to foreign

III) CONTRIBUTION OF TOURISM TO GDP 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee notes that as per the World Travel and Tourism Council (WTTC), prior to 
the COVID -19 pandemic, Travel and Tourism accounted for 10.4% of global GDP. In many 
parts of the world, tourism is a major engine of growth. The Committee in its 275 th Report 
presented to the Parliament on the 3 rd March, 2020 had noted that the contribution of tourism to 
national GDP was over 10% for most countries where tourism happens to be the main driver of 
national economy. However, in India which has unique endowments of biodiversity, forests, 
rivers, its rich culture and heritage and many World Heritage sites, the tourism sector has not 

22 
 
 
proved to be the proverbial engine of growth for our economy. This is evident from the fact that 
India's total share in global international arrivals remains a modest 1.57% against the target of 
3 per cent s et by the NITI Aayog to be achieved by 2022. Similarly, the contribution (direct and 
indirect) of tourism in the GDP and the total jobs in the country are estimated to be 5.16 per cent 
and 15.34 per cent respectively during 2019 -20. The Committee is of the  firm view that if India 
has to move towards becoming a USD 5 trillion economy and a global economic powerhouse, as 
envisioned by our Hon'ble PM Shri Narendra Modi, then the contribution of tourism to India's 
GDP has to be raised from the current 5.16% to 10% in the next five years. The Committee, 
while welcoming the various measures taken by the Ministry to double the contribution of 
tourism to India's GDP, feels that the vast untapped potential of India as a tourism destination 
cannot be realized unless t ourism is included in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India. 
Taking note of the fact that Travel and Tourism does not figure in the Centre, State or 
Concurrent Lists and since in a federal polity like ours, the responsibility for policy making a nd 
implementation of tourism projects are fra gmented across different levels -Central and State 
Governments and coordination between them is often lacking due to absence of clearly defined 
mandate, the Committee in its 288 th Report had recommended inclusion  of tourism in the 
Concurrent List. Since tourism is yet to be included in the Concurrent List, the Committee 
reiterates its recommendation for inclusion of tourism in the Concurrent List of the Constitution 
of India. The Committee is convinced that this w ill go a long way in channelizing the 
development of tourism and positioning and maintaining tourism development as a national 
priority. 
(Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Travel & Tourism Sector has backward and forward linkages with other sectors of the  
economy, like transport, construction, handicrafts, manufacturing, horticulture, agriculture and 
involves multiple issues falling under the purview of both Centre and State Governments. 
Ministry of Tourism being the nodal Ministry for the development of t ourism sector in the 
country has set up several mechanisms for holding consultations with the State Governments, 
Central Ministries and private stakeholders on different subjects to create convergence and 
synergy across multiple agencies and programme for the development & growth of tourism 
sector in the country. These steps have been able to create robust mechanism for facilitating the 
implementation of the tourism policies and programmes, resulting in the growth of the tourism 
sector over the years. The F oreign Tourist Arrivals (FTAs) increased from 5.78 Million in 2010 
to 10.93 Million in 2019. Similarly, Foreign Exchange Earnings (FEEs) from Tourism increased 

23 
 
 
from Rs. 66,172 crore in 2010 to Rs.2,11,661 crore in 2019. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
2.2 The reply of the Ministry does not address the issue. The Committee has time and 
again raised the matter of inclusion of Tourism in Concurrent List in its previous 
recommendations (refer to Para 4.2 of the 298 th Report and Para 72 of the 288 th Report of 
the Committee). The Committee is of the view that inclusion of Tourism in the Concurrent 
List will help in simplifying the issues of the pandemic -hit Indian Tourism Sector since 
tourism is a multi -sectoral activit y and inclusion of tourism in the Concurr ent List will 
play an important role in facilitating the issues involved with multiple Ministries/ 
Organisations at Central level as well as with the States/Union Territories to create 
convergence and synergy of actions across multiple agencies and program mes. The 
Ministry should inform the Committee whether any action has been taken by the Ministry 
on this longstanding recommendation of the Committee. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee observes that Emirate of Dubai does not have the abundant wealth of 
natural oil reserves and nor does it have a pre -existing plethora of natural, historical and 
internationally significant tourist sites. Despite that, it has emerged as a multi -billion dollar 
economy and amongst the world's most visited tourist de stinations, all based on the 
Government's tourism centric approach towards national policy making. The Committe e wishes 
that India should also endeavour  to imbibe creating potential for tourism in the very core of its 
policy making. Although tourism is an important activity in India, its share in global market is 
extremely small and the potential of tourism sector in India is yet to be unleashed. The actual 
implementation of tourist projects takes place at State/UT level but in most of the States/UTs, the 
outlay for Department of Tourism is meager. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in 
order to give policy push to the tourism industry, a National Tourism Council chaired by the 
Prime Minister and composed of Chief Ministers or Tourism Ministers of all States should be 
established. This National Council should be an empowered legislative body on the lines of GST 
Council. This will enable fast -track Centre-State level tourism decision making, leveraging and 
utilizing full synergies of India's tourism potential across all our States.

5. The Committee observes that the tourism and hospitality industry is one of the worst hit 
sectors by COVID -19 pandemic and is in huge financial distress. The highly infectious novel 
coronavirus continues to thwart the sector as new COVID -19 variants keep on  emerging. Apart 
from providing mass employment, income and foreign exchange for the country, this sector has 
an economically beneficial cascading impact on other sectors such as airlines, infrastructure, 
transportation, accommodation, facilitations systems, etc. As per data furnished by the Ministry, 
during the year 2019 -20, this sector provided 79.86 million jobs directly and indirectly and 
generated 5.16% of India's GDP. As per the data furnished by the Ministry in the Table 9 above, 
the potential job lo ss in tourism has been estimated to be 20.8% in the year 2020 falling from 
4.01 crore in 2019 to 3.17 crore in 2020 and the total revenue loss suffered by the hospitality 
sector has been estimated to be Rs. 89,813 crore in 2020. Therefore, this sector need s an urgent 
boost for revival. The Committee notes that a proposal of the Ministry of Tourism regarding 
grant of infrastructure status to investment in hotel industry of Capex over Rs. 25 crore 
(excluding land) is under consideration of the Department of E conomic Affairs since long. The 
Committee observes that construction of hotels is highly capital intensive and it takes long for 
hotel projects to reach operational profitability. COVID has aggravated this and the current 
crisis is threatening the existenc e of hotel business for organizations in the Hospitality Sector 
because availability of lending by banks and financial institutions that have turned risk averse, 
especially towards hospitality sector, have reduced for contact-intensive sectors. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that hotel projects with Capex above Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) be 
accorded infrastructure status and included in the Infrastructure list of the RBI so that long term 
funds are accessible at lower interest rates and the gap bet ween return expectations and debt 

26 
 
 
cost is bridged. The Committee is of the view that according of infrastructure  status to hotel 
projects with C apex above Rs. 25 crore will not only help build quality accommodation supply, 
but will also have an enormous ec onomic multiplier effect across the length and breadth of the 
country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the policy stance of the Government in this 
matter be spelt out within three months from the presentation of this Report.

5.1 The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance.

above Rs. 25 crore (excluding land) to the sector will reduce the operating costs for 
hospitality players through subsidized rates of electricity and water charges, property tax, 
development tax etc. and also attract investments in the Sector. The Committee is confident 
that this move will fuel the Indian economy to achieve „atmanirbharta‟ in the post-
pandemic future.

6. The Committee takes note of the submissions made for relief measures for the survival of 
the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry. The Committee is aware that the Reserve Bank of 
India had consti tuted an Expert Committee with Shri K.V. Kamath as the Chairman to make 
recommendations on the required financial Parameters in respect of borrowers eligible under 
the COVID Resolution Framework and the recommendations of the Expert Committee on the key 
financial parameters, i.e., Total Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net Worth; Total Debt/ 
EBITA; Current Ratio; Debt Service Coverage Ratio; and Average Debt Service Coverage Ratio 
had been accepted by the Reserve Bank of India. The Committee has been inf ormed that the 
timeline to achieve the four ratios has been moved from March, 2022 to September, 2022. 
However, the deadline for the most important financial metric, i.e., Total Outside Liabilities/ 
Adjusted Total Net Worth has remained unchanged, i.e., Ma rch 2022. The Committee observes 
that the Indian economy has encountered a "once in a century" crisis due to COVID -19 

27 
 
 
pandemic and the Travel, Tourism and Hospitality Industry is one of the hardest hit, revival from 
which is unlikely to happen for the next 3-4 years because India is already facing a third wave of 
infections driven by the Omicron variant and tourists' footfall has come down significantly due to 
the vicious cycle of restrictions in the wake of COVID -19. The possibility of many more such 
waves and new variants of coronavirus emerging in India cannot be ruled out. On account of the 
above factors, the Travel and Hospitality Industry has witnessed a huge dip in business. Since 
the Tourism and Hospitality Sector is a major engine of economic growth  in terms of growth of 
GDP, forex earnings and employment generation, it is imperative that the revival of this sector 
should be at the forefront of the efforts of the Government. There is, therefore, an imperative 
need for Government to pull this sector o ut of the COVID -19 recessionary conditions. The 
Committee, therefore, lends its Parliamentary support to the demand of the Travel, Tourism and 
Hospitality industry and recommends that in view of the adverse impact of the third wave of 
COVID-19 pandemic and  the resultant recessionary conditions and the difficulties faced in 
revival of businesses and meeting the operational requirements, the deadline for achievement of 
all five financial parameters, i.e., (i) Total Outside Liabilities/ Adjusted Total Net wort h, (ii) 
Total Debt/ EBITA, (iii) Current Ratio, (iv) Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) and (v) 
Average Debt Service Coverage Ratio under the Resolution Framework relating to operational 
performance of borrowing entities be deferred to September, 2023 and the repayment schedule 
be extended from December 2022 to December, 2023.

IV) IMPACT OF COVID -19 PANDEMIC ON TOURISM, TRAVEL AND

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that Finance Act, 2020 which was announced just before the start 
of COVID -19 crisis, inter alia, came up with new insertion of Tax Collected at Source (TCS) 
provisions under Section 206C (1 G) (a) of Income Tax Act, 1961 pertaining to TC S @ 5% on 
foreign remittance through Liberalized Remittance Scheme (LRS) and under Section 206C 
(1G)(b) pertaining to TCS@5% on selling of overseas tour packages by tour operators. The 
Indian Tour Operators face challenges to match the prices offered for o utbound tours in 
comparison to foreign tour service providers due to additional burden of taxes which include 
GST and newly inserted TCS provisions under Section 206C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 
because overseas agents and Online Travel Agents (OTAs) do no t charge the same since their 
base is out of India. The Committee is of the view that the above TCS provisions will not only 
increase the cost of packages sold by Indian tour operators, they will also shift all sales of 
outbound tourism to overseas suppliers, thereby denying the Government of income tax and GST 
revenue. These newly inserted TCS provisions, therefore, are detrimental to tourism business in 
India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to allow domestic tour operators a 
level playing field in comparison with foreign tour operators in the market of outbound tourism, 
the above mentioned TCS provisions be rolled back. The Committee is of the view that once TCS 
on outbound tourism is withdrawn, it will enable the Indian Travel Agents and Tour Operators to 
stage a recovery post the pandemic. 
(Para 70)

(Para 19.3) 
 With the government‟s agg ressive campaigning of „Make in India‟ and the 
accelerated growth in the economy, the demand for skilled manpower in the country has 
risen. The Committee is constrained to note that against the target of 63,600, only 20,729 
persons have been trained/certified so far. The Committee is of the view that training adds 
structure to an organization/industry‟s learning and development of employees and 
shortage in the trained and skilled workforce may lead to lower customer satisfaction of 
the tourists. The Committee recommends the Ministry to adopt appropriate mechanisms to 
achieve the set target and utilize the „demographic dividend‟ through vigorous branding 
and facilitating the active involvement of PPP since there is a huge scope of generation and 
supply of skilled workforce in India. 
(Para 20.3) 
XI. ASSISTANCE TO CENTRAL AGENCIES FOR TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE  
DEVELOPMENT 
 The Committee may be apprised of the status and outcome of the meeting of the 
Task Force constituted under the Chairmanship of the Secretary, M/o Tourism and the 
steps taken by the Ministry to address the various issues related to tourism as per the 
recommendations of the SGoS for Tourism Sectoral Plan. 
(Para 21.4) 

57 
 
 
 The Committee applauds the Ministry‟s efforts in developing wayside amenities 
under the Swadesh Darshan Scheme since India is fast evolving as a potential economic 
trigger with the development of wayside amenities along the highways and byways across 
the country, consisting of retail fuel outlets, electric re -charging, eating joints, food courts, 
public conveniences and other commuter friendly services like drive -through food pick up 
points, which will not only support small businesses, create jobs, but will also give a big 
boost to the local economy. The Committee would like to know t he percent progress 
achieved in the Wayside Amenities 2018-19 project - „Development of wayside Amenities in 
Uttar Pradesh and Bihar at Varanasi - Gaya - Kushinagar in collaboration with MoRTH,‟ 
and whether more wayside amenity projects have been taken up in remaining Indian States 
and whether any cooperative mechanisms have been created with other Ministries for the 
same. The Committee also desires to know the status of „State Perspective Plan.‟ 
(Para 22.6) 
MISCELLANEOUS 
 The Committee observes that Asian countries - specifically India, China and the 
Caribbean islands are primary hotspots in the adventure tourism industry right now, apart 
from middle-eastern Europe. India having vast amount of adventure locations and a lot of 
potential in development and ex pansion of the Adventure Tourism, taking initiatives for 
Adventure Tour Operators to enable them to operate without much hassle will go a long 
way. However, competitive market pressures may force the Adventure Tour Operators 
(ATOs) to cut corners and operate “close to the edge” in order to remain financially viable, 
which indicates the short -term perspective for the industry. The Committee therefore 
recommends the Ministry to bring out some mandatory accreditation system to ensure 
adequacy of their infrastr ucture to strengthen safety of tourists in the adventure tour 
locations, especially the high -risk adventure zones across the country.  The Committee also 
recommends formulating appropriate policies/guidelines to address issues of the adventure 
tour operators and so that this sector could have a long -term and sustainable future in the 
Indian tourism industry. 
(Para 23.4)

Introduction 
 The Indian Civil Aviation sector is one of the fastest growing sectors of the country as 
well as of the world today. In terms of domestic air passenger traffic, India is the third largest 
aviation market. The unprecedented growth of the Civil Aviation industry can be gauged from 
the fact that in the domestic routes the number of domestic passengers carried by scheduled 
domestic Indian Carriers has witnessed a growth of 48.9 percent in the year 2022, as compared to 
the previous year 2021 (up to 31 st December, 2021) and while in the International Routes during 
the period January to December , 2022 a total of 43.4 million passengers were carried by 
Scheduled India/ foreign carriers as against 17.2 million in the corresponding period in 2021, 
thereby witnessing a growth of 152.7%.   The number of aircrafts registered in the Civil Aviation 
sector is also likely to reach a figure of 1200 in the next few years from the current figure of 744.  
The freighter aircraft deployed by Indian airlines have increased from 7 (2018) to 28 during the 
last three years (2021). 
2.       The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation highlighted the following vision and objectives of 
the Ministry:- 
 To c reate an environment where the a viation industry is sustainable; affordable; safe;  
internationally competitive; and connects to all parts of India and the World;  
 To expand airport capacity more than five times to handle one billion trips a year; 
 To e nhance the availability and affordability of regional air connectivity the Regional 
Connectivity Scheme – Ude Desh Ka Aam Naagrik (RCS-UDAN); and 
 To ensure that airport tar iffs, taxes on fuel, landing charges, passenger services, cargo and 
other charges are determined in an efficient, fair and transparent manner. 
Mandate of the Ministry 
3.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation of national policies and 
programmes for the development and regulation of the Civil Aviation sector in the country. It is 
responsible for the administr ation of the Aircraft Act, 1934;  Aircraft Rules, 1937 ; and various 
other legislations pertaining to the aviation sect or in the country. In addition to the primary 
functions of framing of policies, the Ministry provides guidance to the organizations in the 
implementation of policy guidelines ; monitors and evaluates their activities ; and also provides 
their interface with Parliament. It also supervises the implementation by the organizations of 
special programmes of the Government, particularly those intended for weaker sections of 
society.

12. The Committee notes that the projected demand of the Ministry for B.E. 2023 -24 
was Rs. 3,532.13 /- crore. The Ministry of Finance reduced it to Rs. 3,113.36 /- crore, which 
indicates a reduction of Rs. 418.77 /- crore. The Budget allocation for 2023 -24 is 66.75% 
lower than R.E. 2022 -23. The Ministry also stated that the Ministry of Finance did not 
assign any reasons for the reduction. However, the requirement of additional funds to meet 
the activities of the Ministry will be taken up at R.E. 2023-24 stage. 
13. The Committee notes that the B.E. allocation for 2023 -24 is Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore, 
which is by far the lowest of all the B.E. allocation in the last five years. In fact, the B.E. 
allocation has been steadily decreasing from Rs. 6,602.86/- crore (2018-19), to Rs. 4,500.00/- 
crore (2019-20), to Rs. 3,797.71/ - crore (2020-21), to Rs. 3,224.67/ - crore (2021-22), barring 
the year 2022 -23 when the Ministry received a B.E. allocation of Rs. 10,667/ - crore on 
account of disinvestment of Air India ., and now the lowest at Rs. 3,113.36/ - crore for B.E. 
(2023-24). These decreasing allocations have been made despite the increasing trend of 
inflation in the country, which implies that the effective allocations are ever lower. Even 
during allocations at R.E. stage, the fund allocation remained below the projected demand 
of the Ministry, other than the year 2021 -22, though the Ministry  has shown a good 
capacity to absorb the funds allocated to it, with percentage expenditure as compared to 
R.E. allocations i.e., as high as 98.96% (2018 -19), 98.56% (2019-20), 99.07% (2020-21) and 
98.99% (2021 -22). For the year 2022 -23, the percentage exp enditure was 86.14% as on 
31.01.2023. The Ministry assured the Committee in its Demands for Grants meeting that 
full utilization of the R.E. allocation would be achieved.  
14. The Committee is of the view that the projected demand of the Ministry reflects the 
expenditure on targets and objecti ves it seeks to achieve in that  particular financial year. 
The Committee is aware that the Civil Aviation Industry had suffered a major setback on 
account of Covid -19 pandemic and needs full budgetary support from the Government at 
this critical juncture, where it has to recover its losses and come up to its earlier level in the 
first instance and then grow at an even faster rate. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry of Finance should favourably consider additional grant of funds to the Ministry at 
R.E. stage, to enable the Ministry to achieve its set targets and achieve the aim of the 
Indian Civil Aviation Industry.  
15. The Committee notes that a major part of the B.E. allocation in the financial yea rs 
2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023 -24 consists of the budgetary allocation towards  the 
disinvestment of Air India, which effectively did not create any asset for the Civil Aviation 
Sector in the long run. The Committee hopes that the trend would be reversed with the 
completion process of the disinvestment of Air India and more focus would be laid towards 
asset creation in the Civil Aviation Sector.

Regional Connectivity Scheme – Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik (RCS-UDAN)  
Introduction and Vision 
16. Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) launched Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) – 
Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik (UDAN) on 21st October, 2016. RCS-UDAN is a flagship programme 
of MoCA. The National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 2016 envisages Regional Air 
Connectivity under Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS).  
17. The primary objecti ve of RCS -UDAN is to facilitate / stimulate regional air connectivity 
and by making it affordable to  masses through measures like : (i) Concessions by Centra l 
Government; State Governments / Union Territories (UTs) ; and Airport Operators to reduce the 
cost of airline operations on regional routes / other support measures and (ii ) Viability Gap 
Funding (VGF) to meet the gap, if any, between the cost of airline operations and expected 
revenues on such routes.  
18. Through his presentation, the Secretary deposed before the Committee that the Ministry 
plans to expand UDAN to 1,000 routes and 100 airports . He further enumerated the following 
particulars of the Scheme:- 
 in four rounds of bidding, 1152 valid routes awarded, covering more than 32 States/UTs; 
 467 routes commenced as on 13.02.2023, connecting 73 RCS airports (including 9 
heliports and 2 water aerodromes); 
 more than 114.53 lakh passengers flown in RCS flights; 
 more than 2,19,000 RCS flights operated under UDAN; 
 4th (including 4.1, 4.2 & 4.3) round of bidding of UDAN undertaken; 
 100 airports and 1000 routes to be operationalized by 2024 and 2026, respectively; and 
 during four round s of bidding, 36 airports identified and 142 valid Fixed wing and 
Helicopter routes are awarded in North Eastern States and 64 routes commenced.

regional growth;

iii. MoCA will pursue limitation of CO2 emission in Indian aviation in coordination with 
ICAO under the pri nciples and provisions of the United Nations Framework Convention 
on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and its Paris agreement. At the international level, the 
International Civil Aviation Organizat ion (ICAO) has launched Carbon O ffsetting & 
Reduction Scheme for Aviation (CORSIA) to reduce emissions from international aviation 
which require offsetting of emissions above a baseline value. The CORSIA Scheme is 
envisaged in 3 phases:  
 Pilot Phase: (2021-2023)  
 First Phase: (2024-2026)  
 Second Phase: (2027-2035)  
The Pilot and First phases are voluntary phases whereas Second Phase  is mandatory for all 
the ICAO Member States. The 41 st ICAO Assembly has also adopted a Long -Term Global 
Aspirational Goal (LTAG) for international aviation of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, 
in support of the UNFCCC Paris Agreement's temperature goal. With the launch of 
CORSIA scheme by ICAO, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) has emerged as one of the 
key interventions. As a policy matter, Government of India has decided not to participate 
in t he voluntary phases of CORSIA. Hence, Indian scheduled carriers with international

Use of GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN)  
191. GAGAN is the acronym for Global Positioning System (GPS) Aided Geostationary Earth 
Orbit (GEO) Augmented Navigation, which has been jointly developed by the Indian Space 
Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Airports Authority of India (AAI). The GAGAN uses a 
system of ground stations to provide necessary augmentations to the GPS St andard Positioning 
Service (SPS) navigation signal. A network of precisely surveyed ground reference stations i.e., 
Indian Reference Stations (INRES) is strategically positioned across the country to collect GPS 
satellite data. Using this information, the master control centre i.e., Indian Master Control Centre 
(INMCC) generates messages to correct any signal errors. These correction messages are then 
uplinked through Indian  Land Uplink Station (INLUS) and broadcast through communication 
satellites (Geostat ionary) to receivers onboard aircraft , using the same frequency as GPS.   
192. The GAGAN is designed to provide the additional accuracy, availability, and integrity 
that may be necessary to enable users to rely on GPS, for all phases of flight, from enroute  
through approach for all qualified airports within the GAGAN service volume. GAGAN will 
also provide the capability for increased accuracy in position reporting, allowing for more 
uniform and high -quality Air Traffic Management (ATM). In addition, GAGAN w ill provide 
benefits beyond aviation to all modes of transportation, including maritime, highways, and 
railroads. 
193. The Ministry has informed the Committee that National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 
2016 prescribes that new aircrafts being registered i n India from 1 st January, 2019 (subsequently 
revised to 1 st July, 20 21) will mandatorily have GAGAN -enabled GPS receivers onboard. 
However, exemption from GAGAN mandate has been given to Boeing -787 aircraft till 
31.12.2025 owing to major design changes to be made in the aircraft and subsequent approval of 
the State of Design i.e., Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Moreover, five aircrafts of Air

Surge in Air Fares and Rationalisation 
The Committee during its deliberations expressed concerns about the high fares charged 
by the private airlines in the domestic sector. The Committee also pointed out the wrong 
information published by the private airlines on their websites, regarding the n umber of 
seats left in the flight and the prices of the tickets. The level of misinformation can be 
gauged from the fact that even after the last tickets have been sold, the same number of 
seats show on the website, as indicated before the tickets sale. Th is indicates that airline 
operators are misguiding the public and forcing passengers to pay more. In view of the 
above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should formulate appropriate 
guidelines regarding rationalization of fares and publishing the  correct information on the 
website of the airlines.  
(Para 66) 
The Committee also pointed that 'Predatory Pricing' is being restored to by the domestic 
airlines sector. A particular airline may sell its air tickets at such a low level, that other 
competitors cannot compete and are forced to exit the market. A company that does this 
will see initial losses, but eventually it benefits by driving competitions out of the market 
and raising its prices again. The Committee desired to know whether the DGCA had at any 
point of time, intervened to check the fares of air tickets. The Committee also expressed 
concern at the fact that in the domestic sector, private airlines are charging different fares 
for same sector, route and same direction of flights. This is spec ifically so for the NE 
Region and Hilly areas including Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, where the prices of 
domestic sector tickets are, sometimes even more than the international airline sector 
prices.  
(Para 67) 
The Committee takes note of the fact that afte r the repeal of the Air Corporations Act, 
1953, the airfare is market driven and depends on market fares, and is neither established 
nor regulated by the Government. It notes the DGCA’s comments that the airfares were 

Page 80 of 108 
 
regulated for a fixed period during th e COVID pandemic in compliance with Aircraft Act, 
1934 and the regulation was withdrawn as the COVID pandemic abated and that airlines 
are free to fix reasonable tariffs under the Aircraft Rules, 1937, with regard to cost of 
operation, services, reasonable profit and generally prevailing tariff. 
(Para 71) 
The Committee is fully aware that the Indian domestic Aviation sector is growing in an 
open market and acknowledges that the private airline operators should be given a free 
hand to decide the air fares as they are governed by competition and depends on ma rket 
fares. It also notes that there is a provision in the Aircraft Rules, 1937, which inter-alia has 
a provision for fixing the air fares after considering ‘reasonable profit and generally 
prevailing tariff’ amongst other factors. The Committee observes t hat presently the surge 
in air fares does not reflect any sort of mechanism on part of the Ministry to control the 
fares, based on existing Aircraft Rules, 1937, as during surge in air fares the prices go 
beyond the acceptable or justifiable limits of 'rea sonable profit and generally prevailing 
tariff'.  
(Para 72) 
The Committee notes that while on one hand Government plans to make air transport 
affordable for the common man and the air capacity is being increased, on the other hand 
there is no commensurate expansion of the capacity to bring in aircrafts. This creates lack 
of airline tickets considering the high demand and leads to increase in the prices. The 
Committee recommends that there should be a mechanism with the Ministry such as 
capping of upper and lower prices to stop the practice of 'Predatory Pricing' or the sudden 
surge in prices. The Committee is of the firm opinion that a perfect balance has to be 
maintained between the commercial interest of the private airlines and the interest of the 
passengers so as to enable the private airlines to grow and at the same time the interest of 
passengers should also be kept in mind, so that they are not fleeced in the garb of 
commercialization. The Committee feels that even though price buckets are being create d 
as per international aviation norms, a close watch has to be maintained by the DGCA & 
the Ministry and a mechanism should be devised to monitor the websites of various airlines 
to prevent them from misguiding passengers. And, in case the private airlines  do not 
publish the correct information regarding fares, they should be penalized for it. The 
Committee observes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has a responsibility to the travelling 
public and the nation at large to ensure that predatory pricing mech anism are not adopted 
by the airlines under the cloak of free market economy. The Committee recommends the 
Ministry should formulate a pricing mechanism for air fares to ensure that passengers are 
not charged exorbitant prices. The Committee also recommend s that DGCA may be 
empowered to regulate tariffs based on the data generated by their monitoring Department

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the senior 
officers of the Ministry of Civil Aviation to the meeting . The agenda of the meeting  was 
deliberations of the Demands for Grants (2023 –24) of the M inistry. The Chairman asked the 
Ministry to explain the budgetary allocation for B.E. 2023 -24 and the constraints faced by the 
Ministry. He enquired about the performance of various schemes in both financial & physical 
terms. The Chairman inter-alia sought to know: 
 Ministry’s roadmap for revival and upgradation of 37 Regional Connectivity Scheme 
(RCS) airports;  
 plans to settle the liability arising due to financial restructuring of Air India; 
 actual requirement of commercial pilots in the country and plans  to meet such 
requirements; and   
 details regarding the environment-friendly initiatives to reduce emissions.  
3.         The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation made a detailed presentation about the 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 2023 -24. He stated that an amount of 
₹3,113.36/- crores has been earmarked as Budget Estimates for the F.Y. 2023 -24. The Ministry 
was allocated ₹ 9,363.70/- crores as Revised Estimates (2022 -23). O ut of this, the actual 
expenditure stands at ₹ 8065.54/- crores (till January, 2023) i.e. approximately 86% of the R.E. 
allocation.  
4.         The Secretary stated that Indian Aviation sector is one of the fastest growing Industries of 
the world. The number of domestic passengers in the country has increased by 48.9% in 2022 as 
compared to 2021. The number of registered aircrafts in the country is likely to reach 1,200 from 
the current 744, in the next few years. Post the conduct of ICAO Coordinated Validation Mission 
in November, 2022, India’s safety oversight ranking  has improved from 102 to 48, amongst  the 
193 countries in the world . Also, the implementation score has increased from 69.95% to 
85.49%. 
5.         The Secretary explained that under the RCS, 1152 valid routes have been awarded 
covering more than 32 State s/ Union Territories . Out of this 467 routes have been commenced 
till date. More than 2,19,000 flights carrying approximately 114.53 lakh passengers  have 
operated since the inception of the Scheme. As per the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework 
(2023-24), the Ministry has a target to commence 100 RCS routes (Y ear-on-Year) and increase 
the number of passengers travelled on RCS flights to 30 lakh in the financial year. Further, the 
Ministry aims to operationalize 100 airports and 1000 RCS routes by 2024 and 2 026, 
respectively.      
6.         The Secretary apprised the Committee that under the Greenfield Airport policy,  
Government had accorded ‘in -principle’ approval for setting up 21 Greenfield airports . Out of 

112 
these 21 airports, 10 have already been operatio nalized. Remaining 11 airports are being 
developed in partnership with respective State Governments. The Ministry is carrying out a 
series of reform measures to promote the Unmanned Aircraft System (Drones) in the country . 
Drones are  extensively being used  for the property survey in rural areas under the Swamitva 
Yojana. An amount of ₹ 33/- crores has been earmarked for F.Y. 2023 -24 under the Production 
Linked Incentive Scheme  and Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan  to incentivize manufacturing of 
Drones and Drone components in India respectively.  
7.         The Secretary briefed the Committee about the various digital initiatives viz., e-GCA; e-
BCAS and Digi Yatra to ensure efficient and effective processes ing. He stated that there is a 
need for 1000 pilots per yea r. To meet the  present requirements, a liberalized Flying Training 
Organization (FTO) Policy has been adopted to facilitate the growth of FTOs.  The Ministry has 
actively taken up the issue of reduction in Value Added Tax (VAT) on Aviation Turbine Fuel 
(ATF) with all the States and Union Territories . 18 States/UTs have already reduced VAT on 
ATF. 
8.         Regarding the disinvestment of Air India,  Secretary informed that  the process of 
disinvestment of its four subsidiaries viz. Alliance Air Aviation Ltd.; AI Airport Services Ltd.; 
AI Engineering Services Ltd.; and Hotel Corporation of India Ltd are under process.  The 
Chairman, then enquired into the justification for the Enterprise Valuation Method adopted for 
disinvestment of Air India and the time it will  take to clear the entire liability. Secretary 
responded that the Government had taken over a liability of Rs 62,365/ - crores, and got a cash 
component of Rs . 2,700/- crores. The Chairman also enquired into the details of the amount 
which has been invested by the Government in Air India since it was nationalized in 1953 till the 
date of its disinvestment. 
9.       Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) facilitated the 
disinvestment of Air India in which Enterprise Value (EV) based bidd ing process was adopted. 
The highest bidder i.e., M/s Talace Private Limited, estimated the EV at ₹ 18,000/- crores. Out 
of this the Ministry received cash component of 15% i.e., ₹ 2,700/- crores. The bidder took over 
the balance as debt as prescribed in the bidding process. Also, 68 assets out of the total 211 non -
core assets of the Air India are in the process of being disposed off. The Committee decided that 
the views of the Ministry and Air India Assets Holding Limited on the disinvestment of Air 
India, may be heard at a later date.  
10.       The Chairman also took up the issue of affordability of air tickets for the common man . 
He enquired about the reason for removal of price cap on airfares. He pointed out that by doing 
so, no extra revenue is being generated for the Government or the airport operator . Only the 

113 
airline operators benefit at the cost of the passengers who have to pay for the surge in flight 
tickets. The Director General, Directorate General of Civil Aviation stated that the Minis try does 
not regulate the fares. However, in compliance with the Aircraft Act, 1934, the Ministry 
exercised regulation of fares during the Covid pandemic . This was later withdrawn. The 
Secretary clarified that as per international norms, fare buckets are created by the airlines . 
Ministry only makes them publish their fares on the website. The Committee decided to hear the 
various Private airline operators on this issue, at a later date.  
11.       The Secretary further informed that the long pending issue of opera tionalization of a 
fourth runway at the Indira Gandhi International Airport, Delhi will be resolved by September, 
2023. This will enhance the capacity of the Terminal 1, IGI Airport, Delhi.  
12.       Members raised various queries/issues such as:  
 token allocation under Krishi Udaan Scheme;  
 plans of the Ministry to improve India’s safety oversight rank;  
 India’s capacity to handle MRO operations as per international standards, in view of the 
increasing number of aircrafts in the country;  
 Ministry’s vision to introduce additional national aviation universities to meet the 
increasing requirement of pilots and hence the number of FTOs;  
 Discontinuation of RCS flights in the State of Kerala;  
 Legal issues related to the bidding process of Nagpur airport;  
 Ministry’s plan to include Nagpur-Shirdi-Nagpur under RCS;  
 more flight connectivity for Lakshadweep being a tourism hotspot;  
 Token allocation for Aerosports policy;  
 Capacity constraints at airports;  
 Need to map all the RCS destinations under one comprehensive national plan;  
 Lack of airports in India as compared to other countries;  
 Levy of charges on old aircrafts parked at airports;  
 Need for installation of Instrument Landing System (ILS) at Cuddapah Airport; 
 Use of latest technology such as Artificial Intelligence in security checks, etc. 
13.       The Secretary, MoCA responded to some of the queries raised by the Chairman and 
Members of the Committee and took note of the suggestions made by the Members.  
14.       The Chairman directed that written rep lies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

1, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism,
having, been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on their behalf, present this Thirty Fourth
Report.

2. The Hon'ble Chairman, has referred the Merchant Shipping (second amendment) Bill, 1998 as
introduced in the Rajya Sabha and pending therein, to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport and Tourism for examination and report*

3.The Committee discussed provisions of the Bill at its meeting held on the 11th, 24th August and 7th,
17th September and Sth, 28th Oct., 1998.

4. The Committee heard the views of the Secretary Ministry of Surface Transport and representatives
of the M/o Law, Justice and Company Affairs.

5. The’ Committee decided that the evidence recorded by the Committee should be laid on the table of
both the Houses of Parliament.

6. The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill at its meetings heid on 28th
Oct., 1998.

7. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on 2nd December, 1998.

8. The Ministry of Surface Transport in their note submitted to the Committee explained the need for
introduction of the Bill. In their note the Ministry of Surface Transport stated that keeping in view of
various important developments on the shipping sector, it was decided to appoint a Committee during the
year 1991 to review the provisions of the Act and identify the necessary amendments needed to bring it in
line with important changes in international shipping. The Committee submitted its report in 1992
suggesting about 180 amendments to the Act. Some of the sections were amended during the year 1994,
While action to amend the Act in accordance with the comprehensive recommendations of the Review
Committee is likely to take sometime, in view of certain developments in the shipping section it is felt
that two sections namely sections 76 and 95 of the Act need to be amended expeditiously.

9. OBJECTS AND REASONS FOR PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO SECTIONS 76 AND 95

A. The main objective of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is to ensure development and efficient
maintenance of the Indian Mercantile Marine in a befitting manner in the interest of the nation. The Act
has been amended from time to time in the light of experience gained in its implementation and also to
give effect to various provisions of international conventions or portocols ratified by India.

B. Section 76 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 provides for certificates of competency to be held
by officers on board on ships and the number of officers to be provided on ships. It does not distinguish
between different kinds of vessels or even between coastal and foreign-going vessels so far as manning
scales are concerned. Even small ships operating in coastal waters are required to have certificated officers
on the scale specified for foreign-going vessels. This not only casts additional financiaf‘burden on coastal
ship owners but sometimes causes difficulty in complying with the existing provisions. Coastal vessels
do not require the same level of manning as is required for foreign-going vessels. The Bill proposes to
amend section 76 so that, instead of specifying the manning scales for different kinds of ships in the Act
itself, these may be notified by the Central Government, from time to time, keeping in view operational
and other requirements. if

C. Section 95 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 provides for seamen’s employment office which
regulates supply of different categories of seamen for various classes of ships on the basis of roster
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Par dated the Th August, 1998, August, 1998.

1



system. This system has discouraged employment of young-trained manpower by Indian and foreign ship
owners, In order to facilitate increased employment of Indian seafarers particularly on board foreign flag
vessels so as to realise vast potential of the country in this regard and to augment valuable foreign
exchange earings, the Government seeks to encourage private sector participation in training and placement
of merchant navy seamen. It is, therefore, necessary to minimise Government controls, which have been
perceived by foreign ship owners as a major obstacle in employment of Indian seafarers on their ships.
Accordingly, the Bill proposes to amend section 95 relating to seamen’s employment office so as to allow
both Indian and foreign ship owners to employ merchant navy crew members without going to the
seamen’s employment office.

10. The Committee at its meeting held on 17th September, 1998 discussed the Merchant Shipping
(Second Amendment) Bill, 1998 in the light of the evidence tendered by the Secretary, Ministry of
Surface Transport on the 7th September, 1998.

11. The Representatives of the M/o Law, Justice and Company Affairs informed the Committee at its
meeting held on Sth October, 1998 that in case the existing Amendments to Section 76, as proposed in
this bill, is carried out then consequential amendments may be required to be carried out in sections 436
and 458 of the Parent Act i.e. the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

12. The Committee at its meeting held on 28th October, 1998 heard the representatives of the Ministry
of Law, Justice and Company Affairs and Surface Transport in the light of the written notes furnished by
both the Ministries regarding consequential amendments in Section 436 and 458 of the Merchant Shipping
Act, 1958, in case the existing amendments to section 76 as provided in the Merchant Shipping (Second
Amendmnet) Bill, 1998 are carried out. The representatives of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company
Affairs opined that since section 436 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 provides punishment for
contravention of any provisions of the Act and in case the Section 76, as proposed in the Bill is amended,
then consequential amendment in Sr. No. 17 of Section 436 (2) is also required to be carried out.

13. The Committee, having heard the representaitves of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company
Affairs and Ministry of Surface Transport and having consider the documents on the subject is of the
opinion that there is a need to amend section 76 and section 95 of the Merchant Shipping Act of 1958 with
a view to achieving the objectives set out in the statement of objects and reasons of the amending Bill.
The Committee is in agreement with the provisions of the Bill and recommends that the Bill in its present
form, be passed taking care of certain consequential changes in Sections 436 and 458 of the Merchant
Shipping Act, 1958.

14. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs vide their O.M. dated the 13th November, 1998
sent the draft of the consequential amendments to the sections 436 and 458 of the Merchant Shipping Act,
1958 to the Ministry of Surface Transport.

15. The Ministry of Surface Transport vide their O.M. dated 16th November, 1998 informed the
Committee that the amendments proposed by the Ministy of Law, Justice and Company Affairs are
acceptable to that Ministry and confirm the same (Extracts of the Sections 436 and 458 of the Merchant
Shipping Act, 1958 are at Appendices)

16. The Ministry of Surface Transport during hte deliberations of the meetings of the Committee
desired that rules making powers under amended section 76 of the Merchant Shipping Bill 1998 may be
given to the executive i.e. Ministry of Surface Transport as they have to give effect to various agreements/
treaties ratified by India from time to time and also to keep pace with the fast changes taking place in the
shipping industry and that the rule making takes a lot of time as they have to formulate rules in consultation
with the Law Ministry. The Ministry of Surface Transport therefore requested the Committee to give
some flexibility to the Director General of Shipping in issuing the notification in this regard. However the
representatives of the Ministry of Law opined that in case the mannings scales have already been prescribed
by Rules, the Merchant Shippifg Act should provide that the violation of the rule will be punishable. That
has been given in section 458 of the Merchant Shipping Act. But there is no provision in the Merchant

2


Shipping Act that violation of a notification is punishable. In case the manning scales are to be provided
by way of a notification, then, a separate provision should be made in the Merchant Shipping Act and that
rules and regulations are to be laid on the Tables of the Houses of Parliament. Keeping in view the advise
tendered by the representatives of the Ministry of Law, the Committee expressed its strong reservations
in this regard and did not agree to the views of the Ministry of Surface Transport. The Committee was of
the opinion that there would be no problem in framing rules and the Law Ministry has to be consulted
in the matter of rule making process so as to ensure legality of the subject. The Committee therefore
directed that all the rules/order that would be made under the amended section 76 of the Act would have
to be notified and the notification should be laid on the table of both the houses of Parliament.

17. The Committee further directed that a comprehensive bill considering rest of the amendments of
the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 as suggested by the Review Committee under the Chairmanship of the
Director General Shipping in 1991, so as to bring it in line with the important changes in international
shipping may be brought before the Parliament instead of introducing piecemeal amendments from time
to time.

18. The Committee took note of the views expressed by S/Shri Lakshman Chandra Seth, Anil Basu and
Abani Roy opposing the Bill. The Committee decided to append their views on a note of dissent to its
report.

NOTE OF DISSENT
By
1, Shri Lakshman Chandra Seth
2. Shri Anil Basu
3. Shri Abani Roy

We oppose the amendment of Section 76 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, because the legislative
authority in the matter of specifying the manning scales for different kinds of ship as provided in the Act
itself shall be diminished. Executive Authority will enjoy full liberty in the matter of specifying the
manning scales.

Therefore, we suggest that Rules in respect of manning scales for different kinds of ships according to
tonnage, capacity and the size be framed and passed by Parliament.

We oppose vehemently amendment of Section 95 of the Merchant Shipping Act. This section ensures
employment of Seamen on the basis of roster system. Existing Seamen's Employment office is a result of
long drawn struggle of Seamen.

The First Asian Maritime Conference held in Cylon in October, 1958 under the auspices of the
International Labour Organisation called up on the Government of all countries of world to establish
Seamen's Employment Office in order to regulate employment of Seamen. Dismantling of Seamen's
Employment Office will lead complete chaos in Shipping Industries. Seamen will be thrown as prey to
the brokers and Agents in the matter of employment, bribery, corruption, anarchism will loom large in
this shpere.

Therefore, we record our opposition to this bill strongly and rather we propose to bring the
comprehensive bill with a view to strengthening the Seamen’s Employment Office and ameliorating the
service condition of Seamen.

REPORT 
 
BRIEF BACKGROUND 
Indian culture and heritage is one of the oldest and richest in the world, dating back to 
several millennia. It is a diverse blend of various customs, beliefs, traditions, and values that 
have evolved over time and have been shaped by different religions, languages, and historical 
events. India's cultural and spiritual heritage is reflected in its architecture, literature, music, 
dance, cuisine, and festivals, which continue to fascinate and inspire people from all over the 
world. From the ancient Indus Valley civilization to the present day, Indian culture has 
witnessed numerous influences and transformations. This makes it a unique and dynamic 
tapestry of humanity's collective experience. 
2. Broadly, this Ministry is working on the protection, development and promotion of all 
types of Heritage and Culture namely, Tangible Heritage, Intangible Heritage and 
Knowledge Heritage. In addition, the Ministry also harbour s the responsibility of Gandhian 
Heritage and Commemoration of important historical events and centenaries of great 
personalities. 
3. Major programmes/activities of the Ministry of Culture relating to promotion, 
dissemination, preservation and conservation of the cultural heritage of the country are being 
implemented through a network of two attached offices, six subordinate offices, one statutory 
body, thirty-three Autonomous organisations and one charitable trust under its control. The 
Ministry also implements schemes for promotion and dissemination of Art and Culture under 
umbrella(s) namely; Centenaries & Anniver saries Scheme, Kala Sanskriti Vi kas Yojna, 
Development of Museum, Development of Libraries & Archives, Global Engagement & 
International Coopera tion and National Mission on Cultural Mapping and Roadmap. 
Activities of National Gandhi Heritage Site Mission are undertaken through Kala Sanskriti 
Vikas Yojna. The Ministry has no Centrally Sponsored Schemes.

THE MINISTRY  
B.E. 2023-24: Salient features and Projected Demand vs Allocation 
4. The budget for 2023 -24 for the Ministry of Culture has been pegged at Rs. 3399.65 
crore, consisting of Rs. 3114.25 crore under Revenue and Rs. 285.40 crore under Capital 
heads for undertaking various prioritized programmes/activities/projects. This budgetary 
allocation is about 12.98% more than the budgetary provisions at BE 2022-23. The projected 
demand of the Ministry for 2023-24 was 3989.18 crore.

allocation for 2023 -24 along with allocation made by the Ministry of Culture under each 
Umbrella Scheme/ Group vis-à-vis projected demand, are placed at Annexure-I:

2023-24, and  upon analysing the expenditure trend of FY 2022 -23, it has ensured an optimal 
distribution of funds across various sectors in FY 2023 -24. It furnished the follow ing

8. The Ministry stated that it would have to reorient its activities in such a way that 
important activities would not suffer for want of funds in the Year 2023 -24. However, it is 
expected that deficiency in funds ,if any, would be adequately addressed by the Ministry of 
Finance through an advance from the contingency fund of India/at  the supplementary stage/ 
at the Revised Estimate stage of FY 2023-24. 
 
9. The Committee noted that the allocation  for the Ministry of Culture is just 0.075% of 
the total budget this year. This is in sharp contrast to countries such as China, the UK, the 
USA, Singapore and Australia, which spend roughly 2 – 5% of their budget on the promotion 
of arts and culture.  
 
10. In response, the Ministry stated that it may not be tenable for a developing nation like 
India to allocate a considerable proportion of its public fund in the area of promotion of art 
and culture given the high disparity it experiences in elementary ru ral infrastructures like 
health, education and transportation etc. as against the countries in comparison. However, 
this Ministry has been consistently able to increase its budgetary outlays over the years 
except in the Covid pandemic period where priority  was given to other social sector 
ministries.  Though the approved budget outlay for the Ministry is a relative increase with 
respect to the previous financial year, the Ministry had projected around Rs. 3989 crore as a 
result of an overwhelming increase i n the number of activities by all organisations/offices 
under the ambit of Ministry of Culture. This is an achievable budget at RE 2023 -24 stage 
provided a good pace of expenditure is maintained in the next FY as well.  It may also be 
noted that apart from the union government spending on the promotion of arts and culture, a 
considerable part of the public spending is also made by the state governments in the field of 
art and culture which is not captured in the overall spent. 
11. The Ministry further menti oned that while a majority of the amount spent on art and 
culture is from the non -government sources for the counties in comparison, this may not be 
true for our county. Hence, the Ministry is trying and evolving innovative methods to 
maximise the particip ation of non -government organisations in the field of promotion and 
conservation of art and culture. Monument Mitra, NCF etc. are examples of such initiatives. 
This Ministry believes that Culture should be an area where a large part of expenditure needs 
to be sourced from non -government sources. Moreover, the Ministry of culture is taking a 
phenomenal role in supporting non -governmental organisations/voluntary organisations 
through its schemes/ organisations for participating in overall propagation, preserv ation and 
promotion of all forms of art and culture. This can be considered to have a ripple effect on 
the budget utilised by the Ministry.

Keeping this in mind, the Committee is convinced that the BE allocation of 3399.65

15. The allocation of Rs. 3399 crores for BE 2023 -24 is ~13 percent higher than BE 
2022-23 and ~1 percent higher than RE 2022 -23. However, the Committee notes that 
the increase of 1 percent as compared to RE 2022 -23 is not sufficient to c over the 
impact of inflation. The spending power of the Ministry will actually decrease in 2023 -
24.

underscore the importance of its mandated duties to the Ministry of Finance for higher 
allocation at R.E. stage. Ministry of Finance may be requested to minimise the shortfall

18. The Committee agrees with the submission that a majority of the amount spent 
on art and culture in many countries is from non -government sources. The Committee 
suggests that the Ministry should increase its focus on encouraging private 
participation in the art and culture sector.  
19. The Ministry should try to attract investment from private organisati ons under 
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds, besides seeking investments through

sector. This would enable much better preservation and development of monuments 
and museums in the country. It would also help India become a more attractive tourist

Building Survey Project, Temple Survey Projects and Underwater Archaeology Wing.
