Further, rehabilitation of borrow areas, control of erosion and slope protection, adequate number 
of cross drainage structures to maintain natural water course, silt fencing, use of adequate control 
devices for all construction machineries and their regular maintenance for reduction in pollution 
levels well within their respective permissible limits etc. are  being actively undertaken. 
  
Water & Debris Management: 
a)   Amrit Sarovars: 
Further, the vision of the government of creating 75 ‘Amrit Sarovars’ in each district and around 
50,000 in the country would serve as a major milestone in the conservation of water resources 
and improvement of micro-climate of such areas. It will augment water availability especially in 
water stressed areas of the country besides improving rural livelihoods and productivity. Various 
central and state agencies are part of this noble endeavour. The Ministry had id entified 785 
locations for Amrit Sarovar; 12 locations could not be taken up due to issues of LA, project 
mapping; MoRT&H is identifying alternate 12 locations. Presently work is completed at 343 
locations and in progress at 220 locations. Earth from Amrit  Sarovars is being used in 160 
projects. This pro -poor and environmental friendly endeavour will go in a long way in 
augmenting the water regime in the country. Besides, this will ensure flow of number of 
‘ecosystem services’ for society in the course of development. 
‘Ajadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav’  which is an initiative of the Government of India to celebrate and 
commemorate 75 years of India’s independence  and the glorious history of its people, culture 
and achievements and which is dedicated to its people who hold within them the immense power 
and potential to enable the vision of activating India 2.0, fuelled by the spirit of ‘Aatmanirbhar 
Bharat’ is being celebrated by the MoRTH and its affiliate NHAI by planting 75 lakh saplings. 
 The Ministry and various ex ecuting agencies for NHs are pursuing ‘sabka saath, sabka vikas, 
sabka vishwas and sabka prayas’ mantra given by implementing the sustainable and inclusive 
developmental agenda by following the clarion call of Hon. Prime Minister ‘one earth, many 
efforts’ given on World Environment Day, 5 th June, 2022 . The mission ‘Lifestyle for the 
Environment (LIFE) Movement’  which borrows from the past, operates in the present and

 NHAI is not only building the infrastructure road network of entire country but is equally

 INTRODUCTION 
2023 is the Incredible India! Visit India year and also the year of India‟s presidency of G20, 
presenting the perfect opportunity to establish India as a key tourism destination. This year 
therefore offers the brightest outlook for Indian tourism since the beginning of the pandemic in 
early 2020.   One of the largest Service Sectors in India, Tourism has always played a key role in 
socio-economic progress through employment generation, creation of infrastructure and revenue 
earnings.  Tourism also has the potential to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals, 
particularly, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, sustainable consumption and production 
and sustainable use of oceans and marine resources.  The huge potential of this key sector is set 
to be tapped further this year on Mission Mode with the active participation of states, the 
convergence of government programmes and public private partnerships. 
2. The Nodal Agency for this Mission is the Ministry of Tourism which f ormulates national 
policies and programmes for the development and promotion of Tourism in the country. In the 
process, the Ministry consults and collaborates with other stakeholders in the sector including 
various Central Ministries/ Agencies, State Gover nments/ Union Territory Administrations and 
the representatives of the private sector.

SURRENDER OF SAVINGS  
14. The amount of surrender during the current financial year including th e cut imposed by  
Ministry of Finance at RE stage is Rs. 1409.57 Crores. The final allocation of funds  under RE 
was received by the Ministry on 5th January 2023. On the basis of the RE  allocation, the revised 
requirement of funds for Scheme and non -Scheme components was worked out in consultation 
with the Programme Division, India Tourism Offices in  India and abroad, IISM Gulmarg, etc. 
the final savings were arrived at and surrendered to Ministry of Finance on 08.02.2023. 
 
15. The Committee observes that in the last three years, the allocation at the  Revised 
Estimates stage is half of the Budgetary Estimates and the Actual Expenditure is even less.  
The utilisation percentage of the Ministry for the last two years i.e.  2020-21 & 2021 -22 is 
only 89.85 & 82.89  respectively and for the FY 2022 -23 it is only 34.56% till 31 st January 
2023.While expenditure in 2020 may be understandably low due to the pandemic, the 
status in respect of 2021 and 2022 is no better.  The utilization percentage of only 34.6% in 
2022-23 is unacceptable.  The Committee does not accept the reply of the Ministry that the 
change in procedure of release of funds was a factor in low utilisation of funds. The change 
in procedure was for all Ministries and other Ministries have managed to utilis e most of 
their funds by December, 2022.   
16. The Committee finds that the reduction in Revised Estimates in the past three years 
is across all Central Sector Schemes. The Flagship Scheme of the Ministry, Swadesh  
Darshan has had budgetary cuts of upto 50%  at the Revised Estimates stage in the past 
three years. 
17. The Committee further finds that the entire budget allocation of Rs. 2400 crores is 
under Revenue Head with nil allocation to Capital Head.  The Ministry has submitted that 
a major portion of the  outlay amounting to Rs.1742 crores is earmarked for development 

Page 12 of 136 
 
of infrastructure for tourism development and Rs. 242.00 crores for promotion and 
branding activities.  For tourism infrastructure Schemes, an amount of Rs, 1412.00 crores 
is allocated for Sw adesh Darshan, Rs. 250.00 crores is kept for the Scheme of  PRASHAD 
(Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual and Heritage Augmentation Drive) and Rs 80 
crores is allocated for Scheme for Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism 
Infrastructure Development. 
18. Much of the budgetary outlay is for development of infrastructure. Swadesh  
Darshan, the flagship scheme of the Ministry is focused on development of theme based 
infrastructure. Infrastructure for all tourist amenities like creation of tourist information 
centre, reception centre, convention centres, cafeterias, beautification of tourist attractions 
are covered under this scheme.  The Committee does not find it rational that though 
Capital assets are being created unde r the schemes of the Minist ry, the entire expenditure 
is classified under Revenue.    Revenue expenditure is short -term, recurring expenditure 
mostly pertaining to salaries, operating expenses, administrative costs etc.  Due to its very 
nature, revenue expenditure cannot be reduced as the expenses such as salaries and wages 
are incurred irrespective of the activities carried out.  The Committee finds however that 
for the last five years, the budgetary allocation of the Ministry has been halved at the 
Revised Estimates stage and even this budget has remained unutilised.  The Actual 
expenditure for the past five years has been much less than the budget allocated in Revised 
Estimates. 
19. The Committee notes the submissions of the Ministry that though at the macro level, 
the budget is un der Revenue Head, yet within the Schemes, there would be Object Heads 
pertaining to “Creation of Capital assets.” Under the two Major schemes, Swadesh  
Darshan and PRASHAD, the re is no recurring expenditure on salary etc.  These schemes 
are mainly meant for  asset creation and only 5% funds are given for O&M (Operations 
and Maintenance).  However, though only assets are being created under these schemes, 
the outgo of funds can be reduced depending on the progress of the projects and receipt of 
Utilisation Certificates.   
20. The Committee observes that creation of capital assets leads to value creation and 
generates future cash flows for the economy.  Further, the multiplier effect of Capital 

Page 13 of 136 
 
expenditure is much more than that of the Revenue expenditure. In In dia, the multiplier 
effect of Capital expenditure made by the Central Government is estimated at 2.45 and for 
State Governments, it is around 2 while the multiplier effect of Revenue expenditure is only 
0.99 (RBI  Bulletin, December, 2 020) .  Wrong classif ication therefore may not give  the 
correct picture on total investment in infrastructure and may impact both the Index of 
Industrial Production and the GDP.  The Committee notes that the classification as 
Revenue is arbitrary without following any valid criteria in case of various projects of 
Ministry of Tourism. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take up the 
matter with the Ministry of Finance and submit a detailed explanation to the Committee.

23. The Committee observes that the Ministry had projected a B.E. of Rs. 320 crores for 
promotion and publicity for both domestic and overseas.  The actual B.E is only Rs. 242 
crores.  Keeping in view that 2023 is being promoted as the Visit India Year and the  
promotional schemes drawn up by the Ministry, the Committee feels that the allocated 
amount would not be sufficient for the purpose.

24. The Committee has also been informed that there is no separate budgetary provision for 
G20 and expenditure relating t o the meetings and tourism promotion during G20 would be  met 
from the existing schemes. The Ministry has submitted that more than 200 meetings are being 
organized at 56 destinations across the country. All the State Governments are making efforts to 
provide cultural, traditional and other experiences to these delegates so that they can become 
India‟s Ambassadors for promoting our cultural and tourism offerings.   The Ministry of Tourism 
is also  organizing the Global Tourism Investors Summit, Incredible MICE  Summit, Tourism  
Expo and other events to promote India in G20 Presidency.  
25. The Committee feels that a separate budget allocation should have been kept for a 
major year long event like the G20 which is expected to have much impact on Indian 
tourism. The Committee notes that the budget of Rs. 242 crores would not be enough for all 
the routine promotional activities to be undertaken as  well as the additional events and 
Summits planned for the G20.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry 
may approach the Ministry of Finance for increased allocation for the budget for 
promotional activities.  
26. The Committee observes that the Ministry has cited the National Tourism Policy as a 
focus area. Upon query, the Ministry has stated that a Cabinet n ote has been submitted on the 
policy and approval is awaited.  The Ministry has further submitted that consultation process 
with State Governments, Line Ministries of the Central Government, Industry stakeholders 
etc has been completed.  The Committee reco mmends that the Ministry may make all efforts 
so that the Tourism Policy is enacted during this financial year. 
27. The Committee also observes that the Focus areas of the Ministry for 2023 -24 are 
identical to the Focus areas in the year 2022 -23.  The Committee notes that Focus Areas are 
defined in a budget to ensure that maximum effort and funds are provided to that area during 
that financial year  to ensure success of the project .  The Committee r ecommends that the 
Ministry instead of routinely focusin g on the same goals may set up precise achievable targets

42. Based on the detailed review, the Ministry has now revamped the scheme as Swadesh 
Darshan 2.0 (SD2.0) with the mantra of „vocal for local‟, and with the objective to develop 
sustainable and responsible destinations following a tourist & destination centric approach.  
Swadesh Darshan 2.0 is not an incremental change but a generational shift to evolve Swadesh  
Darshan Scheme as a holistic mission to develop sustainable and responsible to urism 
destinations covering tourism and allied infrastructure, tourism services, human capital 
development, destination management and promotion backed by policy and institutional reforms.  
The aim is to develop fewer locations but with a more visible and impactful development. The 
guidelines of the scheme include an illustrative list of admissible components and covers 
development of toilets, wayside amenities etc. at destinations. 
The key principles to be followed under Swadesh Darshan Scheme 2.0 are  
 (i) Develop benchmarks and standards for major tourism themes 
(ii) Sustainable and responsible tourism 
(iii) Destination and tourist-centric approach 
(iv) Integrated development of tourism destination 
(v) Focus on Domestic Tourism 
(vi) Policy and Institutional Reforms

Impact of PRASHAD scheme: 
55. PRASHAD scheme aimed at integrated development of pilgrimage and / or heritage basic 
tourism infrastructure at the identified destinations on need gap analysis basis with an objective 
of inclusive growth of the local community with employment generation to them and economic 
betterment. The infrastructure includes development/up-gradation of destination entry points viz. 
passenger terminals (of road, rail and water transport), basic conveniences like tourism 
Information / Interpretation / Amenities Centers with ATM/ Money exchange counters, last mile 
connectivity, pathways, procurement of equipment f or eco -friendly modes of transport and 
equipment for tourist activities such as Light & Sound Show, renewable sources of energy like 
Solar Lights, Solar Power Systems, Electric Charging points, Rain Water Harvesting, parking 
facilities, drinking water, toi lets/bathrooms, changing rooms, cloak room, waiting rooms, Craft

The Committee observes that the pandemic has accelerated the need for digitalisation in 
the tourism sector.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry may explore the 
possibilities of integration of the   Digital Portal  with e-visa application system. 
(Para 151)  
ATTRACTING FOREIGN INVESTMENTS IN THE TOURISM SECTOR 
 The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Ministry.  The Ministry may 
give details of the plans of the ID& IP Division regarding FDI promotion.  The Committee 
also feels that the Ministry does not have a roadmap to leverage the G20 opportunity to its 
maximum potential for the promotion of tourism and increase of foreign exchange.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry may develop a more detailed road map for 
attracting FDI in Tourism Sector.  
(Para 156)  
 EASE OF DOING BUSINESS 
 The Committee is pleased to see the initiatives taken by the Ministry in improving 
Ease of Doing Business in the Tourism sector . The Committee observes that Tourism and 
hospitality fall under the purview of several departments and hence face many challenges 
related to regulatory compliances. There is a need to simplify, rationalise and streamline 
the regulations with a focus on deploying digital technologies and self-certifications.

GREEN AND SUSTAINABLE TOURISM 
 
 The Committee asked the Ministry whether any roadmap has been formulated for 
promoting green and sustainable tourism and the steps taken so far to incentivise green 
and sustainable practices in the tourism sector and the key challenges in this regard.  The  
Committee also asked for details of the funds allocated and utilised towards green and 
sustainable tourism in the last 5 years. 
(Para 162)  
 
 The Committee feels that Green tourism must be promoted by mainstreaming 
sustainability into the tourism sector. When tourism is made sustainable, it can create jobs 
and economic growth while avoiding situations where local communities and natural 
ecology are exploited. The Committee observes that sustainable tourism has the potential to 
contribute directly or indire ctly to the UN Sustainable Developmen t Goals in the Agenda 
2030.   The Committee recommends that the Ministry may allocate funds for the promotion 
of green and sustainable tourism in its schemes and projects. 
(Para 168)  
IMPROVING THE CONSULTATION PROCESS WITH MPs 
 The Committee feels that the entire process of selection of the destinations under 
Swadesh Darshan 2.0 was done soliciting no inputs from Members of Parliament who 
represent the public and from important stakeholders.  The Committee recommends th at 
in the future the Ministry may adopt a participatory and consultative approach wit h MPs 
before formulating major schemes and plans. 
(Para 170)

REVISION OF TOURISTS DATA COMPUTING METHOD 
 The Committee observes that as per the verified data sent by the Ministry, the data 
relating to the monument in question was in fact incorrect.  In this particular case, the data 
of the ASI was incorrect.  Due to the incorrect data, the monumen t in question which was 
never on the list of Top Ten Monumen ts of India, was listed in fourth place that year. The 
Committee feels that this shows a lack of scrutiny on part of the Ministry as this should 
have been verified at least at the time of formulating the list of Top Ten Monuments. The 
Committee is of the v iew that data o n tourism from government publications are 
extrapolated and used widely.  The Ministry has submitted that a Standard Tourism 
Methodology has been developed in line with UNWTO for a comprehensive and uniform 
collection of Tourism Statistics from all districts.  The Ministry should take all measures to 
ensure that the data received by it from the ASI and the state governments is accurate.

MINUTES OF THE MEETING OF THE DEPARTMENT-RELATED 
PARLIAMENTARY STANDING COMMITTEE ON TRANSPORT, TOURISM & 
CULTURE (2022-23) 
XII 
TWELFTH MEETING 
  
The    Committee    met    at    11:00 A.M.    on    Friday,   the    17th February, 2023 
in Committee Room „4‟, First Floor, Parliament House Annexe Extension Building, New 
Delhi. 
  
Members present: 
1. Shri V. Vijayasai Reddy             -             Chairman   
RajyaSabha 
 
2. Dr. Sonal Mansingh 
3. Shri A. A. Rahim 
4. Shri Vinay Dinu Tendulkar 
 
LokSabha 
 
5.  Shri Rahul Kaswan 
6. Shri Sunil Baburao Mendhe 
7. Shri Chhedi Paswan 
8.  Shri Rajiv Pratap Rudy 
9.  Shri Ramdas Chandrabhanji Tadas 
10.  Shri Manoj Kumar Tiwari 
 
SECRETARIAT 
 
Shri Sumant Narain, Joint Secretary 
Shri Swarabji B., Director 
Shrimati Monica Baa 
Shrimati Subha Chandrashekar, Deputy Secretary  
Shri Ranajit Chakraborty, Under Secretary  
  
WITNESSES 
Ministry of Tourism 
1. Shri Arvind Singh, Secretary 
 
(Complete list of witnesses attached as Annexure)  
 
 
(After the officers of Ministry of Tourism take their seats) 
 
2. The Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee and the witnesses who were 
present. The Chairman informed that the agenda of the meeting was to examine the Demands 

139 
 
for Grants (2023 -24) of the Ministry of Tourism. The Chairman noted that the budgetary 
allocation for Tourism sector was Rs. 2400 crores, i.e. the same as the allocation in 2022 -
23.  He further noted that the budgetary allocations in the past few years had been much 
reduced at the R.E. stage and that the utilisation percentage in the past two years was 89.85% 
and 82.89% respectively.   Out of the R.E. 2022 -23 allocation of Rs. 1343.13 crores, the 
Ministry has utilised only 34.56% till 31 st January 2023.  The Chairman wished to know the 
reasons why the Ministry was unable to utilize its allocated budget.  
 
3. The Chairman also desired to know the strategies formulated by the Ministry to 
harness India‟s presidency of the G20 to promote Indian tourism on Mission Mode and plans 
to utilise the funds allocated to Swadesh Darshan , the Ministry‟s flagship scheme.   The 
Chairman then highlighted some inaccuracies in statistics in Tourism Statistics for the years 
2021 and 2022 published by the Ministry and desired to know the methodology employed in 
measuring tourist footfalls in Indian states and monuments.  
 
4. The Secretary, the Ministry of Tourism acknowledged that issues regarding data 
collection were being faced as the data from state sources was not reliable.   To resolve this, 
the Ministry organises training in data collection to g round-level staff in states.   The 
Secretary stated that the issue would be looked into and training given to the staff in the 
concerned states. The Secretary then gave an overview of the Indian Tourism scenario – 
 International Tourists Arrivals (ITA) in India in 2021 were 7.01 million as compared to 
6.34 million in 2020, an increase of 10.6%.   
 Foreign Tourist Arrivals (FTA) numbered 61, 91,399 registering a growth of 305.4% 
over 15, 27,144 in 2021.  
 Foreign Exchange Earnings have also risen steadily from R s. 65,070 crore in 2021 to 
Rs. 1,34,543 crores in 2022, an increase of 106.8% over the previous year. Domestic 
tourism grew by 11.05% over the previous year 
 Tourism contribution to GDP in 2020 -21was 1.06% and to share of jobs in overall 
employment was 12.91% 
 
5. The Secretary briefed the Committee about the various offices/organisations under the 
administrative control of the Ministry and informed them that overseas tourism offices are 
being wound up and alternative methods would be used to promote tourism overseas. 
 
6. The Secretary then informed about the budgetary allocations under various Major 
Heads of the Ministry.   Elaborating on the major schemes of the Ministry, the Secretary 
informed that - 
 76 projects had been sanctioned for Rs. 5320.11 crores under its flagship scheme, 
Swadesh Darshan 1.0 out of which 59 have been completed. Progress in 14 projects is 
between 75% -99% and below 75% in the remaining 3 projects.   The scheme was 
implemented from 2014 -15 till 2018 -19. After review at the highest levels, i t was 
revamped in late 2022 as Swadesh Darshan 2.0 to focus on responsible and sustainable 
tourism by following destination centric approach instead of the earlier theme -based 
circuits. 48 destinations have been identified for development under Swadesh Dar shan 
2.0 through a consultative process with the State Governments.    No new projects had 
been undertaken while revamping the scheme and that was one of the reasons for the 
reduced allocations under Revised Estimates along with implementation -related 

140 
 
challenges. The Scheme has the largest budgetary allocation of Rs. 1412 crores this 
year.  
 PRASHAD Scheme aims at rejuvenating pilgrimage, heritage and spiritual experiences 
through well -developed infrastructure. Out of 45 approved projects in 25 states 
amounting to Rs. 1586.10 crores, 20 projects have been completed and progress in 9 
more projects is more than 60%. 250 crores have been allocated to this scheme this 
year. 
 Under the Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development 
Scheme, a total of 60 projects have been sanctioned for an amount of Rs. 841.08 crores 
and 22 projects have been completed till date. 80 crores have been allocated to this 
scheme this year. 
 Under the „Adopt a Heritage Scheme”, 27 MoUs had been awarded to 15 Monument 
Mitras who would take up the responsibility of developing tourist amenities at sites but 
the Scheme has now been transferred to M/o Culture/ASI.  
 Budgetary allocation of Rs. 75 crores has been made for Domestic Promotion and 
Publicity. Overseas Promotion and Publicity Scheme is under review.  
 Allocation of Rs. 70 crores has been done under the Central Financial Assistance for 
the 21 Institutes of Hospitality Management and Sciences and other institutes under the 
Ministry 
 A total of 1,04,371 persons have bee n trained since 2018 -19 till 30/11/2022 under the 
Scheme of Capacity Building for Service Providers (CBSP) through Programmes such 
as Hunar Se Rozgar Tak, Skill Testing & Certification, Entrepreneurship Programme, 
Linguistic Tourist Facilitator, Adventure Tourism Courses, Destination Based Skilled 
Development Programme, etc. 
 An online digital platform to provide training and certification to tourist facilitators was 
launched on 1/1/2020.   IITTM is the implementing agency for this scheme and 4438 
candidates have completed the IITF Basic exam. 
 The Champion Services Sector Scheme has an allocation of Rs. 225 crores for 
extending incentives for improving Air Connectivity. In principle   approval has been 
accorded for 59 Air Tourism routes and 51 have been operati onalized. 140 crores have 
been allocated for the creation of tented accommodation in the Buddhist circuit and 90 
crores for Capacity Building in and around Iconic sites, 75 crores for Incentives to Tour 
Operators in Emerging Markets and 5.40 crores for the Promotion of MICE tourism.  
 The Iconic Destinations Scheme was not approved but some of the concepts have been 
incorporated in the Swadesh Darshan 2.0 Scheme.  
  The Incredible India website with 24 x 7 Live Chat support  interface and Mobile 
application co mprising of features like Maps,  Popular destinations, tourist attractions 
and experiences to assist tourists have been developed with content available in 
multiple foreign languages.  
 
7. A Member commented that none of the Members of the Committee were aware  that 
the Swadesh Darshan Scheme was being revamped and that 57 destinations had been selected 
after the revision of the Scheme. He enquired whether there had been any process of public 
participation or  consultation with Members of Parliament while prepar ing the guidelines for 
the revised Scheme. The representatives of the Ministry replied that State Governments were 
supposed to have public consultations before they submitted their proposals to the Ministry. 

141 
 
Members commented that the Schemes of the Ministry did not have any new components and 
appeared to be a rehash of the past Schemes.    
 
8. The Chairman commented that the Actual expenditure figure for 2022 -23 was very 
low at only 34.6% of the R.E. amount. He then enquired about the reason the entire budget 
allocation of the Ministry was shown in Revenue Expenditure only while infrastructure w as 
being created under some Schemes of the Ministry. He also enquired how the budget for 
Revenue Expenditure which is of recurring nature could be reduced.  The Secretary explained 
that while the overall expenditure is under revenue, the Schemes and projec ts of the Ministry 
are meant for asset creation only.   Further, as per the new policy of the Government, funds 
could be released only after 75% of the earlier funds had been exhausted.   As such the 
Ministry could reduce funds if Utilisation Certificates fo r the projects executed by the State 
Governments were not received.   The Chairman pointed out that the classification of 
budgetary allocations under Revenue and Capital has major impact on the Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) and the Index of Industrial Produc tion (IIP). The representatives of the 
Ministry stated that the anomaly would be taken up with the Ministry of Finance.  
 
9.  A member enquired whether there had been any method to categorize the Consultants 
who were appointed for earlier Swadesh Darshan Sche me and whether some of them had 
been re -appointed. The Ministry affirmed that about ten Consultants with very good track 
records had been appointed and a lot of work had been done to improve the capacity of the 
Consultants.  
 
10. A member enquired about whethe r the Ministry had given any proposal to the 
Transport Ministry for developing ropeways to promote tourism and was informed that 
discussions are going on between the two Ministries for this program.  
 
11. A member suggested that the Committee should recommend for the establishment of 
more Central IHMs and also in partnership with leading hotels.   A Member enquired how the 
50 destinations for iconic had been chosen as some destinations were never given priority.  
 
12. Members drew attention to the innovative concept of “Caravan Tourism” in 
Kerala,  and promotion of sanctuaries, forests, and tiger reserves for tourism. A Member also 
queried about how domestic and foreign tourists are identified for calculation of tourism  
statistics.  There was also discussion about the protection of women at tourist places and the 
usage of the Nirbhaya Fund, the concept of tourist police, training local people to provide 
security for monuments, and the inclusion of Indian festivals and fa irs in the international 
calendar. A Member enquired   whether the Ministry had a tourist portal like the e -Shram 
portal of Ministry of Labour.  
 
13. The Chairman enquired about the pending draft National Tourism Policy and was 
informed that the Cabinet note has been circulated and further instructions are awaited. 
 
14. The Secretary also mentioned about the Ministry‟s involvement in four Tourism 
Working Group Meetings of the G -20 and two major conferences on MICE and Tourism 
investors.   
 

142 
 
15. The representatives of  the Ministry responded to some of the queries raised by the 
Members and took note of the suggestions made by the Members. 
 
16.       The Chairman directed that written replies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week. 
 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
 
17.       A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept. 
 
18.       The meeting adjourned at 1.10 PM.

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, 
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Three Hundred Forty Fourth Repo rt on the Action Taken by the 
Government on the recommendations/ observations of the Committee contained in its Three 
Hundred Thirteenth Report on the subject ‘Promotion of Indian Tourism in Overseas Markets 
– Role of Overseas Tourist Offices and Indian Embassies’. 
2. The Three Hundred Thirteenth Report  of the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Cultur e was presented on the 3 rd  February, 
2022 to the Parliament.

Three Hundred Thirteenth Report were received from the Ministry of Tourism on 21 st  
October, 2022 and 5 th  January, 2023.

March, 2023.

CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee observes that Souvenir shops selli ng miniatures of historical monuments 
are very popular among tourists in foreign countrie s. However, these sorts of souvenir shops are 
very scanty in India. The Committee would, therefor e, recommend that the Government ought to 
take initiatives to help establish genuine outlets for the sale of miniature replicas of historical 
monuments near such monuments. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry  
1.1 Under ‘Adopt a Heritage’ project, advanced amen ities are planned as per the identified 
monument’s tourist footfall and financial feasibility of proposed interventions. Provision of basic 
souvenir shop promoting local art and craftsmanship  is covered under advance amenities and 
may be implemented at the site upon adoption. It wo uld provide a platform to local 
artisans/craftsmen to sell their product and support the local community.  
 
1.2 The Ministry of Tourism has noted the recommend ation of the Committee. The Ministry 
will take up with the States to promote miniature s ouvenirs of historic monuments at various 
tourist destinations to create opportunities for the local community. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Page 3 of 11 
 
CHAPTER-II  
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes that Prime Minister, Shri Na rendra Modi has mooted three 3-Ts -
 Trade, Tourism and Technology - to boost Indian ec onomic diplomacy and suggested that the 
functioning of Indian Missions and embassies should  be judged from their ability to inter alia 
boost tourist inflows. The Committee also takes not e of the submission made by Secretary (ER), 
Ministry of External Affairs before it that his Min istry will be closely working with the Ministry 
of Tourism to ensure greater progress in promotion of tourism and observes that apart from 
providing foreign exchange and mass employment, the  tourism sector has an economically 
beneficial cascading impact on other associated ind ustry segments and, therefore, the Ministry 
of External Affairs in coordination with the Minist ry of tourism and stakeholders needs to move 
quickly towards reworking India's strategy on attra cting foreign tourists to the country and help 
unleash the true potential of tourism sector in Ind ia. The Committee desires to be kept apprised 
of the progress made in this regard. The Committee also recommends that Indian Ambassadors 
as leaders of Indian Missions abroad must set targe ts for the growth of Indian tourism in key 
markets across the world with the objective of incr easing foreign tourist arrivals to the country 
and increasing the share of India in World Tourist Arrivals. The Committee desires to be kept 
apprised of the specific steps taken in this direction. 
(Para 45) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 It has been informed by the Ministry of Externa l Affairs that Indian Missions regularly 
organize events to promote culture and tourism. The se events include around Indian festivals, 
Indian products, performances with Indian/local art ists etc. Missions also regularly engage with 
the Tour Operators, in coordination with Indian Tourism Offices. 
 
1.2 Missions regularly organize quizzes related to India like ‘Bharat ko Jaaniye’ quizzes. 
Through activities such as inviting foreign dignitaries at Kumbh Mela, International Conferences 
in India, their visits to pilgrimage centers and in viting distinguished guests under Gen next 
Democracy Programme, MEA plays an important role in promotion of tourism abroad.  
Likewise ICCR’s Cultural Centers and Chairs program me organize activities promoting Indian 
Culture which reflects every aspect of life.   

Page 4 of 11 
 
CHAPTER-III  
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF 
THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. Modern tourism industry is a key driver of socio -economic growth through creation of 
jobs, infrastructure development and the export rev enues earned because it has potential to 
stimulate other sectors through its backward and fo rward linkages and cross-sectoral synergies 
with airlines, transport, basic infrastructure, agr iculture, handicrafts etc. Despite vast tourism 
resources in the form of its unique endowments of b iodiversity and rich culture and heritage, 
lndia's total share in International Tourist Arriva ls remains a modest l.24%, which is certainly 
below India's huge potential. The Committee is of t he firm view that focused marketing and 
promotion efforts go a long way in promoting growth  of inbound tourism to India. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should formulate an integrated marketing 
and promotional strategy to position India as a fav oured tourism destination in the 
tourism generating markets overseas and increase In dia's share of the global tourism 
market from the present 1.24% to 5% in the years to  come. The Committee feels that one of 
the effective steps in this direction would be re-c asting the website of the Ministry in 
an attractive and user-friendly manner. 
(Para 41) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The Ministry of Tourism, through its India Tour ism Offices Overseas along with Indian 
Missions abroad endeavours to position India as a p referred tourism destination in the tourism 
generating markets to promote various tourism produ cts and destinations and to increase India’s 
share in the global tourism market. The objectives are met through an integrated marketing and 
promotional strategy, global media campaign and syn ergized promotional measures in 
association with the Travel trade, State Governments and Indian Missions overseas. 
 
1.2 On the request of the Ministry of Tourism, the Ministry of External Affairs has 
designated Tourism Officers in the Indian Missions of top 20 source markets in October, 2021. 
The Ministry of Tourism has carried out a detailed benchmarking of global tourism marketing 
strategies and National Tourism Boards of the top 10 source markets.  The Ministry of Tourism is 
in process of revamping the Incredible India Websit e to make it more attractive and user-
friendly. 

Page 5 of 11 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
1.3 The Committee would like to know the details of  the integrated marketing and 
promotional strategy employed by the Ministry to po sition India as a preferred tourism 
destination and the targets set and achieved by the  Ministry to increase International 
Tourist Arrivals (ITAs) and share of India in the g lobal tourist market. The Committee 
believes that empowering tourism industry stakehold ers results in higher tourist 
satisfaction and desires to know whether the said s trategy encourages participation and 
empowerment of various Indian travel agencies and l ocal tourism stakeholders, 
cooperative groups and companies, in identifying ba rriers and enablers for destination 
tourism promotion.  
 
1.4 The Committee would like to be apprised of the outcome of the detailed 
benchmarking of global tourism marketing strategies  and National Tourism Boards of the 
top 10 source markets carried out by the Ministry of Tourism.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The Committee observes that one of the major rea sons for India's Inbound 
Tourism remaining grossly under-utilized has been t he high rates and multiplicity of taxes 
that deter inbound Tourism and have led to tourist packages being out priced vis-a-vis those in 
competing tourist destinations of other countries. The tax structure applicable to hotel 
accommodation, air travel, food and beverages consu mption, etc., not only leads to tourist 
packages being overpriced but also obstructs seamless flow of tourists to our historical sites. The 
Committee notes that despite Inbound Tourism being a major foreign exchange earner with 
foreign exchange earnings of Rs. 2,11,661/- crore i n 2019, the taxes levied on Inbound Tourism 
are among the highest in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tax regime 
applicable to the travel and tourism sector be revi ewed holistically so that with suitable 
amendments India can convert its comparative natura l and economic advantages into 
competitive advantages for the tourism sector. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the 
steps taken and the result achieved in this regard. 
(Para 42) 
Reply of the Ministry  
2.1 The Ministry of Tourism has noted the recommend ation of the Committee. The Ministry 
will take up with the States to promote miniature s ouvenirs of historic monuments at various 
tourist destinations to create opportunities for the local community.  
 

Page 6 of 11 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
2.2 The Committee notes that the Ministry’s reply i s not in line with the 
recommendation of the Committee. The Committee reit erates that higher tax on inbound 
tourism raises tax revenue but can have a detriment al impact on the economy, foreign 
tourist arrivals and tourism competitiveness of a c ountry. Evaluating/reviewing the effect 
of tourism tax on Indian destinations that are entirely tourism dependent is also essential to 
sustain the local communities and various tourism a gencies. The Committee would like to 
be apprised of the steps taken by the Ministry as r egards the holistic review/evaluation of 
the tax regime applicable on the Indian travel and tourism sector. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee takes note of the written submissi ons of the Ministry of Tourism that “In 
order to forge partnership with Indian Missions for  Inbound Tourism and ensure effective 
implementation, a detailed framework has been evolv ed covering the vision and objectives, key 
strategic areas and governance of the institutional  arrangements.” The Committee also takes 
note of the key strategies envisaged by the Ministr y for promotion of Inbound Tourism like a 
holistic approach to it, country-specific strategic  plans, promotion of Medical and Wellness 
Tourism, promotion of MICE Tourism, etc. The Commit tee welcomes these developments but 
would like the Ministry to undertake concurrent and  impact evaluation of these strategies. 
Surveys may also be conducted periodically in impor tant source markets for India to assess the 
impact of the publicity campaigns on the decision of foreign tourists to visit India, the perception 
of the foreign tourists about the various facilitie s at tourist destinations, the preference of 
foreign tourists about the tourism products and destinations. 
(Para 43) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The Country specific strategy papers have been prepared by 20 Indian missions abroad 
for the focused promotion of Incredible India in re spective source markets. After due 
consultation with identified Central Ministries/ St ate Governments/ UT Administrations and 
Industry stakeholders, Ministry of Tourism has form ulated National Strategy and Roadmap for 
Medical  and Wellness Tourism and National strategy  for MICE Industry in January, 2022 and 
April, 2022, respectively. 
 
3.2 The recommendations/observations of the Committ ee are noted.  
 
 

Page 7 of 11 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry has not g iven any details of proposed 
surveys to be conducted in important source markets  for India.  The Committee observes 
that as per the information on the Website of the M inistry, the Market Research Division 
of the Ministry had last conducted surveys in the O verseas Markets of Japan, Germany, 
Russia, South Africa, South Korea and Turkey in Aug ust, 2016. The Tourism Satellite 
Account (TSA) which helps in assessing the size and  contribution of tourism to the 
economy using data from domestic and international tourism surveys was also last 
conducted in 2015-16.  The COVID pandemic had a per vasive effect on tourist behavior, 
impacting travel patterns, destination preferences,  duration of trips etc.  The Committee 
observes that no significant post-COVID surveys app ear to have been conducted by the 
Ministry to assess the changes in travel behaviour and attitudes, the Indian tourism 
industry’s post COVID preparedness and the perceptions of foreign tourists about India as 
a Safe Travel Destination in the post pandemic era.  The Committee desires to know about 
the action taken by the Ministry regarding periodic conduct of such surveys.  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Committee notes that on a request from Minis try of Tourism, the Ministry of External 
Affairs has appointed dedicated tourist officers in  20 Indian Missions abroad, which are key 
tourism source markets or potential markets for Ind ia. The Committee welcomes this step but 
exhorts the Government to create convergence and sy nergy among various ministries and 
stakeholders so that brand 'Incredible India' can b e promoted more effectively. The Committee 
would like to be apprised of the efficacy of appoin ting dedicated tourism officers in Indian 
Missions and embassies in showcasing and promoting the tourism destinations of the country in 
source markets. 
(Para 46) 
Reply of the Ministry  
4.1 The Ministry of External Affairs has informed t hat  Missions/Posts regularly promote 
‘Incredible India’ including Indian culture, herita ge, cinema, food, Indian Perspective, etc. 
through advertisements, seminars, exhibitions, show s, social media handles. The Twitter and 
Facebook page followers of the Missions/Posts have been growing consistently along with an 
increase in percentage of local followers. 
 
4.2 Dedicated Tourism Officers have been appointed in 20 Missions. Tourism Officers in the 
Missions/Embassies are of the rank Second Secretary /First Secretary. They report to

Ambassador/ Consul General/ DCM/ DCG and have 1-2 s upport staff usually. An IFS 
Officer/MEA personnel serving in the Mission is appointed as Tourism Officer. 
 
4.3 The officer working in the Commerce Wing is usu ally given the responsibility of 
handling the tourism work. These Officers have subm itted to Ministry of Tourism, country-
specific strategy papers for promoting tourism to I ndia, in which they have shared valuable 
suggestions like giving free familiarization differ ent parts of India, organizing Thematic 
Conclaves such as on Yoga, Gastronomy, Buddhism; Ma rketing may be increased by Blog 
Writers/ Travel Writers etc. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
4.4 The Committee would like to be informed about t he impact of the appointment of 
Tourism Officers in 20 Indian Missions abroad, the action taken by the Ministry on each of 
the country-specific strategies and suggestions sub mitted by the Tourism officers and the 
outcomes of the same.

4. The Committee observes that the success of a por t project can be ensured only if careful 
planning is made at the formulation stage itself re garding evacuation and connectivity by 
involving Railway Authorities/ NHAI etc., addressin g all technical aspects. The Committee 
emphasizes that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways, waterways etc. should be 
part of the infrastructure planning process right f rom inception stage. Approach to a port from 
the hinterland can be critical enough to make or ma r a Terminal because it determines the 
turnaround time and evacuation time - vital to the functioning of a port. Evacuation is a vital 
component of any port project as the capacity and e fficiency of the port vitally depend on the 
rate at which the cargo can be evacuated from the t erminal. The efficiency, viability and 
business depend on how well connected the port is. The Committee therefore recommends that 
the measures to be taken for the connectivity of a port to the roads and railway networks, to 
airports, to service roads connecting nearby towns and villages should be an essential 
component of the project from its formulation stage itself and be a part of the Detailed Appraisal 
Report so that the integrated infrastructure can be  developed with proper connectivity and 
interlinking. Despite the enormous importance of th e connectivity of ports, the Committee feels

very few connectivity projects relating to minor po rts. The Committee notes that the MMLPs 
planned at strategic locations in the country would  bring down logistics costs and boost the

remaining MMLPs. The importance of a modern and eff icient logistics network can not be 
overemphasized. Poor connectivity across various lo gistic modes not only increases the wear 
and tear of transport means and damages to goods, b ut also leads to uncertainty in supply 
chains leading to further decrease in the route uti lization by trade and thus, increasing rates for

11. The Committee notes that dredging comprises cap ital dredging and maintenance 
dredging. Capital dredging is done to either create  new channels, basins, berths, etc. or to 
deepen the existing such infrastructure. Such dredg ing is highly capital intensive. Presently, 
most of the ports in India are meeting their expend iture towards maintenance and capital 
dredging through their internal resources. The Comm ittee has been informed that dredging 
constitutes a major portion of total project cost a s well as operating cost and if it is funded 
through internal resources and borrowings, it entai ls an increase in overall port cost and 
consequently tariff. The Committee has also been in formed by stakeholders that one of the 
reasons behind high Vessels Related Charges (VRC) i n India is the inclusion of dredging cost in 
computation of tariff and that is why Indian ports are touted as high cost ports. The Committee 
has further been informed by the stakeholders that the concept of full cost recovery from direct 
users/ beneficiaries is not followed in Canada, Jap an and most West European countries. 
Internationally, and especially in developed countries, port channels are used as a national asset 
and dredging projects are funded by local municipal ities or Governments, and not by ports 
themselves. One of the most comprehensive legislati ons on cost sharing in dredging is the US 
Water Resources Development Act, 1987 under which t he Federal Government meets 50% to 
90% of the dredging costs. Similarly, dredging is t he responsibility of the National Government 
at Colombo. Taking into account the above fact, the  Committee recommends that the 
Government should explore the possibility of treati ng the channels as a national asset and 
funding the entire dredging cost. The Committee wou ld also like the Ministry to study different 
practices in other countries for funding dredging, both capital and maintenance, and formulate a 
funding mechanism in respect of Indian ports.

1. The Committee notes that the Deputy Commissioner s of Railway Safety come from 
Ministry of Railways on deputation basis and go bac k to the Ministry after completion of their 
deputation period. The Committee notes that the Deputy CRS is one of the senior most officers in 
the circle offices and comes second in hierarchy af ter the CRS. The Committee feels that such an 
important post should not be filled up on deputatio n basis, as the incumbent may not be inclined 
to give suggestions/ recommendations in his Reports  against the Ministry of Railways, to which 
he originally belongs and would be sent back after his deputation period is over. The Committee 
recommends that the officers of the rank of Deputy CRS should be appointed in the Commission 
on absorption basis, just like the CRS and it should not be a deputation post. The Committee is of 
the firm view that appointing Deputy CRS on absorption basis will ensure grant of full autonomy 
which would make the Commission more independent and effective. 
 (Para 17) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 As per Recruitment Rules of the post of Dy. CRS , the officers are equivalent to Director 
rank officer i.e. level-13 whereas CRSs are of Addi tional Secretary rank officer i.e. Level-15, 
which are recruited on absorption basis from amongs t Railway Officers with minimum 05 years 
service in Level 14. Hence, if Dy. CRSs are selecte d on permanent absorption basis in the 
Commission under Ministry of Civil Aviation, there will hardly be any promotion avenue for 
Dy.CRS. Hence, existing system of taking officers on deputation seems adequate.

are located near the National Highways yet the stat e of the last mile connectivity from the

quality last mile connectivity is important to ensu re a positive experience for tourists visiting a 
tourist destination in the country, which in turn, helps attract more tourists through word-of-
mouth publicity. The Committee therefore recommends  that Ministry may examine the 
state/quality of last mile connectivity roads at al l such tourist spots near the National Highways 
at the earliest and ensure their construction and m aintenance with the concerned 
Ministries/agencies to make the tourist places more  accessible to tourists, both domestic and 
international, which will invariably increase the number of tourists visiting such places.

noted in order to provide more thrust towards this intervention.

Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do

 India has always been one of the richest countries in the world in terms of archaeological and 
cultural wealth but the protection of this rich cultural herit age has always posed a challenge . In 
medieval times, invaders like Nadir Shah carried off a great many priceless gems and jewels and 
ancient fabled treasures. Under British colonial rule, there was a systematic and rapacious looting of 
India’s treasures. British museums today are filled with priceless antiques from India like the 
Sultanganj Bud dha, Maharaja Ranjit Singh’s throne and the sword and rings of Tipu Sultan. The 
looting of India’s treasures did not stop with independence from colonial rule but the heritage theft in 
the post-independence era has not gained as much prominence and visibility.   
2. While the colonial plunder of India’s tangible cultural heritage is well known, the 
contemporary rampant theft and smuggling of countless idols, antiquities and artefacts from the 
temples, forts, archaeological sites and even museums in modern In dia has gone largely unheeded.  
Many of these incidents of heritage theft are often not reported to the law enforcement agencies or to 
the ASI, possibly because no one knows exactly what has been stolen and when it has been stolen. 
As per UNESCO estimates, about 50,000 idols and artefacts had been stolen out of India till 1989. 
Despite various measures taken by the Government to curb smuggling of the Indian cultural wealth, 
many challenges still prevail in the process of  documentation, identification, safe guarding and 
repatriation of antiquities and lost cultural wealth.  
3. Cognizant of the massive scale of looting of our priceless antiquities, the Committee decided 
to take up the subject ‘Heritage Theft – The Illegal Trade in Indian Antiquities and challe nges of 
retrieving and safeguarding our Tangible Cultural Heritage’. The Ministry of Culture and its attached 
office of the Archaeological Survey of India are the nodal organisations concerned with the 
preservation and conservation of antiquities, but the humongous volume of our cultural wealth 
spread throughout the country and the sheer scale of theft of antiquities taking place means that the 
exercise of preservation of our cultural treasures requires the involvement of many government 
departments, NGOs a nd civil society organisations. The Committee , therefore, heard the Ministries 
of Culture, Home Affairs, External Affairs; Archaeological Survey of India (ASI); Directorate of 
Enforcement (ED); Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI); Central Board of In direct Taxes and 
Customs (CBIC); Idol Wing of the Tamil Nadu Police; and Indian National Trust for Art and 
Cultural Heritage (INTACH) in its meetings held on 15 th November, 2022; 25 th November, 2022; 
22nd December, 2022; and 5th January, 2023.

Documentation of Tangible Cultural Heritage 
4. The Ministry of Culture informed the Committee that documentation of antiquities plays a 
very vital role in retrieving or claiming the stolen antiquities and proving the ownership of the said 
antiquity. India has a vast heritage and cultural repositories that are scattered all over the country. 
Some are protected by ASI, some are under state government and some are under Trusts/ local 
authority/ private ownership, etc. A big chunk of movable heritage is unprote cted and scattered all 
over the country without any vigilance and protection. While theft of antiquities in the Centrally 
Protected Monuments/sites under ASI and under State Governments is immediately reported and FIR 
is lodged, theft of unprotected antiquities which are neither documented nor reported makes retrieval 
of stolen property very difficult. The documentation of all such antiquities in the form of digitized 
records alongwith maintenance and periodic auditing of inventory is the first step to ensu re the 
safeguarding of India’s tangible cultural heritage. In this regard, the Government had launched a 
National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (NMMA) to document the country’s monuments 
and antiquities which will help in creating a database of all antiquities and can be referred to readily 
in case of fraudulent dealings or theft in antiquities. 
 
National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities 
5. The National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (NMMA) was launched on 19 th March, 
2007 for an initial pe riod of 5 years from 2007 to 2012. It was extended for a further period of 5 
years till 2017 and was later merged with Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). The objectives of 
NMMA are as follows: 
 Documentation and creation of suitable database on built her itage and sites through published 
and unpublished secondary sources for information and dissemination to planners, researchers, 
etc. and for better management of such cultural resources. 
 Documentation in a uniform manner developed by NMMA, of all Antiquiti es that are available 
in different formats in the form of Registered Antiquities, Catalogued Antiquities with Central as 
well as State Governments, Private museums and Collections, Universities, etc.

 Promote awareness and sensitize people concerning the be nefits of preserving the historical and 
cultural aspects of built heritage, sites and antiquities. 
 Extend training facility and capacity building to the concerned State Departments, Local bodies, 
NGOs, Universities, Museums, Local communities etc. Help in developing synergy between 
Archaeological Survey of India, State Departments, concerned Institutions and NGOs to 
generate close interaction.

27. The Ministry informed the Committee that the creation of database to prevent theft of

49. The Ministry informed the Committee that a certa in category of Antiquities (which ar e more 
than 100 years old) needs  to be registered under the “Antiquities and Art Treasures (AAT) Act, 
1972”. As per S.O.448(E), dated 2.7.1976 as amended by S.O. 397 (E), dated 15.5.1980, painting 
and sculpture in all me diums (which are 100 years old) and Manuscript containing painting 
illustration and illuminations (which are 75 years old); need to be registered by the owners with ASI. 
Till date, ASI has registered approximately 3,52,484 antiquities and all the records a re adequately 
maintained with the Data Bank. It is to mention here that on the basis of records of registration, 
various antiquities have been claimed from Germany (Mahishasurmardini from J&K), USA 
(standing Buddha from Bihar), etc., and brought back to th e country. Section 14 of the AAT Act, 
1972 provides for registration of antiquities, which is as follows:- 
    “14. Registration of antiquities —(1) The Central Government may, from time to time, by 
notification in the Official Gazette, specify those antiquities which shall be registered under this 
Act. (2) In specifying the antiquities under sub -section (1), the Central Government shall have 
regard to the following factors, namely: - (i) the necessity for conserving the objects of art; (ii) the 
need to preserve such objects within India for the better appreciation of the cultural heritage of 
India; (iii) such other factors as will, or are likely to, contribute to the safeguarding of the cultural 
heritage of India. (3) Every person who owns, controls or is in possession of any antiquity specified 
in the notification issued under sub -section (1) shall register such antiquity before the registering 
officer— (a) in the case of a person who owns, controls or possesses such antiquity on the date of 
issue of such notification, within three months of such date; and (b) in the case of any other person, 
within fifteen days of the date on which he comes into ownership, control or possession of such 
antiquity, and obtain a certificate in token of such registration.”

Risk Management System (RMS) 
90. The Risk Management System (RMS) con sistently aims to strike a balance between trade 
facilitation and Customs interdictions. It aims to support the field officers in effective decision 
making by providing them with all the relevant information regarding an incoming or outgoing 
consignment. E valuation of consignments is done by using a host of risk parameters which are 
continuously evolved by using local, national and international risk trends, offence databases and 
feedbacks from the field received. Only the consignments deemed risky on any of the evolved factors 
are sent to the field officers for Assessment or Examination purposes. On the basis of the analysis of 
the self -declaration made by importer/exporter, Shipping Lines, Vessels involved, various risk 
factors are identified. The paramete rs are determined utilizing details such as the countries/ports 
involved; exporter/importer involved; consignee/supplier involved; commodities declared; Import 
General Manifest (IGM)/ Export General Manifest (EGM) declarations; past behaviour of entities 
involved etc.

Amendments to the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972  
138. The Ministry submitted the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act”  of 1972 was implemented in 
1976 to regulate the internal trade in antiquities/ art treasures, prevention of smuggling and export of 
antiquities, and, fraudulent dealings in antiquities/ art treasures. The main provisions of the Act are as 
follows:- 
 Under Section 3 of the Act, only the Central Government can export antiquities.  Generally, this 
is only for the temporary permits for exhibitions or for temporary loans; antiquities are sent 
abroad and they are brought back.   
 One of the main objectives o f this Act is prevention of smuggling and fraudulent dealing, and it 
controls the sale of antiquities.  Under the provisions of this Act, no person, without the licence 
given from the licensing officer who is a senior officer of the Archaeological Survey o f India, 
can sell or offer to sell any antiquity. Antiquities cannot be sold in open market.  Only the licence 
holders can sell these and there are strict provisions in this regard.  They have to keep a proper 
record of all the antiquities which they have received with the details and photographs.  From 
time to time, these stocks are checked and also the sales which they have made.  So, within the 
country, they can sell it following the procedure which has been laid down in the Act. 
 There is also a provisio n of compulsory acquisition.  If the Government feels that any antiquity, 
is of importance and should be displayed or preserved at a public place for the public, any art 
object or any antiquity can be purchased compulsorily or acquired by the Government an d it can 
be displayed in the museum or can be kept in safe custody for the public benefit except the 
objects which are associated with religious practices.   
 There is also a provision for registration of antiquities, for certain classes of antiquities.  Th e 
Government, through a notification, can define as to which antiquities should be registered.  
Once the notification is issued, registration of such antiquities is a must.  
 If cases of theft are to be filed, there are provisions under the Act and the DG g ives the 
authorisation for filing the case in the AAT Act.

158. The early history of Kohinoor  is debatable but it definitely adorned the P eacock Throne of 
Shah Jahan, lodged on the head of a gemstone peacock at the very top of the throne. After the decline 
of the Mughals, the gemstone went into  the possession of various persons until Maharaja Ranjit

the throne eventually passed to Maharaja Duleep Singh, a minor. In 1849, the British annexed Punjab 
and imprisoned Rani Jind Kaur, the Maharaja’s mother. Maharaja Duleep Singh then 10 years old, 
signed the T reaty of Lahore ceding his assets including the Kohinoor diamond to Queen Victoria. 
The Kohinoor is in the hands of the British since then.

Annexure-V 
Modus Operandi adopted for Smuggling of Antiquities 
The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) informed the Committee that the Directorate is investigating a 
number of cases related to smuggling/theft of Art and Antiquities objects under the provisions of 
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. The investigation conducted by the Directorate 
of Enforcement has revealed following modus operandi adopted by the accused persons:- 
Modus Operandi-1 where buyer is the mastermind 
In these types of cases, the antique smugglers first select a temple to carry out thef t/stealing antique 
idols of Hindu deities. Then, they visit the temple site to ascertain the timings, dates, crowding at the 
temple etc. They also enquire from people living around the vicinity of the targeted temples and try 
to gather details of antique i dols which were kept in the temples. After getting these details, the date 
for stealing of the antique idols is decided. The theft is carried out in the night. After theft the antique 
idols are transported from that place to the person (broker) who is hand ling all the activities on 
behalf of the Mastermind Smuggler sitting outside India. The broker gives some money in cash, to 
all the participants of the theft as a commission and keep all the antique idols. 
Thereafter, the broker, who is the owner of an art  gallery, fabricates the letterhead of another art 
gallery as if the stolen idols are newly made handicrafts items and attempts to export the same to the 
mastermind in a foreign country by approaching Handicrafts Department to obtain a Certificate for 
newly made handicrafts. The stolen idols are mixed or replaced with the newly made handicrafts 
items subsequently. The Certificate obtained from the Handicrafts Department is produced before the 
Customs Authority at the time of exporting the stolen idols to th e mastermind. After receiving the 
idols, the mastermind sends commission money to the broker who is in India in his bank accounts in 
the guise of payment made towards the purchase of Handicrafts items. The mastermind sells these 
antique idols in the intern ational market at exorbitant rates and acquires illegal money. The value of 
the smuggled antique idols is estimated to be in several crores in the international market. 
Modus Operandi-2 where buyer is identified after execution of theft 
In these cases, the  accused first steals the antiquities from the unknown historical places, 
archaeological excavation sites, ancient temples etc. Then, the stolen antiquity is taken to another 
place till the buyer is found and deal is materialized. After receipt of desired amount, the antiquities 
are smuggled/exported in the guise of exportable goods to the address of buyer. In one of the cases, 

Page 102 of 108 
 
the accused tried to ship the antiquities through courier in the form of ‘Brass Hindu four handed lord 
Vishnu statue’ and ‘Vintage brass tobacco weighing scale’ before being apprehended. In other case, 
the accused was apprehended with the unknown antiquity in his possession. The accused was 
searching for a buyer for the antiquity for an amount of Rs. 5 crore.

Details of Subhash Kapoor case  
 
Subhash Kapoor, a US citizen and owner of New York based Art Gallery - Art of the Past was found to 
be the mastermind behind smuggling of a large number of Antiques from India.  
 An intelligence was passed on by DRI to its overseas officer in New York on 14.02.2007 
regarding smuggling of antiquities in a shipment that was declared to contain “Garden Tea Sets” 
in the shipping bill presented in India. The said shipment was exported by “ Palace Knit Exports, 
Ludhiana” to “Nimbus Import Export Inc., NY”.  
 The said intelligence was shared by the overseas officer in New York with the officers of US 
Customs and Border Protection (CBP). 
  The shipment was, however, declared to US Customs as cont aining antiquities (in addition to 
items like marble tables). The importer had declared these items as antiquities pertaining to the 
period 2nd Century to 19th Century and valued at USD 60,400, in the invoice dated 05.01.2007.  
 The shipment of seven wooden  crates was detained and later examined by US Customs in the 
presence of overseas officer at New York on 22.02.2007 and it was found to contain, inter alia, 
various idols/figurines (mostly of metals). The Indian exporter and CHA denied having exported 
the consignment. The telephone number given on one of the import documents in USA was 
found to belong to “Art of the Past Inc.” (website: www.artofpast.com), a company located in 
New York, dealing in Asian antiquities and owned by Mr. Subhash Kapoor.  
 The examined antiquities were seized by US CBP and they conducted follow up. 
Simultaneously, surveillance and searches were also carried out by DRI in India on various 
exporters around the country, suspected to have links with smuggling of antiques.  
 A cla im was lodged in New York with the US Customs & Border Protection (CBP) for 
restitution of the seized Indian antiquities in August 2007.  
  Investigations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) of the U.S.A searched various galleries and 
warehouses owned/controlled by Mr. Subash Kapoor in USA on 5th January 2012 and recovered 
more than 2000 antiquities, valued at more than Rs. 1000 Crore. Some of these were of Indian 
origin. It was further revealed that he had supplied a number of antiquities to various US Art 
Galleries/ Museums/Private collectors. In cooperation with US enforcement agencies, these were 
recovered from time to time.

Legal/ Constitutional Position of Retrieval of Antiquities taken out of the Country prior to 
Independence   
Article 253 of the Constitution of India reads as under: 
“ Legislation for giving effect to international agreements.- 
 Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power 
to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any 
treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at 
any international conference, association or other body” 
Section 166A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is as follows: 
“Letter of request competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India. 
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Code, if, in the course of an investigation into 
an offence, an application is made by the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank 
to the investigating officer that evidence may be available in a country or place outside India, 
any Criminal Court may issue a letter of request to a Court or an authority in that country or 
place competent to deal with such request to examine orally any person supposed to be 
acquainted with the facts and circumstances o f the case and to record his statement made in 
the course of such examination and also to require such person or any other person to 
produce any document or thing which may be in his possession pertaining to the case and to 
forward all the evidence so taken or collected or the authenticated copies thereof or the thing 
so collected to the Court issuing such letter. 
(2) The letter of request shall be transmitted in such manner as the Central Government may 
specify in this behalf. 
(3) Every statement recorded or document or thing received under sub - section (1) shall be 
deemed to be the evidence collected during the course of investigation under this Chapter.

that a lot of idols are found while digging/ploughing the land, the Chairman, INTACH 
narrated an incident in Gorakhpur, where INTACH had persuaded villagers to install such 
idols after conservation in t heir temples thus ensuring public participation in conservation of 
heritage.  The Chairman, INTACH also stressed the importance of preservation of 
numismatics, including coins, bank notes, medals, tokens etc, as tangible items of historical 
importance as such small items get less focus than massive sculptures and idols and are more 
liable to be melted in furnaces. He drew the attention of the Committee to the heavy tax of 
about 38 per cent levied on account of packing and insurance charges on items of our c ultural 
heritage, including coins, brought back from abroad through proper channels which may be 
reduced to 5% and the general  lack of laws/guidelines in India in this regard. He mentioned 
that in absence of penal provisions in the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, heritage 
theft is covered under simple theft under IPC.    He urged that stringent penalizing provisions 
should be added to 'The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972' and that an Enforcement 
Agency should be established in every Sta te under this Act.  He also brought to the notice of 
the Committee the large number of art objects lying in police stations across the country as 
Case properties for many years, in neglected conditions. The Chairman, INTACH also 
pointed out that nearly 440 0 objects had vanished from the protected sites of ASI and State 
sites and the situation in the unprotected heritage sites was likely to grow much worse. The 
Chairman of the Committee remarked that Section 25 of the Antiquities Act had penal 
provisions, al beit insufficient,  but INTACH could give in writing their observations and 

113 
 
suggestions regarding penal provisions so that the Committee could make suitably 
incorporate them in its recommendations.  
6.     A Member enquired about the number of antiquities l ost before and after 'The 
Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972' came into being,   the number of antiquities 
recovered and the steps taken by INTACH to recover antiquities lying outside the country

now under the control of Railways, enquired whether such heritage monuments under the

their conservation. The Chairman, INTACH, stressed  that the function of INTACH which is

conservation expertise with the small budget of 13 crores available to the organization. 
 Documentation of art objects is time -consuming and expensive and is the responsibility of 
National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities of the Government of India. Upon a query 
regarding INTACH’s work in preservation of old buildings, the Chairman replied that

10. The Secretary, M/o Culture informed the Committee that the mandate of the Ministry 
is to preserve, prote ct and disseminate Indian culture within and outside the country and the

India and showcase them as tourist sites. The Secretary acknowledged that the subject of 
heritage theft also came under the ASI which implements the Antiquities and Art Treasures 
Act (AAT) 1972 to regulate the internal trade in antiquities/art treasures and prevent 
smuggling/ export/ fraudulent dealing of antiquities and art treasures. The Comm ittee was 
also informed about the compulsory acquisition of antiquities under the AAT Act and 
mandatory requirement of registration of certain classes of antiquities after notification by the

never been done and that the rate of registration, at about Rs 3 to 5 lakhs, was very low due to 
concern among citizens about the consequences of registration. However, ASI was spreading 
awareness about the importance of registration,  and ways of making the registration process 
simpler were being explored. 
  
11. The Committee was informed that legislation, security and retrieval were the 
processes through which Government tries to prevent heritage theft and illegal trade of Indian 
antiquities. Ancient Monuments & Archaeological Sites & Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958 
was modified to authorize the government to issue a notice prohibiting the removal or 
transportation of antiquities from places of their specific locations and punish violators with a 
jail term. Also, ASI communicates/ consults with other nations to bring ba ck smuggled 

119 
 
Indian antiquities from foreign countries under the 1970 United Nations Convention, which 
prohibits and prevents the illicit import, export and transfer of ownership of cultural property 
and which was ratified by India in 1972. ASI apprised the  Committee of the challenges faced 
by it in retrieval and safeguarding Indian tangible/cultural heritage, art and antiquities, such 
as, lack of coordination on part of State Govts and law -enforcement agencies, lack of 
awareness about antiquity documentation, lack of documented database of Indian antiquities, 
distrust and fear among people in case of mandatory antiquity registration, need for a more 
convenient/reliable antiquity registration system, etc.. 
  
12. The ASI informed the Committee that cognizant o f the need to document all antiques 
in the country, including those with private persons/institutions, the Government had, in 
2007, started a National Mission for Monuments and Antiquities. Out of an estimated 54 lakh 
antiquities in the country, this Mission had so far documented 16.7 lakh antiquities, including 
3.52 lakh antiquities which are registered antiquities. The ASI had also initiated 
documentation of its 52 site museums which contain all the excavated material. This  process 
is expected to be completed by the end of 2023. 
  
13.       The Committee was informed that keeping antiquities secure and tracking them in 
case of theft is much easier in monuments under Central Government as round the clock 
security, watch & ward staff, state police and Centr al Industrial Security Force (CISF) have 
been deployed in the monuments/museums under preventive measures. In such cases, FIR is 
lodged immediately and a “Look Out” Notice is issued through the CBI and all the Custom 
exit channels are alerted. In the case of State protected monuments, FIR is generally lodged 
but the relevant information does  not come to the ASI. Tracing and retrieval of antiquities 
which are unprotected or under private ownership is the most challenging as in case of theft, 
they are mostly reported as general theft and the information generally is neither reported to 
the State Government or the ASI. Also, the ASI has interactions with and conducts training 
programmes for various investigative agencies including CBI and customs authorities an d 
from time to time to sensitize their employees about heritage loss.  ASI officials are also 
deputed from time to time to conduct joint or surprise checks to curb fraudulent dealing of 
antiquities, check stocks of different dealers etc. Besides, in case o f suspicious consignments 
in the major customs channels of Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Jodhpur and Thiruvananthapuram, 
Archaeological officers are deputed to examine such objects along with Customs Officials. 
These efforts have resulted in reduction in number of thefts and higher rate of  recovery of 

120 
 
stolen antiquities. Once the objects are held, they become “Case Property” and kept in police 
custody till the case is settled, upon which they are returned to the owner and if the owner is 
not known, they are confi scated by ASI and then generally stored in the Central Antiquity 
Collection, Purana Qila.

between the years 2014 to 2022 as compared to only 13 from 1976 upto 2 014. The process of 
retrieval involves the MEA which plays a key role in negotiations with the foreign 
authorities. However, foreign museums are reluctant to return Indian antiquities despite 
availability of documents/evidence and often took recourse to th eir domestic laws which 
prohibit the export of any antiquity. Thus, use of international fora was necessary for 
consensus among nations for the retrieval of stolen heritage.  It was informed that the 
restitution of cultural property was one of the importan t items on the agenda of the Ministry 
of Culture for the upcoming G20 summit to be presided over by India. ASI was also working 
on the possibility of foreign museums at least acknowledging the provenance of Indian 
antiquities in their possession, even if the objects are not returned to India.

which are difficult to identify without detailed scientific analysis. The Ministry also   apprised
