cultural heritage and also has 165 current research items. Besides, the Sangeet Natak 
Akademi, an autonomous body under the Ministry also works towards preserving and 
promoting the rich Indian intangible cultural heritage.

Shri Mohammed Nadimul Haque, M.P., to present the abovementioned Reports in Rajya 

125 
 
Sabha on 23 rd December, 2022 and Shri Prince Raj, M.P. and in his absence, Shri Ramdas 
Chandrabhanji Tadas, M.P. to lay the Reports on the Table of Lok Sabha on the same date. 
6.         Thereafter, the Chairman welcomed the Director, Enforcement Directorate (ED);  
Special Secretary & Member, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC); 
Director General, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI); and other senior officials of the 
agencies to the meeting. He enquired from the agencies details of the role played by them in 
prevention of smuggling, and retrieving and safeguarding of antiquities. He so ught to know 
their views on the existing legislation/Acts/Rules to curb theft and smuggling of antiquities 
and the changes needed to be incorporated into the existing laws. He asked CBIC and DRI to 
share their views on the efficacy of the existing customs export procedures in tracking and 
prevention of smuggling of antiquities in the country and the loopholes therein. He further 
sought to know about the steps taken to ensure better coordination amongst CBIC, DRI, ED, 
Ministry of Culture, Archaeological Surv ey of India (ASI), State Police agencies and various 
other State Government law enforcing agencies to curb the theft and smuggling of antiquities 
at the State level itself. 
7.         Director, Enforcement Directorate informed the Committee that the smuggl ing of art 
and antiquities is an offence under the Antiquities and Art Treasures (AAT) Act and under 
various provisions of the IPC. He apprised the Committee that ED has two Acts – the 
Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and the Foreign Exchange Mana gement Act 
(FEMA). He stated that the ED registers a case under the PMLA as soon as there is an FIR 
with regard to smuggling of antiquities and there is predicate offence.   He informed that the 
focus of ED is to identify the proceeds of crime and that any person who has dealt with the 
proceeds of crime is dealt with under the provisions of the PMLA. He apprised the 
Committee about the various powers of ED under the PMLA, to seize the proceeds, 
investigate the accused, file a chargesheet upon completion of t he investigation, request the 
competent court to issue letter of request to other countries for obtaining information, for 
collecting evidence from other countries, to request the country concerned to freeze, seize, 
confiscate, and repatriate the assets, a nd for extradition of the accused if they have left the 
country after committing an offence under the PMLA. He further informed that under FEMA, 
ED can levy penalty and, in certain circumstances, attach the proceeds of crime in case 
somebody has parked mon ey which is generated from smuggling of antiquities, outside the 
country. 

126 
 
8.         Director, ED apprised the Committee that ED is investigating a couple of cases under 
the PMLA wherein the amount involved in a particular case pertaining to Tamil Nadu is 
nearly Rs. 800 crores, and that though the middleman in that case has been examined by ED, 
it could not arrest the accused because proceedings cannot be initiated under PMLA against a 
person extradited from a country by an agency not involved in the extrad ition proceedings 
unless and until the competent court in that country permits the same. He stated that 
nowadays both the agencies like CBI and ED jointly go for extradition proceedings to avoid 
facing the problems faced in this case. He informed the Commi ttee that under PMLA, all the 
categories of people involved in the cases of theft and smuggling of antiquity can be 
prosecuted – the person or gang involved in stealing of antiquities, the person involved in 
their sale, the person involved in their smuggli ng, the main kingpin who mostly resides 
outside the country and the person who purchases it. Briefing the Committee about the 
methodology for inter-agency coordination, he informed the Committee that the Customs and 
DRI file a prosecution complaint under S ection 208 of Criminal Procedure Code, on receipt 
of which, ED registers the case under the PMLA. He further stated that the Central Economic 
Intelligence Bureau (CEIB), a Central agency, coordinates among all the agencies. He further 
elaborated that under the provisions of PMLA, ED has sufficient power for the coordination 
and dissemination of information, for example, to the Law Enforcement Agency concerned, 
who is duty-bound to register the case. 
9.         Special Secretary & Member, CBIC informed the C ommittee that CBIC’s role as 
regards antiquities starts when the antiquities are being exported out of India. He stated that 
given a large number of passengers travelling out of India every year and the huge volume of 
trade from India, Customs authorities cannot check each consignment and/ or passenger as it 
would be against ‘Ease of Doing Business’ norms and the larger policy of facilitation of 
cargo exports. He stated that in case of passengers, the main check exercise is from the 
security perspective, with a minimal check of check -in baggage of passengers. He added that 
CBIC uses technological tools by way of advance passenger information system, applies a 
risk-based approach and identifies passengers who may be suspicious for a thorough 
checking. With re gard to cargo, he stated that CBIC employs risk -based management 
approach, which uses artificial intelligence machine -learning tools for identification of cargo 
which may be considered as risky for thorough examination. He informed that less than 10 
percent cargo is subjected to examination at the time of export and that there is possibility of 
concealing items given such large flow of cargo from the country. He stated that on receipt of 
intimation from State police/ ASI or any other authority regarding any  stolen antique, an alert 

127 
 
circular is issued to all customs formations to keep a watch. With regard to coordination with 
other agencies, he informed of forums like CEIB at the Central level and Regional Economic 
Intelligence Committees (REICs) at the State  level. He apprised the Committee about a case 
where Customs, using its channels abroad, informed the U.S. Customs administration about a 
consignment that went out of India, based on which the United States (U.S.) Customs and 
Border Protection agency inter cepted the consignment when it reached U.S. on basis of the 
information passed on by the DRI. 
10.       Special Secretary & Member, CBIC further informed the Committee that AAT 
provides for application of the Customs Act in relation to all antiquities and art treasures, 
allowing CBIC to seize such consignments at the time of export and that as per AAT, the 
determination of whether a suspected item is antique or not is done by a competent officer of 
ASI. He stated that the restitution of stolen antiquities c an be ensured only if the theft has 
already been reported in INTERPOL and it is duly registered. He briefed the Committee 
about two cases of antiquity theft that were detected/ prevented by DRI in the last five years.  
11.       Director General, Directora te of Revenue Intelligence apprised the Committee that 
DRI draws powers from the Customs Act and deals with anti -smuggling work, drug 
trafficking cases and customs duty evasion cases. He informed that the penalty prescribed 
under the Customs Act is three t imes the value of the goods and there is a provision for 
imprisonment of six months to three years, and up to seven years of imprisonment in case of 
repeat offences. He stated that the penal provisions take care of the deterrent effect for such 
crimes. He informed the Committee that DRI does passenger profiling in case of passenger 
movement and employs the techniques of getting the scanning inputs from the security 
agencies at the airports. He added that DRI applies risk parameters to the export 
consignments in the containers and has procedures of collection of intelligence to detect cases 
of smuggling. He stated that the wide definition of antiquities in the AAT Act poses a 
practical problem as the official who has intercepted an item cannot ascertain wheth er the 
item is antique or not. He further added that DRI coordinates with all other intelligence 
agencies and sources available within India and outside and has overseas officers posted in 
the Missions abroad, and these Missions, with the help of the Minis try of External Affairs, 
have been bringing the antiquities which had been seized abroad back to the country. 
12.       Members raised various queries regarding steps taken to curb smuggling of items 
across Bihar -Nepal border, possible measures for profili ng/identification of new persons 
involved in smuggling of antiquities based on risk analysis, restitution of seized antiquities to 

128 
 
respective temples or museums, tracking of illegally exported Indian antiquities being 
auctioned by auction houses, using art ificial intelligence and robotic technology for better 
checking of cargos to curb smuggling of antiquities, valuation of antiquities, list of stolen 
antiquities that have went out of India, trafficking of drugs through Gujarat and Maharashtra 
borders, details of antiquities missing from 12 missing monuments in Delhi, low conviction 
rate under PMLA, inadequacy of manpower available with CBIC at Kochi airport, tackling 
the issue of display of fake antiquities in private galleries and museums, number of Indian  
antiquities brought back to India out of the 2000 antiquities seized by the Investigations and 
Customs Enforcement (ICE) of the U.S.A, feasibility of a barter system to exchange 
antiquities belonging to other nations and compulsory installation of CCTV ca meras at 
archaeological sites and temples, etc. 
13.       On the query raised by one of the Members regarding low conviction rate under 
PMLA, Director, ED replied that their conviction rate is 95.2%. He added that 1,100 cases 
are on trial but in a large nu mber of cases the prosecution is pending because the police has 
not filed a chargesheet. He further informed the Committee that ED has attached the proceeds 
of crimes of Rs. 1,05,000 crores out of which, in four cases, assets of Rs. 15,000 crores have 
been returned to the banks. He apprised the Committee about the problem faced in valuation 
of antiques as there is no standard method of valuation of antiques in the economic sense and 
that ASI follows its own methodology of valuation of antiques and paintings . Citing his 
experience of valuation of antiques as an erstwhile Member of Tirumala Tirupati 
Devasthanam, the Chairman stressed upon the need for a methodology for valuation of 
antiquities by the appropriate agencies which would be useful in case some untoward incident 
happens.  
14.       Special Secretary & Member, CBIC briefed the Committee about the process of 
checks performed by CBIC on containers to be exported. He stated that Customs allowed 
self-sealing of containers in their premises, so the exporter seals the goods in a container with 
an electronic seal and Customs just checks the integrity of the seal,  thus more than 90 
percent of such containers are exported without examination by Customs. Based on the Risk 
Management System, CBIC examines some co ntainers, which strikes a balance between 
enforcement and facilitation. Responding to some of the issues raised by the Member, he 
shared that Customs is aware of the challenges of the Indo -Nepal border and has a number of 
land Customs stations for the bord er. He also informed the Committee about the repatriation 
of seven artefacts from Glasgow Museum, United Kingdom (UK) and a stolen 10 th century 

129 
 
Goat-headed Yogini’s sculpture to the High Commission of India, UK through the efforts of 
overseas Customs Officers of India. He further stated that the recruitment of  Group ‘B’ level 
non-gazetted officials  is presently done through Staff Selection Commission which takes a 
cycle of two to three years and that the  issue of lack of manpower can be tackled if the time 
period for recruitment can be shortened. 
15.       The Chairman directed that written replies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week. 
 (The witnesses then withdrew) 
16.     The Committee further decided to undertake a Study Vis it to Thiruvananthapuram, 
Bekal and Mangaluru for holding meetings and visits from 16th January to 20th January, 2023, 
for detailed examination of various subjects  viz., Progress and Implementation of PM Gati 
Shakti National Master Plan for Multi -modal Connectivity; Development of Greenfield and 
Brownfield Airports and Issues Pertaining to Civil Enclaves in Defence Airports, with 
reference to airports in Kerala and Karnataka; Heritage Theft – The Illegal Trade in Indian 
Antiquities and the Challenges of Retrieving and Safeguarding Our Tangible Cultural 
Heritage; Examination of Draft National Tourism Policy  and ‘Functioning of Major Ports in 
the Country’ with reference to the status of New Mangalore Port Authority.   The Committee 
also decided that it may i nteract with various stakeholders and representatives of the State 
Governments of Kerala and Karnataka on these subjects. The Committee authorized the 
Chairman of the Committee to seek necessary approvals from the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya 
Sabha for the purpose. 
17.    A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept. 
18.     The meeting adjourned at 4:47 PM.

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the various Ministries to expedite the 
implementation of the Port Connectivity Projects. It also notes that the Ministry of Road 
Transport & Highways and NHAI has also carried out a detaile d prioritization exercise and 
had shortlisted 38 road connectivity projects which are at DPR stage and likely to be 
awarded by the F.Y. 2022. The Committee is of the opinion that such a capital -intensive 
infrastructure project which seeks to improve port, rail and road connectivity involving 
various ministries, State Governments can be successful, only if all the concerned agencies 
give utmost attention to the time bound completion of the portion of work allocated to each 
one and maintain close coordination  cooperation amongst themselves. The Committee hopes 
that all out efforts would be made by all the stakeholders to complete the work allocated 
within the time schedule. The Committee also desires to know the status of the award of work 
relating to the 38 road connectivity projects and the percentage of work completed.

1.2 However, after the latest exercise of Comprehensive Port Connectivity Plan (CPCP) 
prepared by DPIIT and shared in September 2022, 55 port road connectivity projects under 
MoRTH were prioritized. The status of these projects as shared by MoRTH is giv en in

Logistics Management Ltd. (NHLML) has been incorporated in 2020 to develop Multimodal

Logistic Parks (MMLPs) and works related to National Highways connectivity to ports. The 
Committee is of the firm opinion that the MMLPs is a step in the right direction and such 
parks, if planned at strategic locations in the country would bring down logistics costs and 
boost the national economy. The parks will enable the shift from a point -to- point to a hub –
and-spoke model in logistics sector, eventually helping to bring down logistics costs and 
enabling more efficient movement through new -generation vehicles. The importance of a 
modern and effic ient logistics network cannot be overemphasized. Poor connectivity across 
various logistics modes not only increases the wear and tear of transport means and damages 
to goods, but also leads to uncertainty in supply chains leading to further decrease in th e 
route utilization by trade and thus, increasing transportation costs for the remaining users. 
Sagarmala aims at construction of wider roads for connectivity of Ports to another point. 
However, unfortunately, the Committee noticed that in some cases the S agarmala Projects 
are undertaken only up to major crossroads on the route and thereafter no effort is made to 
construct road up to point envisaged in the Sagarmala Project. The Committee is constrained 
to note that in such a situation the wider roads/conne ctivity between the Port and the point 
envisaged in the Sagarmala Project beyond the point of cross roads will remain unfulfilled. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the point –to–point Sagarmala connectivity 
envisaged may be implemented irrespective  of the fact that there exists major cross roads in 
between. The Committee stresses that road connectivity under Sagarmala should not be only 
point to point but encompass the entire peripheral network of roadways interlinking nearby 
towns, villages, servic e roads, important tourist places, national monuments etc. for the 
overall development of the areas. The Committee emphasizes that service roads should be 
included in the DPR itself, and given as much importance.

Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee is aware that ports have been centers of commerce for centuries and 
they remain crucial to the economy even today. Every year, hundreds of billions of rupees 
worth of products move through ports. Ports generate substantial business activity through 
their operations. The Committee notes that nation’s Major Ports are an important part o f our 
national economy and transportation system. Over 95% of India’s trading by volume and 
65% by value is done through maritime transport. In addition to their impact on the national 
economy, ports also have an impact on local and regional economies of t he states on which 
the ports are situated. The Committee is also of the opinion that a substantial portion of 
business activity in a variety of industries is driven by international trade, and the value of 
foreign trade has risen substantially over the yea rs. Although trade volumes are affected by 
global economic conditions and have decreased slightly over the past few years due to 
COVID pandemic, trade volumes are expected to rise in the future, increasing the importance 
of ports and waterways in terms of export and import. The Committee recommends that at 
this crucial juncture of expected increase in global maritime trade, appropriate policy 
measures may be taken to increase maritime trade through port connectivity to boost the 
economy of the country. 
(Para 5) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 Connectivity is one of the critical enablers for ports as it is the end -to-end 
effectiveness of the logistics system that drives competitiveness for industry. India's 
hinterland connectivity is mainly based on road and rail n etworks. Railway is the mainstay 
for carrying long lead distance and bulk cargo. But the expansion of rail network has not been 
able to keep up with the growing demand. Hence, the implementation of road and rail 
connectivity projects attains importance for enhancing the country's overall freight efficiency. 
1.2 The Sagarmala Programme has identified connectivity between ports and domestic

production and consumption centres, through rail, road, and domestic waterways (Coastal 
Shipping and Inland Waterways) a s one of the key pillars of this initiative. Under the port 
connectivity pillar of Sagarmala, there are 209 projects (₹1.42 lakh crore) of which 69 
projects (₹32,000 crore) have been completed. 
1.3 Bharatmala Pariyojana is a flagship programme of Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways. Bharatmala focuses on enhanced effectiveness of already built infrastructure, 
multi-modal integration, bridging infrastructure gaps for seamless movement and integrating 
National and Economic Corridors. Bharatmala Pariyojana P hase-I includes development of 
about 24,800 km NH network such as Economic corridors, Inter -corridor & feeder roads, 
National Corridors Efficiency Improvements, Border and International Connectivity roads, 
Coastal and Port Connectivity roads & Expressways. 
1.4 Apart from Sagarmala and Bharatmala Schemes to enhance Port connectivity across 
all Major and Non-Major Ports, Government of India has introduced PM Gati Shakti National 
Master Plan which aims to provide systematic, multi modal connectivity to various  economic 
zones for seamless movement of people, goods & services resulting in efficient conduct of 
logistics and economic activities. In line with Gati Shakti, MoPS&W carried out an extensive 
exercise to find the port connectivity gaps in consultation wit h Major Ports and State 
Maritime Boards through State Multimodal Committees.

RAIL CONNECTIVITY 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee notes that the Go vernment has taken up large number of projects to 
remove the bottlenecks in road and rail connectivity to ports. The Committee has no doubt 
that once the projects are implemented, the connectivity problems may be resolved to a great 
extent. However, despite the enormous importance of the connectivity of ports, the Committee 
feels that the pace of work under the Port, Rail and Road connectivity Projects have been 
slow. The Committee is of the opinion that more coordinated efforts are required to complete 
the connectivity projects by involving Railway Authorities/NHAI etc., addressing all technical 
aspects. The Committee emphasizes that interconnectivity of roads, ports, airports, railways, 
waterways etc. should be part of the infrastructure planning process, right from inception 
stage. The Committee is also of opinion that approach to a port from hinterland can be 
critical enough to make or mar a Terminal, because it determines the turn round time and 
evacuation time-vital to the functioning of the port. Evacu ation is a vital component of any 
port project as the capacity and efficiency of the port vitally depend on the rate at which the 
cargo can be evacuated from the terminal. The efficiency, viability and business depend on 
how well connected the port is. The  Committee, therefore, recommends that the plans for the

Recommendation/Observation 
4. The Com mittee notes the specific instances of connectivity issues. It notes with 
concern the lack of road connectivity from railway sidings at Paradip Port to iron -ore mines

transportation cost. It also notes the lack of railway line to reduce mine -port distance at 
Nayagarh. While at places like Sukinda - Jaroli, iron-ore rake movement is decreased due to 
delay in environmental clearance for doubling projects. The Committee is of the opinio n that 
since railways is the fastest transport mode and can transport huge quantity of ore at one go 
and also causes less environmental pollution as compared to road transport, all out efforts

also recommends that necessary steps may be taken to develop railway sidings near mines 
and for obtaining necessary statutory clearanc es to maximize the rail movement of iron ore.

 international air transport services.

 the Companies Act w.e.f. 1
st March 1994 after the Air Corporations (Transfer of undertakings and repeal) Act 1994
 came into effect.

5. Pursuant to the transfer of the undertaking by virtue of promulgation of the Air Corporations (Transfer of
 Undertakings and Repeal) Act, 1994, the Equity Capital of Rs. 79.48 crores of erstwhile Air-India Corporation has been
 treated as issued and Paid-up Capital of the Company.

 1.4.94 in terms of the Government Notification issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation & Tourism Department No.

12.       The Managing Director Air India while deposing before the Committee has stated that the basic cause for
 declining in profitability is the Company’s own policy for introduction of wetleased Aircraft, without adequate landing
 facilities for purchasing these aircraft heavy burden fell on Air India because of loan repayment and interest payment. 
 Its size rather than quality of services emerged as the critical success factor for the airline. Thus due to three main
 factors i.e. introduction of wet leased aircraft, expansion of aircraft fleet and repayment of loan plus interest cost the Air
 India running into heavy losses. The Committee was informed that the Air India is incurring losses to the tune of rupees
 one crore daily.
 
13.       Another reason for the decline in profitability has been stated to be gulf crisis.  The continuing  recession in the
 world’s major traffic generating economies and over capacity (caused primarily by indiscriminate fleet expansion by
 the major international carriers in an effort to garner market share) have also  diluted revenues and yields and placed
 heavy interest and depreciation burdens on Airlines. The Committee was also informed that  upto the year 1992-93 Air
 India was consistently making profits but with Indian Airlines entry into the gulf sector the position has been changed. 
 There was a sizeable  impact on the profit and from 1992-93 over the years the generation of profits from the gulf as a
 proportion of their total revenue has been falling considerably  though the passenger load factor has remained more or
 less static.  In face it has improved from 1996-97.  The fall in net profit from 1992-93 to the present time is over
 hundred and twenty five crores.
 
 14.      The Committee was further informed  that although Air India has been consistently generating profits since 1985
 (it generated net profit in each year with the exception of 1987/88) its net profits have been negative in 1995-96.  This

 is because its achievements over the last decade in terms of other major performance parameters i.e. growth, market
 standing and health of assets, which affect its ability to generate sustained profits in the future have not been laudatory. 
 Air India has shrunk in size during the last 5 years.  Its marketing standing – measured both in terms of its share of the
 passenger air market to/from India and its First and Executive Class load factors – have continuously deteriorated. 
 Similarly, it has experienced deterioration in the health of its assets – its policy of replacing aircraft after 20/25 years of
 service has led to the aging of its fleet and a consequent deterioration in its operating efficiency and passenger appeal. 
 Additionally, because of the depreciation of the Indian Rupee.  Air India’s Balance Sheet is – in dollar terms – weaker
 than it was five years ago.
 
15.       In reply to question regarding reasons behind the delay in purchasing new aircrafts to replace the ageing fleet,
 the Committee was informed   that it is because of  the long procedure involved in materialising the proposal for the
 purpose. In order to reduce delay in getting government’s approval for acquisition of aircraft a proposal is under
 consideration wherein it is proposed that instead of PIB clearance such projects may be approved by a Committee under
 the Chairmanship of Secretary (Civil Aviation) with members from concerned organisations viz. Ministry of Finance
 and Planning Commission.
 
16.       Regarding status of the aircraft projects for three A 310-200 the Committee has been informed that earlier the
 project report for acquisition of these aircraft was submitted by Air India in December 1993, which was kept in
 abeyance by the Ministry of Civil Aviation because of the surplus A 320 aircraft with Indian Airlines.  In October 1996
 the Ministry requested Air India to recast this Proposal and the same was submitted to the Ministry of Civil Aviation in
 December, 1996 and the Board was apprised of this action.  However, the Ministry directed Air India to seek specific
 approval of the Board for the revised project.  Since then the matter has been under consideration of the Board level and
 a techno-economic evaluation of the A 310-300 vis-à-vis its competitor has been initiated. 
 
17.     Regarding B747-400 aircraft the Committee has been informed that the project report for acquisition of this
 aircraft was originally submitted to the Ministry in August, 1995.  In April, 1997 the Ministry requested Air India to
 formally withdraw this proposal.  In September, 1997 Air India informed the Ministry that the matter was thoroughly
 reviewed in the light of its  changed operating plans.  On July, 24, 1998 the Ministry has indicated  that the project is
 being treated as deferred due to the resource constraints  and difficult financial position of  Air India.  Similarly
 induction of 3 medium capacity long range aircraft (MCLR) in the near future is uncertain in view of the present
 financial position of Air India.
 
18.       During deposition before the Committee the Secretary, Ministry  of Civil Aviation informed  that  some 4-5
 years back whatever profit was earned by Air India were kept in the banks instead of spending it on purchasing new
 aircrafts.  This policy of air India in not spending profits on purchasing new aircrafts has affected the expansion of its
 fleet, where as other airlines like Malaysia, Singapore expanded but Air India’s position remained the same.  However,
 at present their policy is towards purchasing of new aircrafts.
 
19.             Increase in fuel cost is also one of the main reasons for decline in profitability of Air India.  Air India is
 getting air turbine fuel at a very higher cost as compared to international airlines.

 and entered into more Airlines alliances to serve other destinations to which they could not physically operate.  It has
 the approval of the Board and the Government.

Chapter-I 
Background  
The development of airports is crucial for a growing economy like India, which has seen 
a significant increase in air traffic in recent years. India's rapidly expanding middle class, rising 
disposable income, and increasing i nternational trade have contributed to the growth of the 
aviation industry. The development of airports not only improves connectivity but also 
contributes to the growth of various industries, including tourism, manufacturing, and 
agriculture. Indian Government has recognised the importance of airport development and has 
embarked on an ambitious plan to modernize and expand the country's airports. This plan 
includes the construction of new Greenfield airports, as well as the expansion of existing 
Brownfield airports, with the aim of improving access to remote areas and boosting economic 
growth. Additionally, the development of airports has a positive impact on employment 
generation and infrastructure development, making it a crucial aspect of India's overall  economic 
development strategy. 
2. Several issues also persist pertaining to civil enclaves, i.e., aerodromes used for both 
military aviation and civil aviation. At present, there are thirty -one Civil Enclaves in the country, 
out of which twenty-eight are being maintained by the Airports Authority of India (AAI), one is 
to be developed by AAI and the remaining two by the State Government and private Airport 
Operator. 
3. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and 
Culture took cognisance of the crucial role played by the development of greenfield and 
brownfield airports and civil enclaves in facilitating the growth of the aviation sector in India. In 
light of this, the Committee decided to take up the subject „Development  of Greenfield and 
Brownfield Airports and Issues Pertaining to Civil Enclaves in Defence Airports‟ for detailed 
examination and report. 
4. The Committee heard the views of the representatives of various Ministries and 
Departments in its meetings as per details given below:- 
● Ministry of Civil Aviation on 16th November, 2022; 
● Ministry of Civil Aviation on 25th November, 2022;

Limited (DIAL) on 15th December, 2022;

Security Force (CISF) on 6th January, 2023;

2023;  
● Ministry of Civil Aviation, Department of Revenue (Ministry of Finance), 
Department of Expenditure (Ministry of Finance), Department of Economic 
Affairs (Ministry of Finance); and NITI Aayog on 23rd March, 2023.

pertaining to the subject, along with the Committee‟s recommendations thereon, are presented in

Chapter-II 
Development of Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and the 
Challenges thereof 
6. In its background note on the subject,  the Ministry of Civil Aviation furnished the 
following information with respect to greenfield and brownfield airports:- 
I. Greenfield Airport: - 
A Greenfield airport is conventionally referred as an aviation facility being developed on 
empty land or previ ously undeveloped land and an airport whose commissioning, 
planning & construction process is carried out from the scratch / grass route level. 
Ministry of Civil Aviation, in this regard has formulated a Greenfield Airport Policy and 
guidelines for setting  up of Greenfield Airport. The airports, Greenfield in nature are 
given „In -Principle‟ approval as per criteria, guidelines and procedures formulated in 
Greenfield Airport Policy. 
The Ministry informed that before the introduction of the Greenfield Policy,  3 Greenfield 
Airports (GFA) were operationalized namely, Cochin (in 1999), Hyderabad (in 2008) and 
Bangalore International Airports (in 2008). Post 2008, the Government has granted in -
principle approval for 21 GFA projects out of which 11 GFAs have been o perationalised 
since 2008 and In-Principle Approval has been accorded to 10 Greenfield Airports . 
Details are enclosed as Annexure -I. The list of Greenfield Airports for which first stage 
Site Clearance is granted is enclosed as Annexure -II. The list of Gre enfield Airports 
which are under consideration is enclosed as Annexure-III. 
7. The Ministry further informed that the Government of India has formulated Greenfield 
Airports (GFA) Policy, 2008. As per the Policy, a State Government or an Airport Developer, 
willing to establish an airport, is required to send a proposal to the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
(MoCA) for 2 -stages approval i.e. 'Site -Clearance' followed by 'In -Principle' approval. Such 
proposals are considered by MoCA as per the procedure stipulated in the GFA Policy.  
II. Brownfield Airport:- 
A Brownfield airport is conventionally referred to as an airport which has an existing 
infrastructure for the development of an airport such as runway, Terminal Building etc. 
Development works are carried out fu rther on these facilities and additional facilities 
required for safe aircraft operation are created in a phased manner. 
AAI has embarked upon a CAPEX plan of 25000 Crores during year 2019 -2024 
for development/upgradation/modernization of various airports in the country to meet the 
requirement of Air traffic which includes Greenfield airports, expansion/ modification of 
existing terminal, new terminals, expansion/ strengthening of existing runways, aprons, 
ANS works like control tower, technical block etc.  List of New Terminal Buildings/ 
Expansion of existing terminal buildings in progress/ planning stage and New Civil 
Enclaves - work in progress/ planning stage (airports operated by MoD) is at Annexure -
IV.  
8. Given the inherent difference between the approach taken for the development of airports 
in the case of greenfield and brownfield projects, each type has its own set of advantages and 

Page 4 of 111 
 
disadvantages. The Ministry listed the following advantages and disadvantages of greenfield and 
brownfield airports: 
Advantages of Greenfield Airports 
● Airport at Greenfield sites can be planned as per the governing guidelines for 
unrestricted development of Airport and aircraft movement up to full potential. 
● Availability of Land for future expansion of Airport. 
Disadvantages of Greenfield Airports 
● Requirement of more time and money for creation of complete new infrastructure 
at airport as well as Airport connectivity. 
Advantages of Brownfield Airports  
● Brownfield airport already has airport infrastructure. 
● As airport infrastructure is already existing at Brownfield airport and it only needs 
to be upgraded as per requirement, this will lead to cost-effectiveness of airport. 
● Connectivity is already available to places of importance in a city like offices, 
hospitals, institutions etc. 
Disadvantages of Brownfield Airports 
● Limited scope for expansion due to landlocked situation. 
● High cost for acquisition of land for expansion and rehabilitation. 
9. The Committee noted that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has cited „time and money‟

Land Value Capture Mechanism 
53. In its Value Capture Finance Policy Framework, the erstwhile Ministry of Urban 
Development described Value Capture to be based on the principle that private la nd and 
buildings benefit from public investments in infrastructure and policy decisions of Governments 
(e.g. change of land use or FSI). Appropriate VCF tools can be deployed to capture a part of the 
increment in value of land and buildings. In turn, these  can be used to fund projects being set up 
for the public by the Central/ State Governments and Urban Local Bodies ( ULBs). This 
generates a virtuous cycle in which value is created, realized and captured, and used again for 
project investment. As the addit ional value is generated by actions other than landowner‟s direct 
investment, Value Capture is distinct from the user charges or fees that agencies collect for 
providing services. 
54. The Secretary, Department of Expenditure (Ministry of Finance) informed the Committee 
that the Value Capture mechanism is currently operating in the metro rail sector and the National 
Highways. He stated that the Ministry of Housing & Urban Affairs has made it a part of their 
policy that there must be a mechanism by which a pa rt of that increase in the property values 
which arises because of the construction of a metro station, will be given back to the metro rail 
undertaking through either imposition of a betterment levy or some other mechanism to assist in 
financing further g rowth of the metro rail system. He opined that one difference is that both 
metro rail and National Highways are linear projects where there is a ribbon development that is 
possible on either side of the metro or the highway. In the case of an airport, it i s located in one 

Page 13 of 111 
 
place. It may or may not lead to development along the line or the road that leads to the airport 
depending on whether it is completely greenfield or whether it is already in a well -populated 
area. He, however, concluded that theoretically , value capture can be thought of if there is an 
appreciation in value by the creation of an airport that could provide a source of some funding 
for an airport project. 
55. The Committee notes that land acquisition is one of the biggest expenditures

Annexure-VIII  
Advantages and Disadvantages of Civil Enclaves in Defence Airports as informed by the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation. 
1. Advantages:- 
·         By sharing facilities with a defence airport, a Civil Enclave can benefit from the existing 
infrastructure, such as runways and terminal buildings. This can reduce the cost of development 
as compared to building a standalone civilian airport. 
·         Military airports often have enhanced security measures in place,  which can be beneficial 
for the operation of a civil enclave. 
·         The problem of space constraint is solved as both civil and  Military Aviation Operations are 
carried out simultaneously. 
·         Provides better platform for agencies like NSG if any emergency occurs. 
·         Better coordination is achieved between Civil and Defence Agencies. 
·         The civil aviation has n o/or limited capabilities to neutralize or prevent any hostile drone 
attack, so an integrated ecosystem of Civil and Defence Enclave bodies is likely to be in place 
for the security of overall aviation operation. 
 
2. Disadvantages:- 
·         In the Defence Enclave, the length of runway for bigger flights is an issue. While, the fighter 
jets require shorter runways, for civilian flights, the runways have to be upgraded with their 
lengths. 
·         In Civil Enclaves airports, runway is mainly used by the de fence forces for their operational 
exercises. Hence, availability of slots for commercial flights is reduced which leads to bunching 
of flights in a  particular period and subsequently leads to congestion at airports. 
·         The regular mock exercises c onducted by defence forces results in a disturbed schedule of 
the civilian flights. 
·         Restricted operations and constraints for round the clock operations 
·         Challenges for expanding the existing airport to meet the ongoing traffic growth. 
·         CISF‟s role is limited to securing the terminal building only while the concerned defence 
agency is responsible for the  operational  area.  This leads to duality of security agencies for 
Defence Enclave airports. 
 
3. Challenges faced in Civil Enclaves: 

Page 87 of 111 
 
The Committee was apprised that some issues peculiar to defence airfields are faced by AAI, 
when it comes to expansion/ development of a Civil Enclave. These are generally resolved by 
mutual coordination between AAI and Defence Authorities. Some of these issues are as follows: 
·         Obtaining of Working Permission at Defence Aerodromes: AAI is required to obtain 
working permission for carrying out construction/ development activities at Civil Enclaves. In 
few cases, IAF/ Ministry of Defence (MOD)  has granted working permission in lieu of payment 
of lease amount by AAI. Accordingly, the issue of de -linking the working permission with the 
lease amount was taken up with IAF/ MOD, who assured to consider the request of AAI on case 
to case basis. 
·         At times, there is a requirement of swapping of land between AAI and Defence Authorities 
for development of a civil enclave. In order to deal with such cases of swapping of land between 
IAF/MOD and AAI, a Land Barter Matrix is being developed and has been sent by AAI to MoD 
to resolve the land related requirements on equal value of land basis. 
·         The watch hours for operation of civil flights at Defence Enclaves are limited. The civilian 
flights get second priority in the matter. The issue is ta ken up with the concerned defence 
authorities on case-to-case basis depending upon demand from the airlines. 
 
4. The Committee was apprised of some other challenges faced by the Ministry of Civil 
Aviation in obtaining approval from the Defence agencies and  the solutions thereto are 
enumerated as follows: 
i)        The opposing issues of IAF and AAI are generally related to accessibility of air space, 
operational watch hours and land. For accessibility of air space issues and watch hour issues 
regular coordination meetings are held. For land issues a Land Barter Matrix between MoD and 
AAI has been approved by Ministry of Defence, wherein equal value of land will be transferred 
between IAF and MoD. 
ii)   Obtaining of NOC from MoD for the Greenfield airport pro ject is another challenge. On 
few occasions, MoD has withdrawn its NOC after giving the initial permission. 
iii) High levy of Property Tax by the MoD in respect of the airport land which is under 
jurisdiction of Defence Forces. This higher charges result i nto higher aeronautical charges being 
levied from the Passengers. 
iv) Lease rental charged by IAF/MoD for land leased out with working permission to AAI if 
the land is not to be used jointly by IAF & AAI. 
v)   Delay in physical possession of land by AAI even after getting working permission.

Aviation from the Ministry of Defence in the following areas:

•                Extension of watch hours for civilian flights.

Details of Green and sustainable initiatives at airports and civil enclaves:- 
1. The Ministry informed that it has taken an initiative for working towards Carbon 
neutrality and to achieve Net Zero Emission at Indian airports on the lines of the country's 
reduction of Green House Gases (GHG) emission goals. Towards this objective, MoCA has 
written to the operators of all the Brownfield Airports with scheduled operations and developers 
of the upcoming Greenfield Airports, advising them to work towards achieving C arbon 
Neutrality & Net Zero, to get Accreditation by Airports Council International (ACI)/ISO 14064 
through empanelled verifiers and adopt Carbon Mitigation Measures as well as Carbon 
Management Plans. MoCA has also written to all the State Governments/UTs , advising them to 
ensure Carbon Emission reduction measures and Net Zero achievement targets are incorporated 
ab-initio in design/standards of the Greenfield airport development proposals, DPR, Airport 
Master plan etc. 
 
2. The Ministry added that airports have shown positive response to the initiative of MoCA. 
While Cochin Airport was already the first green airport functioning on solar power, the airports 
of Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Bengaluru have also achieved the status of being Carbon 
Neutral. Othe r non -AAI airports like Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Mangaluru, Guwahati, Jaipur, 
Thiruvananthapuram, Nasik, Sindhudurg, Kannur, Durgapur etc. have also taken steps to reduce 
their carbon footprint with the ultimate goal of Net Zero Emission. AAI has also taken var ious 
initiatives to achieve use of 100% Green Energy at its airports. Renewable energy sources for 
Airports can be Solar, Wind, Biomass, Hydro, Geothermal, Tidal. However each source has its 
constraints/limitations and is site specific. Key considerations for any airports renewable energy 
generation involve the following: 
i)     Resource availability – land, solar intensity, wind speed, proximity to sea and 
dams 
ii)    Techno commercial feasibility – Power generation vs. cost of investment, ROI 
and power intensity 
iii)   Adherence to airport specific requirement – Glare and reflection from the panels, 
current load design of terminal roof.

approval and also the policies/regulations/acts proposed policy changes regarding the 
development of these airports.   He also desired to know the steps taken to ensure coordination 
and cooperation between State and Central Governme nts for the development of these airports. 
He enquired about the advantages and disadvantages of both Green field and Brownfield airports 
and the challenges faced by the Ministry in site -searching and the criteria for site selection/land 
acquisition regarding these airports. The Chairman asked the Ministry to apprise the Committee 
of the number of Greenfield/Brownfield airport projects which are facing delay due to legal 
issues. The Chairman also desired to know why some of the projects like Mopa Airport in Goa, 
Navi Mumbai International Airpor t in Maharashtra etc. have been  inordinately delayed by a 
decade or more, even after obtaining the in-principle approval. 
5. The Chairman, also asked the Airports Authority of India (AAI) to apprise the Committee 
of the number of operational Civil Enclaves in the country, the issues faced in land acquisition 
and obtaining working permission by IAF/Ministry of Defence to carry out 
construction/development activities, budgetary allocations and constraints, and coordination  
mechanisms employed by the AAI with the Ministry of Defence for developing and enhancing 
facilities in Civil Enclaves. He also asked the AAI to brief the Committee on the issue of delay in 
land acquisition for new airports, ‘Land Barter Matrix’ Formula an d how it can resolve the lan d-
related issues in development of Civil Enclaves. 
6. The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, through his presentation, gave an overview of 
the Greenfield policy, 2008, development of Greenfield and Brownfi eld Airports and is sues 
pertaining to Civil Enclave in Defence Airports. The Secretary informed the Committee that 
Greenfield airports are basically new airports built on fresh , unencumbered land while 
Brownfield airports are already existing airports which are further devel oped as    per 
requirement. The Secretary further informed that b efore introduction of the Greenfi eld policy in 
2008, only 3 Greenfi eld Airports were in operation i.e. Cochin, Hyderabad and Bangalore 
International Airports. Post 2008, the Ministry has grant ed in -principle approval for 21 
Greenfield Airport projects of which 8 are operational and 9 are nearing completion while 4 have 
been granted in -principle approval but development is yet to start. The Secretary informed that 
the projects at Dabra in Madhya  Pradesh and Karaikal in Puducherry are sub -judice while the 
legal impediments in Bhogapuram, Andhra Pradesh have been cleared. There is not much 
progress in the Dagadarthi project in Andhra Pradesh. 

116 
 
7. The Secretary further informed the Committee that the re are 145 operational Airports in 
India (including water aerodromes and heliports) out of which 71 airports and 28 Civil Enclaves 
are operated by AAI, 9 are Joint Ventures under AAI, 6 are under Public Private Partnership, 22 
are under State Governments, 5 are Private airports, 2 are under Ministry of Defence and 2 Civil 
Enclaves are under State Government and Private Operator respectively. The Secretary also 
informed the Committee that the target of Ministry of Civil Aviation is to develop 220 airports 
(including aerodromes and heliports), by the end of Financial Year 2025. A budgetary allocation 
of Rs. 4500 crore has been provided under the RCS UDAN Infrastructure Scheme for a period of 
four years for this purpose and more than half of it has been spent. 
8. The Committee was also informed that Civil Enclaves are joint use airports where the air 
side is entirely controlled by the  Defence forces and the city side terminal is controlled by the 
AAI. There are 31 such Civil Enclaves in country an d development of infrastructure in them is 
undertaken by  IAF under Modernisation of Airfi eld Infrastructure  (MAFI) scheme.   The 
advantage of making Civil Enclaves is that the airports were already existing but the biggest 
challenge is sharing of land or making available  land for expansion of airport. Further, as these 
airports are controlled and managed by the defence services they have ‘watch hours’, which are 
the hours during which the airport is availab le for operations by Civilian fli ghts. The Ministry 
has however worked out a "Land Barter  Matrix" where land identifi ed by the AAI is assigned a 
value as per the local Circle Rate and the total cost of which is required to be paid by AAI to the 
defence services. Likewise, airports where defence services required land fro m the AAI are 
similarly mapped on this matrix. The Ministry has been able to successfully resolve some of the 
long pending issues on exchange of land and extension of watch hours for civilian flights. 
9. Thereafter, Members raised various querie s regarding  the status of 
Greenfield/Brownfield/Civil        Enclave    Airports    at    Bihta,    Darbhanga, Thanjavur, 
Sabrimala, Calicut, Nagpur, Kannur, Parandur, Kotkasim, Navi Mumbai, Jhalawar, Neemuch, 
Gaucher, Dehradun, Pantnagar, Dimapur,   Mopa,   Kaddapa, Begumpet etc. Issues   regarding 
Night Landing Facilities at airports, status of airports which exist but have no scheduled 
commercial operations, di fferent User Development Fees (UDF) at different Airports, ‘funnel 
policy’ etc. were also raised. 
10. The Members wanted to know about airstrip development scheme in the country to which 
Secretary replied that Rs. 4500 crores have been allocated which will be spent over a period of 
four years. Members also enquired a bout non -scheduled cargo fli ghts operations wh ich are 

117 
 
restricted to only 6 Indian cities presently. A Member pointed out that Kerala is a very good 
destination for Cargo flights and this restriction is having   a negative impact and desired that the 
Ministry may intervene on this issue. Dela y in completion of Sabarimala project was also 
affecting the interests of passengers. The issue of delay in land acquisition for Dimapur airpor t 
was also  a  grave issue.  A Member wanted to know about the  delay in development of the 
Dehradun and Pantnagar airports  and another Member commented on the impact of taxi and 
hotel lobbies on development of airports and also remarked that though 40 crores had been 
allotted for the development of the Jolly Grant Airport in 2003, due to faulty planning the new 
terminal recently built had not been connected to the old terminal.   Similarly, fourth runway has 
come up in Delhi at cost of about 1000 crores but is still lying unutilized.  
11. Commenting on the "UDAN" scheme, a Member pointed out tha t  3 helicopter services 
were to b e started in Uttarakhand but only 2 or 3 have been started and even these are not 
affordable for the middle clas s people.  A  Member expressed concern at the slow pace of 
development             of Greenfield airports and wished to know whether every district headquarters in 
the country would one day, have an airport, even a small one. He pointed out that by 
2025, India would still have only 25 0 airports compared to the approximately 20,000 airports in 
the USA. Another Member raised a query on the level of futuristic planning of Indian airports, 
whether the planning had been done for the next 20, 30 or 50 years.  
12. A Member pointed out the delay in providing simulator training of Pilots to nearly 62,000 
pilots waiting for it and desired to know of the action being taken by the Ministry in this regard. 
It was also suggested that pilot shortage in India, is caused due to the fact tha t a pilot having 
expertise can fl y only one  specific type of plane, while in other countries like USA, pilots are 
permitted to fly different types of planes. 
13. A Member stated that there are only around 200 chartered and private aircrafts in India, 
but even very small countries like UAE have 758 chartered/private aircrafts which may be due to 
the reason that a lot of formalities and permissions are required for operating private aircrafts in 
India. In this connection, the Chairman expressed concern that DGCA  takes more than 6 months 
to give clearance to new aircrafts in India and directed that in the next meeting, the DGCA may 
provide the Committee with data regarding the number  of applications received and clearances 
given by DGCA in the last 3 years. 
14. A Member inquired about the development of infra structure of Patna airport  for which 
just 20 kms from the airport nearly  2300 acres land is available. He wanted to know the action 

118 
 
taken if any on the limitations in Bagdogra and Dimapur airports and on the safety aspects of 
Patna and Jolly Grant airports both of which are critical airports in the country.   He also queried 
why Civil Enclaves are made even in places where there is huge demand for airports. He cited 
the example of Darbhanga airport which has been made a civil enclave despite huge demand for 
an airport and much inconve nience is caused to passengers   who are    forced to carry their bags 
to main road for about a kilometre, and Chandigarh airport where pilots are called to park their 
planes not through RT but by a hand waving.   He reiterated the need for night landing fac ilities 
at airports. The M ember also opined that Greenfield projects have far more advantages in every  
parameter as compared to other  investments in civil enclaves or brownfi eld projects. The 
argument that Greenfield projects require more time and money fo r creation was fallacious and 
sought to know the reasons why airports are not being proposed in some States even though the 
State Governments are willing to provide land for the same. He stated that as per Entry 29 in the 
Union List of the Seventh Schedule  of the Constitution of India, the construction, regulation and 
functioning of the airports within the country is the exclusive and sole responsibility of the 
Union of India. In 2014 however the policy was tweaked so that a State Government would have 
to provide land free of encumbrance and free of cost before an airport could be made in the State 
which, in effect, is against national interest. He contrasted the situation in aviation sector with the 
National Highways where the Central Government, by virtue of its right enshrined in the 
Constitution, notifies any road in the country to serve the national interest. The Member opined 
that a holistic, futuristic vision is lacking and tweaking policy retrospectively does not benefit 
either the individual tax paye r or the nation as a whole.   The Ministry should work at its Civil 
Aviation Policy to bring out the desired results.   
15. The Chairman specifically requested the Secr etary, Ministry of Civil Aviation to give 
clarification on each and every qu estion raised  by the Hon. Members with direction that no 
question should be left unanswered by the Ministry. He also requested to furnish written re plies 
to the questionnaire before the next meeting of the Committee on 25 th November, 2022 or to 
intimate in case it is not possible for the Ministry to respond. 
(The witnesses then withdrew) 
16.    A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept. 
17. The meeting adjourned at 1:40 PM.

22. The Chairman welcomed all the Members of the Committee; Shri Rajiv Bansal, 
Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA); Shri Sanjeev Kumar, Chairman, Airports 
Authority of India (AAI); Shri Arun Kumar, Director General Civil Aviation (DGCA); and  
other officials, to the afternoon session of the meeting. He informed that the Committee had  
heard the views of t he Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation on the subject ‘Development of  

121 
 
Greenfield and Brownfield Airports and Issues pertaining to Civil Enclaves in Defence 
Airports’ in its meeting held on 16 th November, 2022. From the deliberations in the said  
meeting, the Committee felt the need to further hear the views of the DGCA and other senior  
officers of the Ministry. 
 
23. The Chairman then asked the Ministry to brief the Committee about the roadmap of 
the Ministry in the near future and the coordination mechanis ms employed by the MoCA, 
AAI and DGCA to develop the projected target of 220 airports by year 2025. He further asked 
the MoCA, DGCA and AAI to put forth their views regarding various Greenfield/Brownfield  
airport projects facing inordinate delays and other issues which were pointed out by the 
Members in the earlier meeting. 
 
24. The Chairman asked the DGCA to brief the Committee about its functions and 
responsibilities handled by it in the Indian aviation sector with specific reference to the 
subject under examination. He also inquired about the reasons for the undue delay in the 
grant of  clearances to new aircraft for operating in the country, construction of the 
Greenfield/Brownfield airports/Civil Enclaves projects that have been delayed for more than  
five years due to site clearance, license process or in-principle approval by the DGCA 
and concerned agencies and whether any steps have been taken to tackle such delays. The 
Chairman also desired to know the reasons for delay/denial of clearance in cases where States 
are willing to allocate land for the construction of airports.  He also pointed out that replies to  
the questionnaires sent by a Member of the Committee and some questions sent by the 
Secretariat, have not been received and desired that the replies may be expedited. 
 
25. The Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, assured the Committee that the replies to 
the remaining questions would be sent shortly. He then shared with the Committee two recent 
important developments in the Indian aviation sector, the first being the recent inauguration 
of the Hollongi Airport in Arunachal Pradesh adjacent to Itanagar, its capital city,  by the 
Hon’ble Prime Minister and the second being the elimination of the necessity of filling up the 
Air Suvidha form, due to declining Covid cases, by international travelers to India which is 
believed to further facilitate the inward flow of international tourists.  Referring to the issues  
raised by the Committee in its earlier meeting and in the questionnaires, the Secretar y stated 
that the Heads of the attached offices of the Ministry would address the issues concerning 
their organizations. 

122 
 
 
26. The Chairman, Airports Authority of India (AAI) addressed the issues regarding 
operational airports, nigh-landing facilities, profitability of airports, use of renewable energy 
in airports etc. He informed that presently there are 134 operational airports out of which 119  
airports are carrying out scheduled operations and 15 airports are carrying out non -scheduled 
operations and the figure keeps changing slightly due to operational reasons.  Out of the 119  
airports, 28 are run on Visual Flight Rules (VFR) and 90 use Instrument Flight Rules (IFR)  
procedure. He further informed that there are 43 airports which have CAT -I facility, 16  
airports with CAT -II facility and 6 airports have CAT -III facility. The AAI is trying to 
convert many of  the VFR airports into IFR airports but the problem arises due to lack of 
space as most of the old VFR airports are in congested areas. As regards Night Landing 
Facility, the Committee was  informed that out of the 134 airports, 89 airports have Night 
Landing Facility and 45 airports, presently do not have this facility. For Night landing facility 
the airports needs to be an IFR  airport and sufficient  land should be available for lighting 
arrangement and the Ministry is in discussion with the State Governments to provide land for 
installation of said facility at airports which do not have it. He further added that AAI is in the 
process of procuring of 34 Instrument Landing System (ILS) from Russia. Informing the 
Committee of the profitability of  the airports, the representative of AAI informed that out of 
110 odd airports,  only 10 -15 airports are consistently making operational profits. On the 
issue of airstrips, the Ministry  informed that as per the records of DGCA, there are 452 
airstrips, including the airports  mentioned before, some of which are owned by the State 
Governments and Defence authorities while some of the airstrips are also owned by the 
private owners. The Ministry  further informed that wherever land becomes available and 
opportunity arises, efforts are being made to convert airstrips into proper airports. 
 
27. The Committee was further informed by the AAI that there are 17 Flying Trainin g 
Organisations (FTOs) which are operational and 9 FTOs have been approved on AAI land in  
phase-I and are on the verge of becoming operational within next 6-8 months. Thereafter, 
in the next phase, FTOs are going to be setup at 6 more airports. Regarding use of renewable 
energy, the AAI informed that efforts are being made to convert all its 100 odd airports for  
renewable energy by December, 2024, either installing by solar plant or by procuring renewal 
energy through the distribution companies. 
 
28. The Director General of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) while 

123 
 
informing the Committee of the aviation safety aspects, stated that India is a signatory to the  
Chicago Convention, 1944 which has set the international standards for civil aviation and  is 
followed by 193 countries across the world. There are 11,000 safety standards in the said  
Convention and it is obligatory for all the signatory countries to follow those standards, 
failing which a country may be declared an “outlaw”. He further informe d that this had 
happened once in a limited way to India in 2013 but India has now got 70 per cent rating and 
is going up to  85% rating consequent to the recent successful audit of the International Civil 
Aviation Organisation (ICAO).  India is now comparabl e to the rating of New Zealand, 
Belgium etc, thus, which indicates the significant strides made by India in this regard. The 
Director-General then informed the Committee that the primary role of DGCA was to 
implement the ICAO  SARPS (Standards and Recommended Practices).  There are eight 
critical elements in safety  oversight, namely Primary Aviation Legislation, Specific 
Operating Regulations, State Systems, Qualified Technical Personnel, Technical Guidance 
Tools, Licensing Certification,  Authorisations and Approval Obligations, Surveillance 
Obligations and Resolution of Safety  Issue. The Committee was informed out of the eight 
parameters, there are issues only regarding insufficient number of Flight Operating Inspectors 
(FOIs) which are being looked into. As  regards the certification of an airport, the DGCA 
informed that the process is slightly time  consuming as all the 350 check points as per the 
ICAO document have to be certified. Similarly for aircrafts certification, there is a detailed 
procedure involving numerous parameters and manuals that has to be followed and it takes 
time to grant clearance to a new  aircraft. However, the Ministry has implemented the e-
Governance of Civil Aviation (eGCA) to reduce  human interface which has considerably 
reduced the delays. 
 
29. Thereafter, the Ministry informed the Committee that presently, in -principle approval 
has been given to 21 airports out of which 9 have already been operationalised and the 
Ministry is expediting the operationalisation of the remaining 12 airports. Issues regarding 
some Greenfield airports at Karaikal (Pondicherry); Dabra (Madhya Pradesh); Dagadarthi 
(Andhra Pradesh); Parandur (Tamil Nadu); and Kottayam (Kerala) were also discussed. In 
reply to a  specific query of the Chairman of the Committee regarding exchange of land 
between the Defence Authorities and the Ministry of Civil Aviation for Thanjavur Airport, 
the Ministry stated that a Board of Officers comprising of both AAI and Indian Air Force 
(IAF) Officers, has been constituted to carry out survey, physical demarcation etc. and 
thereafter, the exchange of land will take place. 

124 
 
 
30. A Member stated that development of airports which are further away from the State  
capitals should be given more preference and specifically raised the issue of Kota and 
Jhalawar in Rajasthan. He also desired to know about funnels in various airports. Another 
Member pointed out that the Ministry had not given any reply to the query of the Chairman 
in the last meeting as to the time taken for the certification process and data on the number of 
aircrafts cleared in the last three years. He also pointed that some Air Operator Permits 
(AOPs) have been delayed by over a year causing inconvenience to the aircraft owners. The 
Member also  enquired about how much time it takes for aircraft clearance process in the 
USA and whether the same rules can be followed here as well to reduce the clearance time as 
both the countries  are parties to the Chicago Convention. The Member also raised issues 
regarding “type certification” for the  aircrafts brought into  the country  and enquired  as to 
what the DGCA is doing about it. Director General, DGCA informed about the various types 
of induction of  aircrafts and the time taken to certify them.  He explained that the delay 
generally takes place  when a new type of aircraft is being inducted, for which a Flight 
Operating Inspector (FOI) is has to be trained for the ‘safety oversight’ of that particular type 
of aircraft and since DGCA is  governed by global norms,  shortcuts are not possible. The 
Member also raised the issue of  training pilots to fly two -three types of aircrafts as is 
admissible in other countries. A Member  raised the issue of non -operational airport at 
Nanded (Maharashtra) and desired to know the reasons for it. 
 
31. A Member also requested the DGCA to look into the issues like Flight Duty Time  
Limitation (FDTL) and other norms and allow relaxation of rules for hours of flying of 
aircrafts. In reply, DGCA stated that they are thinking of bringing some relaxation of flying  
hours in general aviation and for this, a time consuming study has to be done keeping in mind 
the global standards. Another Member raised the issue of (eGCA) e -Governance of Civil  
Aviation and enquired about its smooth functioning , especially as regards licensing where 
there are undue delays. 
 
32. A Member expressed concerns about airports which have been constructed but 
no commercial scheduled flights are operating there. He raised the issue of Gondia Airport 
(Maharashtra) which was constructed in 2008 and flight operations were started only in 2022  
but due to lack of Night Landing Facility, operations have been discontinued and desired to  
know when the said facility will be installed. He further stated that there are 25 -30 airports in 

125 
 
the country which do not have commercial flight operations which indicates the lack of 
planning, faulty Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) and market surveys, on part of the Ministry. 
The DGCA clarified that the airports are generally constructed based on future requirements 
and growth and not based on current requirements. Hence, in some cases, commercial flight  
operations may start from day one, while in some other cases, flights may start but may be  
stopped due to operational reasons and restarted aga in after there is growth in demand for 
such flights. The Member suggested that airports should be futuristically planned based on 
latest technology, so that  the requirement  of frequent  expansions does  not arise and 
specifically raised the issue of expansion of Navi Mumbai airport where expansion has 
been planned for the fourth time. Another Member agreed that that the Ministry was making 
policies in bits and pieces instead of planning ahead for a substantial period of time. 
 
33. A Member while congratulating the Ministry for the inauguration of the Donyi Polo  
Airport at Hollongi (Arunachal Pradesh) and start of Ziro -Dibrugarh-Pasighat sector, desired 
that flight operations of seven Advanced Landing Grounds (ALGs) in Arunachal, which are  
defunct, may be made operational soon.  He also highlighted the requirement of an airport 
with Cargo facility in upper Assam at Dibrugarh, so that fruits and horticulture produce can 
be transported across the country from the North -Eastern States. The Chairman of t he 
Committee also asked the Ministry to check the feasibility of operationalization of Mechuka 
and Tuting  airports in view of National security as both the ALGs are close to the 
international border. Another Member requested for consideration of construction of an ALG 
at Mon district (Nagaland) and also raised the issue of the existing airport at Dimapur 
(Nagaland) which  required urgent expansion and increase  in number of flights  keeping in 
view the present demand. The AAI stated that the Ministry has been engaging with the State 
Government for  provision of land for expansion of the runway at Dimapur and facilitate 
landing of bigger aircraft. 
 
34. A Member pointed out that under the Seventh Schedule of Constitution of India,  land 
for construction of airports , inter-alia, is the prerogative of the Central Government in 
addition to the provision for national connectivity; whereas the State Government is only 
required to facilitate the process of acquiring the land under the Land Acquisition Act.  He 
criticized the flaw in the National Civil Aviation Policy (NCAP), 2016 which as per para 13 
(a) (iii) requires  the States to provide the land free of cost and free from all encumbrances 
without treating it as equity, before AAI takes up new airport projects. He queried the 

126 
 
rationale behind this rule which requires States to give land for airports when the same would 
not be treated  as equity  and also wanted to know why the nation’s priorities and 
infrastructure essential for a state  should be dismissed because of a flaw in the government 
policy. Giving the example of the  requirement of airport in Mon district as stated  by another 
Member, he queried that, in the event the State government does not take any action, why 
the Central Government could not exercise its authority and prepare a feasibilit y report on an 
airport in Mon, especially when  AAI would not be investing but would be  advertising for 
investing partners. The Member also  pointed out that as per  Para 5.1 of the ‘Guidelines for 
Setting up of Greenfield Airp orts’, 2008 land for such airports would have to be provided by 
the Airports Authority of India.  Thus the 2008 guidelines contradicts the NCAP, 2016 with 
regard to acquiring land for airports yet the  2008 guidelines  was reproduced again in 
December, 2016, the year the NCAP was brought out  and is on the website of the Ministry 
and quoted in all their documents.  There is however no  clarity on when this provision was 
changed and the contradiction still exists.  The Member decried that due to such flaws, states 
like Bihar do not have a Greenfield project till now, since  the Ministry keeps vacillating 
under the contradictory provisions. The Member also expressed that the Ministry of Law and 
Justice should be called before the Committee to explain the  Constitutional provisions as to 
the AAI as an entity, the Union List and the responsibility of the  GOI and how such changes 
can be made under the Constitutional provisions.  In this context,  the Chairman also desired 
the Ministry of Law and Justice may be called to seek an explanation on the applicability of 
the guidelines and the policy, vis-à-vis the Constitutional obligation as it is not a Concurrent 
Subject but a Subject under the Union List. 
 
35. A Member pointed out that the Ministry had not given any reply to the issue 
regarding the ‘Point of Call’ status to Kannur International airport (Kerala) that he had 
raised in the earlier meeting and letters to the Ministry and further suggested that it would be 
convenient for  Haj pilgrims to have an Embarkation  Point at the Kannur airport. He also 
raised the issue of  establishment of Aviation Training Academies and initiating Aircraft 
Maintenance Courses in  the State of Kerala. The Chairman reiterated that the Ministry 
may look into the issue of making Mechuka and Tuting airports operational as Civilian 
terminal has been approved at  these airports by the Ministry. Another Member also enquired 
as to whether after the operationalization of the new Mopa Airport (Goa), the Goa 
International Airport will continue  to exist, to which the  AAI clarified that both  the airports 
will remain functional. 

127 
 
 
(The witnesses then withdrew)

India Act, 1994 and 2008 Guidelines for setting up of Greenfield Airports and stated that the 
2016 NCAP is in contravention of the Act and the Union List of the Constitution . In response to 
a query of the Committee, Law Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs informed the Committee 
that 2016 NCAP is legal and valid as per the provisions of the AAI Act and the Constitution. 
The Law Secretary was of the view that the law may need improvements. 

146 
 
5. Joint Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that the Ministry had 
consulted the Ministry of Law and Justice, Ministry of Finance and NITI Aayog before  
finalizing the NCAP. The Committee decided that the views / comments of the said Ministries  
and NITI Aayog on the subject and the NCAP issue, may be heard at a later date. 
6. On a query of the Chairman, DG, DGCA informed the Committee that airlines have been 
empowered to deal with unruly passengers and that  Tokyo Convention regulates misbehavior of 
passengers and that  there is a provision for penalizing the airlines in case of non -reporting of 
such incidents.  He stated that action is initiated under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) where 
applicable and that 143 persons have been  placed in the restricted list so far.  The Committee 
suggested that special Airline Wing should be formed for dealing with police and courts in cases 
of unruly passengers  since the pilot and crew members have to attend the court at present for 
prosecuting the unruly passenger.  
7. Members raised various queries regarding lack of airports in Bihar, issues relating to land 
and night landing at Bagdogra Airport, delays in civilian flights at civil enclaves due to Defence 
activities, need for futuristic plannin g for development of airports, plan to decongest airports, 
improving metro connectivity to airports, tackling the increasing number of incidents of 
misbehavior by passengers in flights, scope for development of heliport facility at Varanasi, 
absence of direct flight from Delhi to Itanagar especially in view of the G20 Summit, exorbitant 
pricing of tickets especially from/to North-East States, development of airports at Kota -Jhalawar 
in Rajasthan, status of development of Sabarimala Airport, no more Advanced  Landing Grounds 
(ALGs) in Arunachal Pradesh, extension of runway at Dibrugarh and Dimapur Airports, need for 
installation of Instrument Landing System (ILS) at Pasighat Airport, etc. 
8. The representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation and Department of Legal Affairs  
responded to some of the queries raised by the Members and took note of the suggestions made 
by the Members. 
9. The Chairman directed that written replies to the points which had not been answered 
may be sent within a week.
